summary: First NAS shares set up on the Synology: media, backups and docs volumes exist, with an NFS export for the Proxmox host and SMB for the laptop.
body:
Started the homelab repository today and put the NAS layout into notes/nas.md so it can be rebuilt. Three shared folders were created on the Synology: media, backups and docs. Each has its own user, so no single account can write everywhere.

The backups share is the important one. Its user can only reach that folder and has no shell. The recycle bin is on for docs and media but off for backups, because restic manages its own pruning and deleted chunks would only eat space.

NFS was enabled for the Proxmox host at its fixed address. The export for media is read-only, squash set to map all users to the media user. The first mount from Proxmox failed with 'access denied by server'. The cause was that the NAS rule listed the subnet but the host had a second address on the bridge. Adding the real address to the rule fixed it, and the mount worked after that.

SMB was set to minimum protocol version 2 and the signing option stays on. A test copy of a 4 GB file from the laptop ran at about 105 MB/s, which is the limit of the gigabit link. Snapshots are not enabled yet, since the volume is Ext4 and not Btrfs; this is noted as a limit.

In the repository there is now an fstab snippet for the Proxmox host and a small script, scripts/check-mounts.sh, that tests each mount and prints OK or FAIL. Next step is the first restic repository on the backups share. DSM updates stay manual for now. The notes file lists all users and which share each can reach.

summary: Created the first restic repository on the NAS backups share and ran a first backup of the Proxmox host configs; 2.1 GB went in, 38 seconds on the second run.
body:
Initialised a restic repository over SFTP on the NAS, using the backup user with the key stored only on the Proxmox host. The password lives in a file outside the repository, mode 600, and a copy is in the password manager. Without that copy the backups would be worthless, so I checked the copy first.

The first backup covered /etc, /root and the Proxmox config directory /etc/pve. Result was 2.1 GB read, about 1.4 GB stored after deduplication. The second run found almost nothing new and finished in 38 seconds.

I wrote scripts/backup-host.sh with an exclude file for caches and temp folders. It exits non-zero if restic fails, so a later check can notice it. A cron entry runs it at 03:00. The retention is not set yet; that comes with the forget and prune step.

Open: the cloud bucket copy and a restore test.

summary: Pi-hole installed in an LXC container on Proxmox with a fixed address; the router now hands it out as the DNS server and ads drop on all devices.
body:
Created an LXC container with Debian, 512 MB RAM and 2 GB disk, and gave it a fixed address outside the DHCP range. Pi-hole was installed with the unattended installer using a setupVars file from the repository, so the choices are recorded.

Upstream is Cloudflare and Quad9 for now. The plan is to replace this with Unbound later so queries do not leave the house in the clear.

I set the router DHCP to give out the Pi-hole address as DNS. Old leases kept the router as DNS for a while, so the phone did not see the change until I toggled wifi. After that the dashboard showed 4,100 queries in the first hour and about 22 percent blocked.

One problem: the smart TV hardcodes 8.8.8.8 and ignored it. I left that alone for now and wrote it down.

The container config and the adlist file are in the repository under pihole/. Backup of /etc/pihole is added to the host backup script. Next, a local DNS name for each service so I don't type addresses.

summary: Added local DNS records for the NAS, Proxmox and Pi-hole in a custom dnsmasq file, so they answer as nas.home.lan, pve.home.lan and dns.home.lan.
body:
Wrote pihole/02-local.conf with address records for the three machines, and chose home.lan as the internal domain. Pi-hole reads the file from /etc/dnsmasq.d, which first needed the option 'misc.etc_dnsmasq_d' turned on, otherwise the file was silently ignored.

Tested with dig from the laptop: all three names resolved. A reverse lookup of the NAS address returned nothing, so I added ptr records as well.

I noted that .lan is fine for now, but certificates for it will not work from a public CA. This matters for the reverse proxy step, and a real domain with DNS challenge is the likely answer. Decision on that next time.

summary: Picked Caddy as the reverse proxy and ran it in Docker Compose on a small VM; first service proxied over plain HTTP with a Caddyfile kept in the repository.
body:
Compared Caddy and Nginx Proxy Manager. Caddy won because the whole configuration is one text file that lives in git, and it handles certificates itself. A web UI with its own database would be one more thing to back up.

Created a VM with 1 core and 1 GB, Debian, Docker installed from the official repository. The compose file in caddy/ mounts the Caddyfile read-only and two named volumes for data and config.

The first site block proxies dns.home.lan to the Pi-hole admin page on port 80. It worked at once over HTTP. Caddy tries to get a certificate for any name with a public look; for .lan it uses its internal CA, so the browser warns about trust. I will install the root certificate on the devices, or switch to a real domain.

Next: decide on the domain and DNS challenge.

summary: Bought a domain for internal use and set up DNS challenge certificates in Caddy, so https://dns.example-home works without browser warnings.
body:
Registered a cheap domain and moved its DNS to a provider with an API, since the registrar had none. A scoped API token that can only edit the TXT records of that zone was created.

The stock Caddy image has no DNS plugin, so I built a custom image with xcaddy and the provider module. The Dockerfile is in caddy/ and the build takes about two minutes.

The token is passed as an environment variable from an .env file that is in .gitignore. A .env.example is committed instead.

First request for a certificate worked: the log showed 'certificate obtained successfully' for the Pi-hole name. Pi-hole local DNS now maps the subdomain to the Caddy VM, so names resolve privately while certificates are real. Tested from the phone: green lock, no warning.

Open: renewal check and the other services behind it.

summary: Moved the NAS admin page and Proxmox behind Caddy with valid certificates; Proxmox needed the upstream marked as skip-verify because of its self-signed cert.
body:
Added two more site blocks. The NAS on port 5001 and Proxmox on 8006 both speak HTTPS with their own self-signed certificates, so Caddy returned 502 at first with 'x509: certificate signed by unknown authority'.

The fix was a transport block with tls_insecure_skip_verify on those two upstreams. This is acceptable because the link is inside the LAN, but I wrote the reason as a comment in the Caddyfile.

Proxmox console over websocket worked without extra settings. Both sites show the right certificate, and expiry is about ninety days out. Caddy renews at thirty days left, so I will look at the log in a few weeks to confirm.

summary: Ran into a Caddy renewal failure after the first DNS challenge worked, traced it to a stale API token scope, and fixed it so certificates renew cleanly.
body:
The certificates from the DNS challenge issued fine two days ago, but today I wanted to be sure renewal would work too, so I forced a renewal test instead of waiting for the real one. It failed with 'adding challenge record: 403 Forbidden' in the Caddy log.

The cause was the API token I had created at the DNS provider. It was scoped to read zone data only, and the first issuance had gone through because I had briefly used a broader token while testing. When I moved the token into the .env file for the compose stack, I used the narrow one by mistake. The two tokens had similar names, which did not help.

I created a new token limited to a single zone with edit rights on DNS records and nothing else. I put it into stacks/caddy/.env, which is listed in .gitignore, and added a stacks/caddy/.env.example with a placeholder so the variable name is documented in the repository. Then I ran docker compose up -d in the stack folder to recreate the container with the new value.

After that I used the Caddy admin API to reload and checked the log. Caddy created the TXT record, waited for propagation, got the certificate and removed the record again. The whole round took about 40 seconds. I repeated it once more to be sure that cleanup of the challenge record works, and the zone showed no leftover records.

One more thing I checked was the resolver used for the propagation check. The Pi-hole answers for the internal names, and I wanted to be sure it did not interfere. I set the propagation resolvers in the Caddyfile to two public resolvers, so the check does not depend on the local DNS. This removed a warning about a slow lookup that had appeared in the log.

I deleted the old broad token at the provider, so only the narrow one exists now. A short note in the README of the stack says which scope the token needs and where it is stored.

What is left: a check that warns me before a certificate runs out, so a silent renewal failure does not show up as browser warnings. I will look at that when monitoring comes up.

summary: Added VM and container backups using Proxmox vzdump to the NAS, excluding the media disk, and kept restic for configs only; nightly run uses 38 GB.
body:
The restic job so far saves only configuration. For the guests I turned on Proxmox vzdump in a scheduled job at 02:00, storing to the NAS over NFS, mode snapshot with zstd compression.

The first full run produced about 38 GB for four guests. Most of it is the Caddy VM image and a Debian template VM that nobody uses; I removed the template from the job. That brought the size to 24 GB.

Retention in the storage is keep-last 3 and keep-weekly 2. That fits the space on the backups share with room to spare.

One guest, the Pi-hole container, failed once with 'unable to freeze filesystem'. In snapshot mode LXC on directory storage can't always do that. Switching that container to stop mode for the backup made it work, with about 20 seconds of downtime at 02:00. I accepted that.

I considered sending vzdump files to the cloud too, but the bandwidth makes it slow: 24 GB would take half a day for each full set. So the offsite stays config only for now, and the guests can be rebuilt from Ansible later.

Documented the schedule in notes/backups.md, listing what is in which copy, and what is missing: the NAS data itself has no copy anywhere, which I flagged as the next risk.

summary: Wrote the first Hyper Backup plan for the NAS shares to the cloud and found that the docs share restores fine, while the photo folder is too large for the uplink.
body:
The NAS data had no second copy, which was the gap noted last time. Today I set up Hyper Backup on the Synology for the docs share and the photos folder.

Sizes first: docs is 14 GB, photos 310 GB, media 2.4 TB. Media is replaceable, so it is excluded. Photos are not replaceable.

I used the same cloud provider as for restic but a separate bucket and a separate key. The Hyper Backup task is encrypted client side, and the key file was exported and stored in the password manager as well as on paper.

Docs uploaded in under an hour. For photos the estimate at 0.6 MB/s uplink was about six days. I limited the upload rate to 0.4 MB/s during the day and to unlimited from midnight until 07:00, so that video calls are fine.

To test the thing I restored one folder of docs to a temp location through the Hyper Backup explorer. File count and checksums matched on 120 files.

The photo task will run for days; Hyper Backup shows it as 'backing up' and survives interrupted runs. I will check the progress each morning.

A scheduling issue: the vzdump job at 02:00 and the Hyper Backup both read from the NAS disks. They overlap and the NAS CPU hit 90 percent. I did not change it yet since it is only for the first upload.

Cost estimate for 324 GB is about 2 euro a month. Rotation: keep 30 versions with smart recycle. Next: the first real restore of a VM from vzdump, to see that these files work.

summary: Photo upload to the cloud finished after four nights; Hyper Backup integrity check passed and the NAS load problem went away on its own.
body:
The first full upload of the photos ended overnight. Hyper Backup reports 324 GB stored, and the task moved to its normal incremental schedule at 04:30.

I started the integrity check from the task settings. It ran for about three hours and finished with 'no errors found'. This check re-reads data from the bucket, so it also uses download traffic; the provider counts that, but at this size the cost is cents.

The overlap with vzdump no longer matters, since incremental runs finish in a few minutes. NAS CPU stays below 30 percent during the night.

I wrote the setup in notes/backups.md: what Hyper Backup covers, the rate limit, and where the key file is. Remaining item is a restore test of a VM.

summary: First VM restore test from a vzdump file worked: the Caddy VM came back on a new ID in 6 minutes and served its sites, but needed its network device fixed.
body:
Today I tested a real restore. I picked the Caddy VM because it is small and I know what a healthy one looks like.

Command: qmrestore from the NFS path to a new VM ID 900 with --unique so the MAC address changes. It took about 6 minutes for 8 GB. I kept the original running, and left the new one with its network disconnected until I had changed its address.

Problem: after boot the guest had no network. The interface name in the guest config was tied to the old MAC, so netplan matched nothing. I changed the file to match on the name and the VM got its address. Then I gave it a temporary address and tested the Caddyfile by pointing a hosts entry at it: all sites answered with valid certificates, as the certificate data are in the Docker volume.

I stopped and deleted VM 900 afterwards.

Lessons: use a name-based match, not MAC, in the guest netplan; add this to the Ansible plan later. Restore time is acceptable. The restore of the Pi-hole container is the next test, since it is stop mode and a different type.

summary: WireGuard server set up in an LXC container with one phone and one laptop peer; the tunnel works from mobile data, with split routing to the home subnet only.
body:
Chose WireGuard for the VPN. It lives in its own unprivileged LXC container on Proxmox. The tun device was the first obstacle: the container needed the lines for /dev/net/tun in its config file on the host, and 'wg-quick up' failed with 'Operation not permitted' until I added them and restarted.

The router forwards UDP port 51820 to the container. The domain has a dynamic DNS record so the clients have a stable name; the updater runs on the Pi-hole container with a 5 minute timer.

Server config uses 10.8.0.1/24. I generated keys on the server and then each client got its own key pair and a preshared key. Peers: phone at 10.8.0.2, laptop at 10.8.0.3. The AllowedIPs on the clients are only the home subnet and the VPN subnet, so normal internet traffic does not go through the house. DNS for clients is the Pi-hole, so ad blocking and local names also work abroad.

Test: phone on mobile data, wifi off. Handshake in under a second, ping to the NAS 31 ms, the NAS admin page opened through the Caddy name with a valid certificate.

IPv4 forwarding and a masquerade rule were needed in PostUp so that the clients can reach the LAN hosts, which have no route back to 10.8.0.0/24. I put them in the config file with matching PostDown lines.

The private keys are not in git. The repository has a template wg0.conf.example with placeholders and a script that renders client configs with a QR code.

Next: add the container to the backup job and test that a lost phone can be removed quickly, which is just removing its peer block.

summary: Added the WireGuard container to vzdump and wrote a short runbook for revoking a lost device; revocation tested with the old laptop peer in under a minute.
body:
The WireGuard container was not in the guest backup job yet. I added it and ran the job by hand. The size is 420 MB, and it worked in snapshot mode, no freeze problem here.

Then I wrote notes/vpn.md with three procedures: adding a peer, revoking a peer, and rotating the server key. For revoking, the step is to remove the peer block from wg0.conf and run 'wg syncconf wg0 <(wg-quick strip wg0)', which drops the peer without disturbing the others.

Tested it with the old laptop peer. Before: 'wg show' listed the last handshake 12 seconds ago. After the sync it was gone from the output, and the laptop could no longer connect. It took under a minute including the edit.

I also noted that the preshared keys are per peer, so a leak of one does not affect the rest.

One small fix: the QR script printed the config to the terminal history. I changed it to read from a temp file in /dev/shm and delete it after.

summary: Jellyfin installed as a Docker Compose service on a new VM with the media NFS share mounted read-only; libraries scanned 1,900 items.
body:
Created a VM with 4 cores and 4 GB for Jellyfin. The compose file is in jellyfin/ and mounts the media share from the NAS read-only at /media, with config and cache on local volumes.

The NFS mount in the VM is done through fstab with the _netdev and nofail options, so a slow NAS does not block boot.

First scan found 1,900 items in movies and series. About 60 were shown with the wrong title because of folder names with years in brackets and release tags. I renamed them following the Jellyfin naming guide, and a rescan fixed most.

Hardware transcoding is not set up yet, since the host CPU has an iGPU that still needs passing through. Direct play works for most clients, so it can wait.

Next: Caddy block for the new name and a user for each family member.

summary: Got Intel Quick Sync transcoding working in Jellyfin by passing /dev/dri into the VM; a 4K to 1080p test used 12 percent CPU instead of 380.
body:
Jellyfin on the CPU stalled when two clients needed transcoding, so today I enabled the iGPU.

First choice: PCI passthrough versus using a container. Passing the whole iGPU to the VM would take the display from the host, which I did not want. Simpler path: move Jellyfin from a VM to an LXC container and bind the render device. That is what I did.

Steps: created a privileged LXC container with Debian and Docker, added to its config the lxc.cgroup2.devices.allow line for the DRI major number (226) and a mount entry for /dev/dri. Inside, the user is in the render group, and the compose file passes /dev/dri to the Jellyfin container with group_add for the render group id. The group id differed between host and guest, which cost me a half hour: ffmpeg said 'Failed to open VAAPI device' until I used the id from the container, 104, not from the host.

In Jellyfin I set hardware acceleration to VAAPI, enabled tone mapping and the H.264 and HEVC decoders. I turned off AV1 since this iGPU can't do it.

Test: a 4K HEVC HDR film to a 1080p client. With CPU only, the load was around 380 percent on the 4 cores and playback stuttered. With VAAPI, CPU was about 12 percent, and the transcode ran at 5x realtime.

I moved the config volume from the old VM into the new container by rsync and shut the VM down but did not delete it. The new container is added to the vzdump job. Using a privileged container is a trade-off; I wrote it into the notes. I'll delete the old VM after a week.

summary: Created Home Assistant OS as a VM on Proxmox and restored nothing yet; it sees the router and Jellyfin as auto-discovered integrations.
body:
Downloaded the Home Assistant OS qcow2 image and imported it with qm importdisk into a new VM with 2 cores, 2 GB and UEFI boot. The first boot got an address from DHCP; I reserved that address in the router.

Onboarding took about 10 minutes. HA found the router and the Jellyfin server by itself and offered both integrations. I accepted Jellyfin and skipped the router.

The VM needs a USB Zigbee stick later, which means USB passthrough by vendor and product id. I did not do this today.

Added the VM to vzdump. The HA built-in backup is also on, with a copy to the NAS via Samba.

summary: Zigbee stick passed through to the Home Assistant VM and nine sensors paired; the stick path changed after a reboot, so the config now uses the vendor and product id.
body:
Plugged the Zigbee coordinator into the Proxmox host and passed it through to the Home Assistant VM. The first try used the host port path (bus and port), and it worked.

Then I rebooted the host for a kernel update and the VM stayed without the stick: Zigbee showed as 'not connected'. The USB port number had changed. Passing through by vendor and product id fixed this, and the line in the VM config is now usb0: host=10c4:ea60. This survives moves between ports, with the limit that two identical sticks would clash, which is not the case here.

In Home Assistant I used the ZHA integration with the stick, choosing a channel away from my wifi, channel 25, since wifi is on channel 6 and 11 neighbours. Pairing: 4 temperature sensors, 3 door contacts and 2 smart plugs. The plugs act as routers and make the mesh better. Two door sensors at the far end of the flat needed to be paired after the plugs were in place, as they otherwise found no parent.

I renamed all devices consistently by room and function, for example 'hall door contact', since entity ids are difficult to change later.

One automation was made: the hall light turns on for 3 minutes after the door opens, only after sunset. It worked on the first test.

Backup: the ZHA network key is inside the HA backup. Without it, all devices must be paired again, so I downloaded a full backup and put a copy on the NAS and in the password manager storage. A note about this is in notes/homeassistant.md.

Next time: Caddy block for HA, which needs trusted_proxies in configuration.yaml or it answers 400.

summary: Caddy block for Home Assistant added; HA needed trusted_proxies set to the Caddy VM address, otherwise it returned 400 Bad Request.
body:
Added a site block for the HA name with reverse_proxy to port 8123. The page answered with 400 Bad Request straight away.

The HA log said 'A request from a reverse proxy was received from 192.168.1.20, but your HTTP integration is not set up for reverse proxies'. In configuration.yaml I added use_x_forwarded_for: true and trusted_proxies with the Caddy address. After restarting HA core the app opened with a valid certificate.

Websockets worked without further settings. The companion app on the phone was switched to the new https name and keeps its connection through the VPN.

summary: Replaced the hand-copied compose files with one stack folder per service in git and a README table; Jellyfin, Caddy and Pi-hole now start with docker compose up -d from their folder.
body:
The compose files had spread over three machines and some only existed on the server. Today I pulled them all into the repository.

Layout: one folder per service with docker-compose.yml, an .env.example, and a short README line about volumes. A top-level table in README.md lists service, host, port and where data lives.

While doing this I found that the Pi-hole container was started by hand with docker run and a long command line that existed only in shell history. I translated it into compose, stopped the old one and started the new one with the same volumes. DNS was down for about 15 seconds, which was noticed by nobody.

I also found that the Jellyfin compose had the image tag latest. I pinned it to the current version number. The same for Caddy. Floating tags caused a surprise update on a restart in the earlier test, so this is better.

The real .env files stay on the hosts and are in the restic job: I added their paths to the include list and checked that the next backup contained them with 'restic ls latest | grep .env'.

Not done: a script to update everything. That is the next topic.

summary: Wrote scripts/update-all.sh that pulls and recreates every compose stack on a host, with a dry-run flag and a log; first run updated 5 images and left Pi-hole alone on purpose.
body:
The script loops over the stack folders listed in a text file per host. For each it runs docker compose pull, shows which images changed, and only then runs up -d. With --dry-run it stops after the pull and prints what would change.

Pi-hole is on a skip list since a DNS restart in the middle of the script would break the pulls of the next stacks. It gets updated by hand at the end.

The first run on the Jellyfin host pulled 5 images, took 3 minutes and used 410 MB. After it, I called each service by curl to see an HTTP 200; the script now does this for stacks that have a health URL in the list.

Log goes to /var/log/update-all.log. Old images are cleaned with docker image prune -f at the end. Since versions are pinned, the script only changes things when I bump the tag in git, which is what I want.

summary: Added a second NAS disk to the Synology and expanded the storage pool from one drive to a mirror; the initial sync took 11 hours and no data was moved off first.
body:
The NAS had one 4 TB disk without redundancy, which was the known weak point. Today I added an identical 4 TB drive.

Before touching anything I checked that the Hyper Backup photo task and the docs task had finished within the last day, and that the last restic run was clean. I also ran a SMART extended test on the old disk: it passed with 0 reallocated sectors.

The new disk was put in the empty bay while the NAS was running (it supports hot swap). DSM saw it at once. I ran its own drive test on the new one first, a quick test of about 10 minutes, and it showed healthy.

In Storage Manager I used the action to change the RAID type of the pool from Basic to RAID 1 and selected the new disk. DSM warned that this takes a long time and that performance is lower during it. The estimate was 10 hours.

The sync took 11 hours. During it the media streaming was fine, but a vzdump run at 02:00 became about twice as slow, 41 minutes instead of 20. I did not stop it.

After the sync the pool showed 'Healthy' and the volume had the same size as before, 3.6 TB usable, as expected for a mirror.

I turned on the notification mail for disk problems and set a monthly data scrubbing task on the first night of the month.

Important point in the notes: RAID is not a backup. The cloud copy and the restic repositories stay as they are. The next step in the plan is a bigger disk pair when the media share passes 80 percent; it is now at 64 percent.

summary: Wrote and ran the first full restore test of restic data: a config directory and the Home Assistant backup file came back byte-identical from both the NAS and cloud repositories.
body:
The goal was to prove that the backups can be read back, not only that they exist. I ran the test from the laptop to be sure that nothing depends on the Proxmox host.

Setup: installed restic on the laptop, copied the repository password from the password manager (not from the server), and used the NAS over SFTP with a read-only key I made for the test. For the bucket, the access key from the notes.

Test 1, NAS repository: 'restic snapshots' listed 14 snapshots. I restored the latest into /tmp/restore-nas with --include /etc/pihole and the HA backup file path. The restore finished in 9 seconds. Compared with sha256sum against the live files on the servers: all 23 files matched, except gravity.db, which had changed since the snapshot, as expected with a live DNS service.

Test 2, cloud bucket: same snapshot selection and same include. It took 2 minutes 40 seconds because of the download. Again the files matched. This was the real proof that the offsite copy has a complete and readable set, including the key handling.

Test 3: the wrong password case, to see the message. restic says 'Fatal: wrong password or no key found', and this is the one I would see if the copy in the password manager were out of date.

A finding: the notes did not say which of the two repositories uses which password. They are in fact the same, but I created a separate one for the bucket in the plan. I decided to leave them the same for simplicity and wrote that down; a different password per repository would be cleaner, though it adds a second secret to lose.

I added scripts/restore-test.sh that does the NAS part automatically and compares checksums, and put a reminder to run it every quarter. Clean up: removed /tmp/restore-* and the test key from the NAS user list.

Still open: the restore test for the NAS Hyper Backup photos beyond a few samples, and an alert if the nightly backup does not run.

summary: Backup jobs now report to a healthcheck URL on success and a missed night raises a mail within 26 hours; tested by disabling the cron entry once.
body:
Until today a failed or missing backup would only show up when I looked. I wanted the absence of a success to raise an alarm.

I used a simple method: after a successful run, backup-host.sh calls curl on a ping URL of a free healthchecks service, and calls the /fail endpoint when restic exits with an error. The service expects a ping every 24 hours with a grace time of 2 hours, and mails me when that is missed. The URL contains a secret token, so it lives in the env file and not in git.

I did the same for the weekly forget and prune job, with a 7 day period and 12 hours grace, and for the vzdump job through its hook script. The hook is a small shell file in /usr/local/bin that Proxmox calls at job-end and that receives the status as an argument.

Testing: I commented out the cron entry for one night. After 26 hours the mail arrived with the subject 'DOWN: backup-host'. I turned the entry on again, ran the script by hand, and the check went back to up with the next ping.

I also tried the fail path by temporarily giving the script a wrong repository path. The /fail ping came in at once and mail followed in less than a minute.

One limit: the check only tells that the script said it succeeded, not that the data can be restored. The quarterly restore test covers that part.

The Hyper Backup tasks on the NAS already send DSM mails on failure, so I did not add pings there. Later I want to move these checks into Uptime Kuma, which is planned for the monitoring work, using push monitors so there is one place to look.

summary: Pinned Jellyfin and Pi-hole image tags in their compose files after a latest pull changed the Jellyfin config path, so update-all.sh no longer jumps versions blindly.
body:
After the first real use of update-all.sh, Jellyfin came up on a newer image and logged a warning about its cache directory moving. Nothing broke, but it showed that pulling latest on every run is a gamble. I looked at the compose files in stacks/ and replaced the latest tags with explicit version tags for Jellyfin, Pi-hole and Caddy.

The script got a small addition: it prints the image tag before and after each recreate, so the log shows what changed. The dry-run flag now lists tags too. I ran it on the Jellyfin VM and it reported no changes, which is correct.

For Home Assistant nothing is needed, because it is a full OS VM with its own update button. I wrote a note in the README table with a column for the pinned version. Raising a tag is now a deliberate commit with a one-line reason.

Next step is a monthly reminder to look at release notes before bumping anything.

summary: Jellyfin library scans were hammering the NAS every hour; limited the scan to a nightly task and enabled real-time monitoring off, which dropped NAS load from 60 percent to idle.
body:
The NAS fan was audible in the afternoons, and the Synology resource monitor showed disk reads of 80 MB/s with no one watching anything. The cause was Jellyfin: the library scan task ran hourly and the real-time monitor was on for an NFS mount, where it polls instead of using inotify events.

I changed the libraries in the Jellyfin admin page to turn off real-time monitoring, and set the scheduled scan to once a night at 04:00. The NFS mount is read-only, so there was no risk of Jellyfin changing files.

I also checked the trickplay and chapter image extraction tasks. Both were set to run during scans, which made the reads worse. I moved chapter extraction to the same nightly window and limited it to one thread.

After a day of watching, NAS disk activity in the afternoon stayed near zero and the fan stayed quiet. The nightly window overlaps nothing important, because restic runs at 02:30 and finishes in under ten minutes. I noted the settings in the stack README, since they live in the Jellyfin database and not in git.

Open point: a way to export the Jellyfin settings into the repository so they survive a rebuild.

summary: Added a DHCP reservation for the Home Assistant VM and a DNS record ha.home.lan, because its address had changed after a router reboot and the Caddy block pointed at the old one.
body:
Home Assistant was unreachable through Caddy this morning, returning 502. The VM had taken a new lease after the router rebooted, and the Caddy upstream still held the old address.

I fixed it in three steps. First I created a DHCP reservation on the router for the VM MAC address. Second I added ha.home.lan to the custom dnsmasq file on Pi-hole. Third I changed the Caddyfile upstream to use that name instead of the raw address, and reloaded Caddy.

The trusted_proxies setting in Home Assistant still uses the Caddy VM address, which has been a reservation since the start, so it needed no change. I tested from the laptop and from the phone over WireGuard, both fine.

I went through the other VMs and all of them now have reservations except the test VM, which I left alone on purpose.

summary: Wrote an Ansible playbook skeleton for the Proxmox host and Docker VMs, covering packages, users and SSH hardening, and ran it in check mode against the Jellyfin VM with two differences reported.
body:
The goal for the coming weeks is to stop configuring machines by hand, so I started the Ansible layout in the repository: ansible/inventory.ini, group_vars, and a roles directory with common, docker and ssh roles. Ansible runs from the laptop over SSH with key auth.

The common role installs the base packages (curl, htop, vim, unattended-upgrades), sets the timezone and configures chrony. The docker role adds the official apt repository, installs docker-ce and the compose plugin, and adds the admin user to the docker group. The ssh role disables password login and root login via a drop-in file in sshd_config.d.

I wrote the inventory with three groups: pve, dockervms and pi. The Raspberry Pi is in the inventory but only the common role applies to it so far.

The first run was ansible-playbook site.yml --check --diff --limit jellyfin. It reported two changes: unattended-upgrades was not installed, and the ssh drop-in was missing. Both matched what I expected, so I ran it for real. It finished with changed=4 and no failures, and SSH still worked in a second terminal that I kept open as a safety net.

The Caddy VM came next. It showed the same two differences plus an old docker apt source in the legacy format, which the role replaced. I did not touch the Proxmox host yet, because I want to read what the role would change there very carefully.

The secrets question is open. For now there are none in the playbooks, but the DNS API token for Caddy will need ansible-vault or a file outside git.

summary: Ran the common and ssh roles on the Raspberry Pi; the first attempt locked out the pi user because the key was not yet in authorized_keys, fixed with a keyboard and monitor.
body:
I added the Raspberry Pi to the Ansible run today. The playbook disabled password login as designed, but I had never copied my public key to the Pi, only to the VMs. After the run, SSH refused me with Permission denied (publickey).

I plugged in a monitor and keyboard, logged in locally and put the key into authorized_keys. After that SSH worked again.

To prevent this in future, I added a pre-task to the ssh role. It uses the authorized_key module to install the admin key before it touches sshd_config, and it asserts that the key file is not empty. I tested it by removing the key from a VM and running the role, and the key came back first.

The Pi also had a different default user than the VMs, so the inventory now sets ansible_user per host. The rest of the common role ran clean, changed=6.

Lesson noted in the README: never disable password login in the same run that is meant to install the key without a prior check.

summary: Replaced the hand-built Pi-hole LXC with a documented compose-based setup and an Unbound upstream, and verified DNSSEC works with the dnssec-failed test domain.
body:
Pi-hole had been forwarding to a public resolver, which meant every query left the house. I added Unbound as a recursive resolver so the upstream is the root servers themselves.

Unbound runs as a second container in the same compose stack, listening on 127.0.0.1 port 5335 inside a dedicated network. The config file unbound.conf lives in the stack folder in git. It enables DNSSEC validation with the root trust anchor, prefetching, a 4 MB message cache and hides identity and version. Pi-hole's upstream is now unbound#5335 with the public resolvers removed.

First problem: Unbound started but logged a warning about a too small receive buffer, so I raised net.core.rmem_max on the host to 1 MB in a sysctl drop-in. The warning went away.

Second problem: first lookups were slow. A cold query for a new domain took around 300 ms, against 20 ms with the public resolver. After the cache warmed, repeated queries came back in under 2 ms. I accept the cold cost for the privacy gain.

To verify DNSSEC, I resolved dnssec-failed.org, which returned SERVFAIL as it should, and cloudflare.com, which resolved with the ad flag set. dig +dnssec confirmed it.

The local records for nas.home.lan and friends still work, as they are served by dnsmasq inside Pi-hole before any upstream is asked.

I moved the old LXC aside but did not delete it. The new compose stack was started on the same VM that runs Caddy for now, and I will watch it for a week before cleaning up. The router DNS setting is unchanged, because the address stays the same.

summary: Pi-hole with Unbound ran a week without problems; deleted the old LXC and added it to the vzdump job and update-all.sh exclusions.
body:
After a week of the new Pi-hole and Unbound stack, the query log looks healthy. Average response time on the dashboard is 4 ms and there have been no SERVFAIL spikes apart from the test domain.

I deleted the old Pi-hole LXC container from Proxmox after checking that the new stack really answers on the fixed address, by running dig against it from the laptop and from the phone.

The host with the stack is already in the vzdump schedule, so no change was needed there. In update-all.sh the Pi-hole stack is still excluded on purpose, since an update that fails would take down DNS for the whole house. I wrote the manual update procedure into the stack README: pull, stop, up, then test with dig.

One item remains for later: a second DNS server so a reboot does not cut the network. I put it on the todo list in the README.

I also exported the Pi-hole teleporter archive and stored it in the backups share.

summary: Looked at why the restic job reported success but snapshots stopped growing: the config directory exclude pattern had swallowed a whole folder, fixed and verified.
body:
Reviewing the restic stats I noticed the Home Assistant folder was missing from recent snapshots. The exclude file had a pattern, *cache*, written to skip cache directories, but it also matched a directory called homeassistant-cache-backup that holds the real backup files.

I replaced the broad pattern with explicit paths, such as /srv/*/cache and **/__pycache__. Then I ran restic backup with --dry-run -vv and confirmed the folder was listed as new.

A real run added 410 MB. I restored one file from the new snapshot to check it. The healthcheck had stayed green all the time, which is the weakness: it only knows the job ended. I added a note to check the snapshot size trend monthly.

summary: A Jellyfin container update broke hardware transcoding because the render group id changed, so the compose file now sets group_add by numeric id and a check was added to update-all.sh.
body:
After the last run of update-all.sh, Jellyfin on its VM went back to software transcoding and a 4K test pushed the CPU to 370 percent again. The Jellyfin log showed a VA-API initialisation error and a permission denied on /dev/dri/renderD128. I checked inside the container and found the render group there had a different numeric id than the one on the VM, because the new image created its groups in another order. The compose file had used the group name render, which resolved to the wrong id inside the container.

I changed the stack to use group_add with the numeric id of the render group on the VM, 104, which is the same on the host and is what the device node carries. After recreating the container, vainfo listed the Quick Sync profiles again. The same 4K to 1080p test went back to about 12 percent CPU.

To catch this earlier, I added a small post-update check to scripts/update-all.sh. It runs vainfo inside the Jellyfin container and prints a warning in the log if it fails. I tested it by temporarily removing the group line, and the warning showed up as expected. The tag pinning from earlier would not have helped here, since the problem came from a minor version bump that I had allowed. Still to do is a note in the stack README about the numeric id, and a look at whether the Ansible role should template it from a variable once the Jellyfin stack moves there.

summary: Moved the Caddy and Pi-hole stacks into an Ansible role that templates compose files, and a full rebuild of the Caddy VM from the playbook came up serving all sites in 14 minutes.
body:
The aim was to prove that a machine can be rebuilt from git alone. I wrote a role called stacks that copies the stack folder of each service to /opt/stacks on its host, templates the .env file from variables, and runs docker compose up -d through the community.docker module.

The Caddy stack was the first. The Caddyfile is copied as is, and the DNS API token is an ansible-vault encrypted variable in group_vars/dockervms/vault.yml, written into the .env file with mode 0600. I created the vault password file outside the repository and added it to .gitignore and to ansible.cfg.

First run failed: the module complained that the docker python package was missing on the target. I added python3-docker to the docker role.

Second run ran through, but Caddy could not obtain certificates, logging a 403 from the DNS provider. The cause was a trailing newline in the vault string that ended up in the token. I switched to a folded value without a newline and the problem went away.

Then the real test. I cloned the Caddy VM template, ran the common, docker and stacks roles and measured the time. From a bare Debian clone to serving https was 14 minutes, of which 9 were package installs. Certificates were stored in a volume, so a fresh VM had to request new ones, which took about 40 seconds.

I checked three sites in the browser, the NAS, Proxmox and Home Assistant, and all gave valid certificates.

One caveat: certificate state is not in git, which is right, but a rebuild repeats the issuance, and doing that many times could hit the rate limit. For tests I will use the staging endpoint.

Next is the same role for Jellyfin, which has a database that needs a restore step.

summary: Jellyfin stack now deploys from Ansible, with its config volume backed up by restic and a documented restore step; watch history survived a test rebuild.
body:
I applied the stacks role to the Jellyfin VM. The compose file is the same as before, with the pinned tag, and the media NFS mount is declared with the ansible.posix.mount module so fstab is managed too.

The config and database live in /srv/jellyfin/config. I added that folder to the restic path list, and stopped nothing during backup, because the sqlite files are small and a copy mid-write is a known risk. To be safer I added a pre-backup hook that runs a quick docker exec sqlite3 .backup of the library database into the same folder.

For the test I rebuilt the VM from a clone, ran the playbook, then restored the config folder from restic with restic restore latest --target /. Jellyfin started, found the libraries and showed the watch history for both users. The only thing missing was the transcoding device, because the clone had no /dev/dri passthrough; I re-added that in the VM hardware.

The passthrough is a Proxmox setting, not an Ansible one yet. I put it on the list for the Proxmox host role.

Total rebuild time was about 20 minutes plus the restore.

summary: Wrote a Proxmox host role that only manages safe things, such as the apt repositories, chrony and mail relay, and left storage and network config out on purpose.
body:
Today I turned to the Proxmox host itself. I decided early that Ansible should not touch the network config or the storage definitions, because a mistake there costs a trip to the keyboard and screen, and the host rarely changes.

The role pve covers the no-subscription apt repository and removal of the enterprise one, which had been giving 401 errors on apt update. It also sets up chrony, installs a small postfix relay that sends mail through the ISP smarter host, and deploys the vzdump hook script that pings the healthcheck URL.

I ran it with --check --diff first. The diff showed the enterprise list file would be removed and the no-subscription file added, which was right. The postfix change was more intrusive, so I read the main.cf template twice before running it.

Test mail: I sent one with the mail command and it arrived within a minute. I also triggered a failing vzdump on a test VM and the failure mail came through with the log attached.

The real run ended with changed=7. I rebooted nothing.

One snag was the apt pin for the proxmox-ve package. I left it alone because it is a manual choice.

The README now has a section on what Ansible owns and what it never touches. The host passthrough settings stay documented as manual steps.

summary: Fixed a failing Ansible run caused by the vault password file path being relative; ansible.cfg now uses an absolute path through an environment variable.
body:
A run from a different directory failed with Attempting to decrypt but no vault secrets found. I had put vault_password_file = .vault-pass in ansible.cfg, which only works when started in the repository root.

I changed ansible.cfg to read ANSIBLE_VAULT_PASSWORD_FILE from the shell profile, with the file at ~/.config/homelab/vault-pass. I removed the in-repo path and confirmed .vault-pass was never committed, with git log --all -- .vault-pass showing nothing.

I ran the playbook from the home directory with -i pointing to the inventory and it worked. The README setup section lists the file location and says to keep a copy in the password manager.

summary: Installed Uptime Kuma in Docker Compose on the Raspberry Pi and added 14 monitors for the web services, DNS and the NAS, with mail alerts; the Pi sits outside the Proxmox failure domain.
body:
For monitoring I chose Uptime Kuma, and put it on the Raspberry Pi so that a Proxmox outage is still noticed. The stack folder has the compose file with a named volume and a fixed port, and the Ansible stacks role deploys it.

First problem: the Pi image was 32-bit and the Kuma image needed 64-bit. docker compose pull failed with no matching manifest for linux/arm/v7. I checked uname -m, which printed armv7l. The OS was an old Raspberry Pi OS lite 32-bit. I reflashed the SD card with the 64-bit version, ran the common and docker roles and then the stack, which took about 25 minutes in all.

Then the monitors. I created 14:
- HTTPS checks for Caddy sites: Jellyfin, Home Assistant, NAS, Proxmox.
- DNS checks that resolve nas.home.lan and a public name against Pi-hole.
- A TCP check for the WireGuard UDP port is not possible, so I ping the container address.
- Ping for the router, NAS and the Proxmox host.
- Push monitors for the backup jobs, which complement the healthcheck mails.

The interval is 60 seconds with 3 retries before an alert, to avoid noise from a single dropped packet. Alerts go by mail through the same relay as the Proxmox mail.

I tested by stopping the Jellyfin container: the monitor went red after about three minutes and the mail came. After starting it again, a recovery mail followed.

A status page for the family is not done; the user asked about it, but only for the Home Assistant and Jellyfin state, so I will make one with those two later.

The Kuma data volume is in the restic path list now.

summary: Added a Kuma status page for the family showing only Jellyfin, Home Assistant and internet reachability, served at status.home.lan through Caddy.
body:
The user wanted a page the family can check before asking whether the server is down. In Uptime Kuma I created a status page with three monitors: Jellyfin, Home Assistant and a ping to a public address as an internet check. The other monitors stay hidden.

Caddy got a new block for status.home.lan, proxying to the Pi on the Kuma port. I added the DNS record in the dnsmasq file and reloaded Pi-hole.

Kuma needed no extra header setup, but WebSocket for the admin page works through Caddy without changes, as it supports upgrades by default. I tested the admin login and the page from the phone.

I set the page theme to dark and the title to Home status. The admin interface is still reachable on the Pi port from the LAN, which I left.

summary: Uptime Kuma checks were missing the services that fail quietly, so I added a push monitor for each backup job and a certificate expiry check for the Caddy sites.
body:
Kuma had been running on the Pi for a few weeks with 14 monitors, and they all covered whether a web page answers. Looking back at the restic problem from before, I saw that nothing would tell me if a backup quietly stopped producing snapshots. I added push monitors in Kuma for the restic job, the vzdump job and the Hyper Backup task. Each one expects a heartbeat within 26 hours and sends a mail if it is missed.

The backup scripts now call the Kuma push URL at the end of a successful run, next to the healthcheck call that already exists. I kept both on purpose, so a single service going down does not leave me blind. To test it, I disabled the restic cron entry for one night and the alert mail arrived on time the next morning.

I also added certificate expiry monitors for the Caddy sites, with a warning at 14 days. Caddy renews at 30 days, so a warning at 14 means a renewal has failed for two weeks. That is the same situation as the stale token problem from the early setup, which I only noticed by luck. The push URLs are stored in the scripts env file, not in git. Next I want to add a check on the NAS disk SMART status through the Synology, but that needs an SNMP or script monitor and I have not decided which.

summary: Bought and installed a UPS for the NAS, Proxmox host and router, and read its runtime: about 28 minutes at the current 85 W load.
body:
The UPS arrived, a 900 VA line-interactive model with a USB port. I plugged in the NAS, the Proxmox host, the switch and the router, and left the monitors and other peripherals on the wall.

The load shown on its display was 85 W. After a test where I pulled the mains plug, the display estimated 28 minutes, and the actual run during a ten-minute test dropped the battery by 36 percent, which fits.

The USB cable goes to the Raspberry Pi for now. Next is NUT: the Pi will act as the server, and the NAS and Proxmox will be clients that shut down cleanly before the battery runs out.

summary: Set up NUT on the Raspberry Pi as the UPS server and connected the Synology as a client; the NAS now sees the battery state and is set to shut down at 20 percent.
body:
I installed nut on the Pi through the Ansible common role extension and created a new role called nut. The ups.conf uses the usbhid-ups driver, and upsc showed battery.charge 100 and ups.status OL right away.

The NUT server config needed three files: ups.conf, upsd.users with a monitor user for the clients, and upsd.conf to listen on the LAN address instead of only localhost. The password for the user is in the vault.

On the Synology I opened Control Panel, then Hardware and Power, then UPS, and chose a Synology UPS server with the Pi address. The NAS accepted the connection and displayed the battery state immediately.

I first set the shutdown trigger to Time before shutdown, but changed it to the low battery state, so the NAS stays up as long as possible and shuts down at the end. The Pi itself will be the last to go.

Test: I ran upsmon -c fsd from the Pi to simulate a forced shutdown. The NAS received it and began a clean shutdown, which took about two minutes. I then had to power it back on by hand.

The NUT port 3493 is only open to the LAN. Proxmox is still to be done, and it is the more important client because of the VMs.

summary: Proxmox host now shuts down its VMs and itself through NUT when the UPS reaches low battery; a simulated power cut stopped all guests cleanly in 3 minutes 40 seconds.
body:
I installed nut-client on the Proxmox host from the pve role and set MODE=netclient. upsmon.conf points to the Pi with the monitor user and the vault password.

The shutdown command in upsmon.conf is the default, which stops the host, but I wanted guests to be stopped first. Proxmox already does this on shutdown, using each guest's shutdown timeout. I checked the VM options: Home Assistant had 30 seconds, Jellyfin 60 and Caddy 30. Those were enough in the test.

The order matters for the NAS. The NFS mounts on the Jellyfin VM must go away before the NAS shuts down. The NAS shuts down at the same low battery event, so I added a delay in the NUT config: the NAS is a client with a slower timeout, and Proxmox is set to react as soon as the status is OB LB.

Test with the real UPS: I unplugged mains, and to avoid waiting for the battery to drain I used upsmon -c fsd on the Pi, which acts like low battery for all clients.

The results: the Proxmox host started shutting down the VMs one after another, and the host powered off after 3 minutes 40 seconds. The NAS started its own shutdown right after and was off about two minutes later. The Pi stayed up until I switched it off.

Things found: the Home Assistant VM took 45 seconds, longer than its timeout, so Proxmox killed it. I raised the timeout to 90 seconds. Also Pi-hole went down with the VM, which is the expected result.

After power was back, the host did not start on its own. I set the BIOS option for power on after AC loss to Last State and checked it with a mains pull.

Still open: the VMs start order after boot. I need to set the boot order with delays so Caddy and Pi-hole come first.

summary: Set Proxmox boot order with startup delays so Pi-hole and Caddy come first, then Home Assistant and Jellyfin, and checked it through a full host reboot in about 5 minutes.
body:
After the power cut test I set the start order in each guest's Options tab under Start at boot. The order is Pi-hole VM at 1 with a 30 second delay, Caddy VM at 2 with 20 seconds, Home Assistant at 3 with 20 seconds and Jellyfin at 4 without delay.

The NAS has to be up before Jellyfin mounts its NFS share. In the Jellyfin VM fstab the mount has the options _netdev and nofail, plus x-systemd.automount, so a late NAS does not block boot and the share appears when it is there. I confirmed that the Ansible mount entry has those options too.

I rebooted the host. DNS answered after about 90 seconds, Caddy sites after 2 minutes and Home Assistant after 4. Jellyfin was fully usable at 5 minutes. Kuma on the Pi recorded the outage and recovery, which also served as a check of the alerts.

I wrote the boot order as a table in the README. A problem to remember: if the NAS is off, Jellyfin starts with empty libraries but recovers when the share returns.

summary: Added the UPS battery charge and load to Home Assistant through the NUT integration, with a phone notification when the system runs on battery.
body:
In Home Assistant I added the NUT integration pointing at the Pi on port 3493 with the monitor user. It created sensors for battery charge, load, input voltage and status.

I built an automation: when the UPS status changes to on battery for more than 30 seconds, it sends a notification to the phone with the battery percentage. The delay avoids alerts for the short blips that happen with the heater next door.

Test: I pulled the mains plug of the UPS for a minute. The notification arrived at about 40 seconds, and a second one when mains came back. The load sensor shows 82 W.

The sensors are also on the dashboard now. The automation lives in the HA config, which is part of the HA backup file.

summary: Enabled IPv6 planning: checked what the ISP delivers, a /56 prefix with SLAAC on the router, and found that Pi-hole and Caddy are not yet reachable over IPv6 on the LAN.
body:
I started the IPv6 topic with a survey instead of changes. The router receives a /56 prefix from the ISP by DHCPv6 prefix delegation and gives each LAN a /64 using SLAAC. The laptop already had a global address and ipv6test confirmed it.

On the servers the picture was mixed. The Proxmox host had only a link-local address on vmbr0. The VMs with Debian had SLAAC addresses, since the kernel accepts router advertisements by default. Docker containers have no IPv6 at all, because the daemon has it disabled.

DNS: Pi-hole listens on IPv6 too, but the router only hands out the IPv4 address as the DNS server, so clients with IPv6 only would not find it. The AAAA records for the local names do not exist yet.

A stability concern is the prefix. The ISP prefix may change after a router reboot or a long outage, so hard-coding global addresses in configs would break. The cleaner way is ULA addresses for internal use, with a fixed fd00 prefix, next to the global ones.

Plan written to the README:
1. Generate a ULA /64 and announce it from the router if it supports a second prefix.
2. Give the Pi-hole and Caddy VMs fixed ULA addresses.
3. Add AAAA records to dnsmasq.
4. Enable IPv6 in the Docker daemon for Caddy only.
5. Open WireGuard to IPv6 last.

I did not change anything on the live system today. The router has a menu for a ULA prefix, which I found, but I want to read its documentation before touching it.

summary: Announced a ULA prefix from the router and gave Pi-hole and Caddy VMs fixed ULA addresses, with AAAA records for the local names; dig over IPv6 now answers for nas.home.lan.
body:
I followed the plan from last week. First I generated a random ULA prefix with the RFC 4193 method, and entered it in the router as an additional prefix on the LAN with the SLAAC flags on. After a few minutes the laptop showed a second IPv6 address in the fd range.

For the servers I wanted fixed addresses, so I used netplan-like entries through the Debian interfaces file, via an Ansible template in the common role. The Pi-hole VM got the ::53 host suffix, and the Caddy VM got ::443. The suffixes are easy to remember and live in group_vars.

Then I added AAAA records to the custom dnsmasq file for dns, nas, pve and the Caddy sites. The NAS got a ULA address too, which I set in Control Panel under Network.

Testing: dig AAAA nas.home.lan @fd..::53 answered with the right address, and ping -6 reached the NAS from the laptop. Pi-hole shows the queries over IPv6 in its log.

A problem showed up with Unbound. It tried to reach root servers over IPv6, which timed out, because the Pi-hole VM had no global route. After a look at ip -6 route, I saw the default route was missing, as the VM accepted router advertisements only for the ULA. I switched on accept_ra for the interface, and the default route returned.

I told the router to hand out the Pi-hole ULA address through RDNSS, so IPv6 clients know where to ask. Android ignores RDNSS, as expected, so it falls back to IPv4 DNS, which is fine.

Docker for Caddy is next.

summary: Enabled IPv6 in the Docker daemon on the Caddy VM; Caddy now answers on both stacks, but real client addresses were lost behind NAT66 until ip6tables was switched on.
body:
On the Caddy VM I edited /etc/docker/daemon.json to set ipv6 true, a fixed-cidr-v6 from the ULA space and ip6tables true with experimental on, as the Docker version here still requires. The change is in the Ansible docker role as a template with a variable, so only the Caddy host gets it.

After restarting Docker, the compose network was recreated. I added enable_ipv6 to the network in the compose file with a subnet, and ran docker compose up -d. Caddy listened on the host ports for both stacks.

First test: curl -6 https://nas.home.lan worked from the laptop. But the Caddy access log showed the client as the Docker gateway address, not the laptop. That happens when Docker's userland proxy accepts the IPv6 connection and forwards it.

The logs were useless for debugging with this. I turned on ip6tables, as mentioned, and restarted again. After this, the log lines showed the real source addresses. For IPv4 the real addresses were already shown.

Home Assistant has trusted_proxies with the Caddy IPv4 address only. When Caddy contacts it over IPv6 it would return 400, so I made sure the upstream in the Caddyfile uses the IPv4 name. I tested HA through Caddy over both stacks, and it worked.

I checked certificates: they stay the same on both stacks, since they are bound to the name.

Kuma monitors still use IPv4. I added one extra monitor for IPv6 on the status page name, using a ping6-like check of the Caddy ULA address.

Open: WireGuard over IPv6, and the firewall rules for global addresses. Today the global addresses of the servers are reachable from outside only if the router allows it. I checked that the router's IPv6 firewall blocks inbound by default, which it does.

summary: Closed the IPv6 topic: WireGuard stays IPv4-only for the tunnel, the router firewall blocks inbound, and the README documents the ULA scheme and the choices.
body:
Last step of the IPv6 work was a decision. WireGuard could carry IPv6 inside the tunnel, but the peers only need the home IPv4 subnet, and the split routing works well. I chose to leave the tunnel on IPv4. The server endpoint is IPv4 only too, because the ISP's IPv4 address is stable enough.

I then checked the external exposure. From a phone on mobile data I scanned the global addresses of the Caddy VM and the NAS with an IPv6 port scanner app. All ports were filtered. That matches the router's default of dropping inbound IPv6, and I made no pinholes.

I reviewed what changed over the whole topic:
- a ULA prefix announced by the router,
- fixed ULA suffixes for Pi-hole, Caddy and the NAS,
- AAAA records in dnsmasq,
- accept_ra fixed on the Pi-hole VM,
- Docker IPv6 on the Caddy VM only.

The Ansible run is idempotent for all of it. I ran the full site.yml twice and the second pass said changed=0.

I rewrote the README section on networking with a table of the addresses and the reason for the ULA choice, which is that the global prefix can change. A short troubleshooting list covers the two issues found: the missing default route and the lost client addresses.

There is no further IPv6 work planned. The next topic will be the second DNS server.

summary: Started a plan to move the WireGuard VPN off the router onto a small LXC on Proxmox, because the router firmware cannot show per-peer traffic or handshakes.
body:
The router's built-in WireGuard works, but it exposes only an on/off switch and one peer list. I could not tell which phone or laptop was connected, and a stale peer had been in the list for months. I spent the evening writing down what I want from the VPN.

The list: one peer per device, split tunnel for the home subnets only, DNS through Pi-hole, and a handshake check that Uptime Kuma can read. I also want the whole config in git, with keys in the Ansible vault, in the same way as the other services.

I looked at three options. The first was a wg-easy container in Docker on the Caddy VM. The second was plain wg-quick in a dedicated LXC. The third was to keep the router. I rejected the first because the web UI keeps its state in a volume and I would rather template the config. The router stays as a fallback until the new one has run for a while.

The LXC needs a TUN device, so I read the Proxmox notes for unprivileged containers. The lines needed are lxc.cgroup2.devices.allow for c 10:200 and a mount entry for /dev/net/tun. I did not change anything on the host yet. The router still needs a port forward of UDP 51820 to the new address, and I will leave the old forward until the cutover.

Next step is to create the LXC with a fixed address and write the Ansible role for it. I also have to decide on the tunnel subnet; 10.8.0.0/24 does not clash with anything at home. Nothing was changed on any machine today, this was planning only.

summary: Chose the VPN addressing plan: tunnel subnet 10.8.0.0/24, a fixed LXC address, split-tunnel AllowedIPs and Pi-hole as DNS, written into the README before any build.
body:
Right after the planning entry I turned the decisions into a short section in the README, so the Ansible role has a spec to follow.

The tunnel subnet is 10.8.0.0/24, with the server at .1. Peers get fixed addresses from .10 upward, one per device, and the README has a table of device name and address. The LXC itself gets a fixed LAN address outside the DHCP pool, with a reservation noted on the router.

For the split tunnel the client AllowedIPs are the LAN subnet, the ULA prefix is deliberately not included, and 10.8.0.0/24. That matches the earlier decision that WireGuard stays IPv4-only. The client DNS entry is the Pi-hole address, so names like nas.home.lan resolve over the tunnel.

I checked that Pi-hole accepts queries from 10.8.0.0/24. By default it listens only on the local interface in some modes, so I looked at the compose environment. The setting is permit all origins off, and I will have to add the tunnel subnet as an allowed origin, or Pi-hole will refuse the queries. I wrote that as a TODO in the README.

Keepalive is 25 seconds for phones behind mobile NAT and off for the laptop that is mostly at home. I also wrote down how to add a peer: add one entry to the vars file, run the playbook, and show the QR code from the generated client file. The private keys go into the vault, not into git in plain text.

Nothing was deployed. The next session creates the LXC and writes the role.

summary: Created the WireGuard LXC on Proxmox with a TUN device and fixed address, and confirmed that wg-quick starts there with a test key pair before any role exists.
body:
I created an unprivileged Debian LXC with 1 core, 256 MB of RAM and 2 GB of disk on local storage. The address is the fixed one from the README plan.

The first start showed the known problem: wg-quick failed with 'RTNETLINK answers: Operation not permitted'. The container had no TUN device. I added the two lines to the container's config file on the host, allowing device 10:200 and bind-mounting /dev/net/tun, and restarted it. After that the interface came up.

I generated a throwaway key pair, wrote a minimal wg0.conf with address 10.8.0.1/24 and listen port 51820, and ran wg-quick up wg0. wg show listed the interface with no peers, which is right. I also turned on IP forwarding with a sysctl file, since the tunnel has to reach the LAN.

Then I checked the packages. wireguard-tools is in the Debian repository, and the kernel module comes from the Proxmox host kernel, so nothing has to be built. That matters because the host kernel gets updated separately.

I took the test key out again and removed the config, because the real config will come from Ansible. The container is in the Proxmox backup job already because it is covered by the whole-pool vzdump schedule; I checked the job's selection to be sure.

What is left is the role: package, template for wg0.conf, a peer list from vars, firewall rules with nftables for masquerade, and the service enabled.

summary: Wrote the Ansible wireguard role with a peer list, vaulted keys, templated wg0.conf and masquerade rules, and brought up the tunnel with the first test peer, my phone.
body:
The role lives in roles/wireguard and has tasks, a template for the server config, a template for each client file, and defaults. The peer list is a variable of name, address and public key. Server private key and peer preshared keys are in the vault.

First problem: the template wrote the keys with the default file mode, so wg-quick complained that the config file was world-accessible. I set mode 0600 and owner root on the config and the generated client files. The warning is gone.

Second problem: forwarding. Packets from the phone reached the LXC and the handshake worked, but nothing went further. The cause was the missing masquerade. I added a small nftables ruleset: forward accept for wg0 to the LAN, and masquerade on eth0 for 10.8.0.0/24. With that the phone could ping the NAS.

I generated the phone's client file on the control machine, in a folder that is git-ignored, and showed it as a QR code with qrencode. The phone connected from the mobile network. The handshake appeared in wg show within a second, and the transfer counters moved.

DNS did not work at first. Names did not resolve and the phone fell back to nothing. This was the Pi-hole TODO from the README: it ignored queries from 10.8.0.0/24. I set the Pi-hole listening option to allow all origins, which is acceptable because only the LAN and the tunnel can reach it, and the router blocks inbound from the internet. After the restart of the stack, nas.home.lan resolved over the tunnel.

I also tested that the split tunnel works: a public IP check from the phone still shows the mobile provider address, so only home traffic goes through. The check mode run of the role against the LXC afterwards reported no changes.

To do: the router port forward, the other devices, and a monitor in Kuma.

summary: Pointed the router's UDP 51820 forward at the new WireGuard LXC and tested from a mobile hotspot; the old router VPN is switched off but its config is kept for a week.
body:
I changed the port forward on the router so that UDP 51820 goes to the LXC address instead of the router itself. The router's own WireGuard server was listening on the same port, so I had to disable it first; otherwise the forward does not apply.

Test from the phone on mobile data with Wi-Fi off: the handshake came within two seconds and the NAS web interface opened. I repeated it from the laptop on the phone's hotspot and it worked too.

I exported the old router config as a file and saved it outside git, in the password manager notes, in case I need to roll back. The old peers were two devices I still use and one that I no longer have. The unknown one is not carried over.

I left the old config in place for a week, switched off, before deleting it.

summary: Added the laptop and tablet as WireGuard peers and a Kuma push monitor that fails when the newest handshake is older than a day, using a small script on the LXC.
body:
The two additional peers went into the vars file with the next free addresses, .11 for the laptop and .12 for the tablet. After a run of the playbook the client files appeared and I imported them. The laptop worked at once; the tablet needed a retype of the endpoint, since I had mistyped the port in the manual setup.

For monitoring, Kuma cannot see inside the tunnel. I wrote scripts/wg-check.sh, which reads the latest handshake times with wg show wg0 latest-handshakes and prints the youngest age in seconds. The role installs it with a systemd timer that runs every 5 minutes.

The script has one decision in it. A peer that is never used would always look stale, so it checks the age of the youngest handshake over all peers, not each one. If the newest is older than 86400 seconds, it sends nothing and Kuma raises the alarm after the push interval. Otherwise it calls the push URL. A day is generous, but the phone reconnects often.

I tested it by stopping the timer and waiting for the heartbeat interval. The monitor went red after the grace period and recovered after I started the timer again. The mail alert came as before.

One oddity: with persistent keepalive the phone shows a handshake only when traffic flows, so overnight the youngest age grows to a few hours. That is still within the limit.

summary: Wrote the VPN section of the README and a restore note, then rebuilt the WireGuard LXC from scratch with the playbook; the phone reconnected without any change on the device.
body:
To prove that the setup is reproducible I destroyed the LXC and rebuilt it. First I wrote the documentation: how to add and remove a peer, where the keys live, how the port forward is set, and the pitfalls found earlier, namely the TUN device lines, the file mode and the Pi-hole origin setting.

The rebuild went in steps. I created the container with the same ID and address using the Proxmox command line, added the TUN lines, and ran the playbook. It took about 4 minutes from an empty container to a running tunnel.

The important check was the server key. Since it comes from the vault, the public key stayed the same, so no client had to be updated. The phone reconnected within a few seconds of the interface coming up, and the laptop on a hotspot did too.

One item broke in the rebuild: the TUN device lines are not part of the playbook, because the playbook runs inside the container and cannot edit the host config. I added them to the Proxmox host role as a small task instead, keyed on the container ID, and put a comment in the README so I do not forget why. I have not run that host task yet.

I also confirmed that the vzdump backup of the container restores. I did not do a full restore; I only listed the archive contents.

Deleted the old router VPN export from the notes after a final look, since the new one has worked for several days.

summary: Looked at Jellyfin playback stuttering on the TV and found it direct-streaming a high-bitrate file over Wi-Fi; set the TV client to a bitrate cap instead of changing the server.
body:
A family member said that one film stutters every few minutes on the living room TV. I looked at the Jellyfin dashboard while it played. The session showed direct play, so the server was not transcoding and its load was low.

The file is a 4K remux at about 62 Mbit/s. The TV is on Wi-Fi, and iperf3 from a laptop in that room showed about 90 Mbit/s with large swings, down to 40. So the peaks of the file exceed what the link gives at times.

I considered three options. The first was to wire the TV, which is not easy in that room. The second was to transcode on the server with hardware acceleration, which works since the render group fix, but a 4K to 1080p transcode costs quality and the GPU time. The third was to cap the client bitrate. I picked the third for now: on the TV client I set the internet streaming quality to 20 Mbit/s, and Jellyfin then transcodes only this kind of file and direct-plays the rest.

The film played through without a stall. The dashboard showed a hardware transcode with the GPU at about 30 percent and the CPU near idle.

I added a line to the README under Jellyfin about this limit. I might look at a powerline adapter later, but nothing is bought.

summary: Deleted the disabled router VPN config and checked all three peers still connect, which closes the WireGuard move to its own container.
body:
The week of the fallback is over. I looked at the Kuma monitor for the handshake check and it had stayed green the whole time, with no alerts.

I removed the disabled WireGuard server from the router and also deleted the exported config from my notes. Before that I made sure that none of the peers used the old keys: phone, laptop and tablet all showed recent handshakes in wg show on the LXC.

One last test from outside: the laptop on a hotspot opened ha.home.lan and the Jellyfin page through the tunnel, and a DNS lookup of nas.home.lan returned the right address from Pi-hole.

The README section is complete and matches the live setup. The only open item is the host task for the TUN lines, which I have not run, since the container works. I will run it at the next Proxmox role pass.

summary: Ran the Proxmox host role with the new TUN device task in check mode and for real; it only touched the WireGuard container config, and the container survived a restart.
body:
This was the open item from the VPN rebuild. The task adds the two device lines to the container config file on the host if they are missing, using lineinfile with a validation of the container ID variable.

Check mode first: it reported one change, the container was missing no lines, so I expected zero. The reason was a trailing space in my regex, which did not match the manual lines I had typed. I fixed the pattern to match the lines exactly and ran the check again: no changes, as it should be.

Then I tested the task by removing the lines by hand on the host and running the role. It restored both. I restarted the container with pct reboot and the interface came back. Handshakes from the phone appeared within 10 seconds.

The rest of the role ran clean: apt repositories, chrony, mail relay all unchanged. I also checked the chrony offset, which was 2 ms.

I noted in the README that adding a second VPN container would need the container ID in the host variables. Nothing else needs to be done for this topic.

summary: Investigated a Jellyfin 'database is locked' error during a library scan and found that the SQLite file sat on an NFS mount from the NAS; moved the config volume to local VM disk.
body:
Jellyfin showed 'SQLite Error 5: database is locked' in the log during the nightly scan, and a few items vanished from the library until the next restart. I started with the log in the config volume and counted the errors: 37 in one night, all around the scan window.

I checked how the volumes are mounted. The media sits on the NAS over NFS, which is fine, but the config volume was a path under the same NFS mount. I had set it up that way early, to have the data on the mirror. SQLite does not lock files reliably over NFS, so concurrent writers from the scan and the playback reporting collide.

The fix was to move the config to the local disk of the Jellyfin VM. Steps:

- stopped the stack with docker compose down
- copied the config folder with rsync -a to /srv/jellyfin/config on the VM
- changed the volume path in the Ansible template
- ran the playbook and started the stack

The copy was 1.4 GB, mostly metadata and images. The cache folder stayed local too, as it was before.

After the start I checked the library counts against a screenshot of the dashboard from before: movies and shows matched. Watch history was intact, as the user data lives in the same database.

Because the config is now on the VM disk, the restic job has to cover it. The earlier backup included the old NFS path, which is on the NAS and therefore backed up differently.
