I changed the restic include list to the new path and ran the job by hand. The snapshot grew by about 1.3 GB, and restic ls showed the database files.

I also updated the restore step in the README, which still pointed to the old path. A forced scan ran that night without errors; I will look at the log once more tomorrow.

summary: The nightly Jellyfin scan after the config move produced zero lock errors, and the restic snapshot of the new config path restored a copy of the database that opens fine.
body:
I read the Jellyfin log after the first full night on local disk. The scan ran from 03:00 to 03:22 and there were no SQLite errors at all, compared with 37 the night before.

Then I tested the restore of the new path, since the backup is only worth something if it comes back. I restored the latest snapshot into a temporary folder with restic restore, picking the jellyfin config include. The library database was in it at the expected size.

To be sure it was usable, I ran sqlite3 on the restored file with PRAGMA integrity_check, which returned ok. I did not start a second Jellyfin on it.

One detail: the database is in WAL mode, so a copy taken while the server is running might miss recent writes. The restic job runs at 02:00, before the scan, when little is written. That is acceptable for now. A cleaner way would be a pre-backup hook that stops the container for a minute. I put that in the notes as an option but did not do it.

I deleted the old config folder on the NAS after one more check that nothing mounts it. It was 1.4 GB.

summary: Home Assistant's backup file had grown to 2.1 GB because the recorder kept 30 days of history; set it to 10 days and excluded noisy sensors, which cut the backup to 380 MB.
body:
The restic cloud upload had been getting slower, so I looked at what changed. The largest item was the Home Assistant backup file, at 2.1 GB, up from about 600 MB a few months ago.

Inside the config the home-assistant_v2.db file was the cause, close to 1.8 GB. The recorder keeps 30 days by default in my setup, and the NUT integration added several sensors that update every few seconds, such as the UPS load and the input voltage.

I looked at the biggest entities by row count with a query on the states table grouped by entity. The top five were all UPS sensors and a power plug reporting watts, with together about 60 percent of the rows.

I made two changes in the recorder section of configuration.yaml. The first was purge_keep_days set to 10. The second was an exclude for the UPS voltage and the plug's watts entities. I kept the battery charge and the load, since I use them in the notification.

After a restart I ran the purge service with repack set. The database went from 1.8 GB to 290 MB. A new backup came out at 380 MB.

The energy dashboard uses long-term statistics, which are separate from the states table, so the graphs for earlier weeks stayed. I checked the last month in the dashboard to be sure.

The cloud backup duration will show over the next nights.

summary: The first restic cloud run after the Home Assistant database shrink took 9 minutes instead of 34, so the recorder change also fixed most of the slow upload.
body:
I looked at the log of last night's job. The cloud part of the run took 9 minutes, whereas the run before the change took 34 minutes. The data added was 410 MB, compared with 2.3 GB.

The NAS repository part was also faster, 3 minutes against 11. The healthcheck ping arrived on time and Kuma showed all backup monitors green.

One remaining slow part is the media metadata folder, which changes a little each night, but it is small. I do not plan any change there.

I wrote the recorder settings in the Home Assistant section of the README, together with the reason, so that nobody raises the days again without knowing what it costs.

summary: Planned the replacement of the failing-smart-test path for the Proxmox SSD: read the SMART data, found wear at 11 percent and no errors, and decided only to monitor it.
body:
A Proxmox mail reported a SMART attribute change on the boot SSD, so I looked at it over SSH with smartctl -a. The drive reports percentage used at 11 percent, available spare at 100 percent, and zero media errors. The attribute that changed was the power-on hours counter crossing a threshold the mail relay treats as a change.

There is nothing to replace. At the current write rate the drive would last many years. I checked the write total: about 18 TB written since install, with a rating of 600 TBW.

I decided to add smartd monitoring with a short test weekly and a mail on any error, and to look at the wear value again in six months. The smartd.conf line goes into the Proxmox host role.

summary: Replaced the cron-driven apt upgrades on the Docker VMs with unattended security-only updates and a Kuma push monitor, after a manual kernel patch was missed for weeks.
body:
While checking the VMs for the Proxmox host role I found that two of the three Docker VMs were running a kernel several security releases behind. The apt upgrades had depended on me running the playbook by hand, and nothing reminded me when I did not. This session closed that gap.

I added an Ansible role called autoupdate that installs unattended-upgrades and templates /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades. It allows only the security origin, never the regular updates pocket, so Docker and other third-party packages stay under manual control. Automatic reboots are off, because the boot order on the Proxmox host matters and I do not want a VM to restart on its own at an odd hour. Instead the role writes a flag when /var/run/reboot-required appears.

A small script, scripts/reboot-needed.sh, runs from cron every morning at 07:00 and pushes to a new Kuma push monitor. It reports down when the flag file is older than 7 days, so a pending kernel update shows up as an alert rather than being forgotten. The monitor sends the usual mail.

I ran the role in check mode against all three Docker VMs first, which reported 4 changes per host, all expected. Then I applied it for real. A dry run of unattended-upgrades with --dry-run -d on the Caddy VM listed 9 security packages it would install, none of them Docker or containerd, which was what I wanted.

One snag: the Jellyfin VM had the old Docker apt source with a deprecated key, which made apt print a warning on every run. I fixed the source file in the same role, and the warning is gone.

The two lagging VMs got their pending kernel updates and I rebooted them one at a time by hand, with Pi-hole and Caddy staying up throughout. Both came back in under 2 minutes and all Kuma checks went green again. Next I will watch the logs in /var/log/unattended-upgrades for a week to confirm nothing unexpected is touched.

summary: Fixed Uptime Kuma flapping on the Jellyfin monitor: the check hit the web root during the nightly scan and timed out, so it now uses the lightweight /health endpoint.
body:
Kuma sent a down and up pair of mails at 03:05 and 03:11 for Jellyfin. Nothing was really down; I confirmed by looking at the access log, which showed normal answers.

The monitor was an HTTP check on the Jellyfin home page with a 10 second timeout. During the library scan the page took 12 to 14 seconds to render once, so the check failed.

Jellyfin has a /health endpoint that returns 'Healthy' without touching the library. I changed the monitor to that URL and expect the keyword Healthy in the answer. I also set retries to 2, so a single slow answer does not send a mail.

To verify, I started a manual library scan and watched the monitor: the response time stayed around 40 ms and nothing alerted. The check also still turns red when I stop the container, which I tried for a minute.

I looked at the other monitors for the same pattern. Home Assistant checks its login page, which is light enough. The Pi-hole check uses a DNS query, not the web page. So only Jellyfin needed the change.

The monitor export, kept in git as JSON, is updated with the new settings.

summary: Wrote a small script that tests all five WireGuard-relevant paths from the LXC after changes and ran it once; it caught that the tablet peer had a duplicate address with the laptop.
body:
After adding the peers I wanted a single check to run after any VPN change. scripts/vpn-selftest.sh runs on the LXC and checks five things: the interface is up, IP forwarding is on, the nftables masquerade rule is present, Pi-hole answers a DNS query from the tunnel address, and the NAS is reachable by ping.

The script prints one line per check and exits non-zero if any fails. It is plain bash and uses only wg, sysctl, nft, dig and ping.

The first run printed all five as ok, but I also added a sixth check after reading the peer table: each address must appear once. That one failed. The tablet and the laptop both had 10.8.0.11 in the vars file, because I had edited the list by hand when the tablet misconnected earlier. WireGuard accepts the second entry and moves the allowed IP to the later peer, so the laptop would silently lose its tunnel whenever the tablet connected.

I had not noticed because I never used both at once. I changed the tablet to .12, as the README says, and ran the playbook. The test passed all six checks.

I also made the playbook assert unique addresses in the peer list before templating, with a fail message that names the duplicate. I checked it by introducing a duplicate on purpose, and the run stopped at the assertion.

The selftest script is mentioned in the README next to the add-a-peer steps.

summary: A Docker update on the Caddy VM filled the root disk with old images and logs; pruned 6.8 GB, capped the json log size, and added a disk-usage monitor in Kuma.
body:
Caddy stopped answering at around 22:00 and Kuma raised the alarm for all the web services at once, since they all go through the proxy. The VM itself was up.

Over SSH, df showed the root filesystem at 100 percent. The Caddy container had crashed because it could not write its certificate storage. The reason was disk space, not Caddy.

I looked for the big items with du. The Docker data directory held 6.8 GB that could be freed. The container logs were the largest part: the json-file log of the Caddy container was 3.1 GB, since access logging is on and the default driver has no limit. Old images from earlier update-all.sh runs made up the rest.

The repair steps:

- docker image prune -a to remove unused images, which freed about 3.2 GB
- truncated the container log file after stopping the stack
- started Caddy again; it came up and served all sites within seconds

The permanent fixes went into the Ansible role. The Docker daemon.json now sets log-opts with max-size 10m and max-file 3, which applies to new containers, so the Caddy stack was recreated to pick it up. I also made update-all.sh run docker image prune -f after a successful update, with the dry-run flag showing what it would remove.

For detection I wanted a warning before the disk is full. I added a push monitor with a small script on each VM that reports only if the root usage is below 85 percent. That means the Kuma alert fires on silence, which is how the other push monitors work too. The script runs from a systemd timer every 10 minutes.

I tested by creating a large file with fallocate to cross 85 percent on the Caddy VM; the alert mail arrived after the grace period and cleared after I deleted the file. I also checked the Jellyfin and Home Assistant VMs: both below 50 percent.

Root cause summed up: unlimited logs plus image build-up. The VM disk could also be enlarged, but I left it at its size.

summary: Replaced the single vzdump schedule with two jobs, nightly for the critical guests and weekly for the rest, after a full-pool backup ran 5 hours and overlapped the restic window.
body:
I noticed that the backup mails came late, and the vzdump log showed the whole job taking 5 hours 10 minutes, from 01:00 to after 06:00. It overlapped the restic run at 02:00 and the Jellyfin scan at 03:00. The NAS was busy during that whole time.

The job selected every guest in the pool. Looking at the sizes in the log, the bulk came from two guests: the Jellyfin VM with its 80 GB disk at 2 hours, and an old test VM that I no longer use at 40 minutes.

I made these changes in the Proxmox datacenter backup settings, and wrote them down in the README since they are not in git:

- Nightly at 00:30: Pi-hole, Caddy, WireGuard and Home Assistant. These are small and cannot be rebuilt as quickly. Mode snapshot, zstd compression.
- Weekly, early in the morning when nobody is watching a film: the Jellyfin VM.
- The test VM is excluded; I shut it down and set it for removal after a month.

The Jellyfin VM can be rebuilt from the playbook, and its config is protected by restic, so a weekly image is enough. The media itself lives on the NAS.

I ran the nightly job by hand once. It finished in 14 minutes with 22 GB of output before dedup on the target. Then I started the weekly job manually to measure it: 1 hour 48 minutes, and the NAS load showed up in the graphs, so I put it in a time slot far from restic.

The retention was another point. Before, it kept 7 daily and 4 weekly for everything. For the nightly job I kept 7 daily and 4 weekly, and for the weekly job 3 weekly, as the images are large. The NAS backup share had 410 GB free, and this reduces the use.

I also pointed the Kuma push monitor at the new schedule. It had a 26 hour window, which works for the nightly job, and I added a second monitor for the weekly job with 8 days.

Next night I will check that the times line up and that nothing overlaps.

summary: Verified the new vzdump schedule over two nights: the nightly run took 15 minutes and finished before restic started, and both Kuma push monitors stayed green.
body:
I read the vzdump logs for the two nights since the change. The nightly job started at 00:30 and ended at 00:45 both times. That is clear of the restic job at 02:00.

The NAS load graph shows a short peak at 00:30, and then idle until restic. In the earlier setup the load was high for five hours.

Both push monitors, the nightly and the weekly one, are green. I had to check the weekly one by waiting for its first run, which happened in the early morning. It took 1 hour 52 minutes and sent its ping on completion.

One mistake showed up: the weekly job was set to send mail only on failure, and I had not noticed that the nightly job was configured to send mail always. That gave me a mail per night again. I set the nightly one to failures only, since Kuma covers the success case.

Then I tested a restore of the smallest guest, the WireGuard LXC, to a new ID from last night's archive. It restored in 20 seconds and started. I did not give it the same address, so there was no conflict, and I checked wg show before destroying it. The restored copy had the correct interface and keys.

The old test VM was removed from the Proxmox host after the retention period of a month would apply; I left it off for now. The topic is closed unless the Jellyfin VM image grows noticeably.

I added the numbers to the README so I can compare them later.

summary: Checked Pi-hole's long-term query database after the web page got slow and found 1.9 GB of history; set retention to 90 days and flushed, and the dashboard loads in under 2 seconds.
body:
The Pi-hole dashboard had become slow, with the query log taking about 25 seconds to open. DNS itself answered fine, so it was only the web interface.

The cause was the FTL database, pihole-FTL.db, at 1.9 GB. Retention was set to 365 days, which I had chosen long ago when the network had few devices. With the IoT devices and the phones, there are about 60,000 queries a day, so the table has grown large.

I changed MAXDBDAYS to 90 in the compose environment of the stack, which goes through the Ansible template. Then I stopped the container and ran VACUUM with sqlite3 on the database. The file shrank to 520 MB. I started the stack and checked the dashboard: the log page now opened in under 2 seconds.

Before the vacuum I copied the database aside as a precaution; I deleted the copy after the check. The restic job includes the Pi-hole config but not the query database, which is fine because the history has no value for a restore.

I also looked at which clients make most queries. One smart plug sent 9,000 queries a day to a cloud name that is blocked, and the plug retried constantly. I did not change that, but I noted the device name for later.

The settings page now shows a database size of 520 MB, and I noted the retention in the README. I will see in a few months if 90 days is enough. Home Assistant's own long-term view is unaffected, as it does not use Pi-hole's data.

summary: Wrote a one-page recovery runbook in the repository that lists the order of rebuilding the homelab after a total loss, with the time each step took in the tests so far.
body:
I had many separate README sections but no single document for the case where everything is gone. I spent the evening on docs/recovery.md, based on the real tests done in the last months and not on guesses.

The order in the runbook is this:

- Network first: router settings, the DHCP reservations and the ULA prefix, which are all documented but not in git.
- Then the Proxmox host with the host role, then the Pi-hole and Caddy VMs from the playbook, because DNS and the proxy are needed for everything else.
- WireGuard LXC, the Home Assistant VM from its backup file, and Jellyfin with its config from restic.
- Last the monitoring checks and a look at Kuma.

Each step has a measured time. The Caddy VM rebuild took 14 minutes in the test. The WireGuard LXC took 4 minutes. A Jellyfin rebuild including the config restore took about 25 minutes, mostly the restic download from the NAS. I did not have a number for the Home Assistant restore, so I marked it as not measured.

The runbook also records where the secrets are: the vault password is in the password manager and on a paper copy, and the restic repository passwords are in the vault and the same paper copy. If the vault password is lost, the backups cannot be opened, so I stated this at the top.

A gap I found while writing: the Raspberry Pi, which runs Uptime Kuma and NUT, has no backup of its Kuma data. The monitors are exported as JSON in git, but the history and the status page settings are not. I added a restic include for the Kuma volume on the Pi and ran it once; the snapshot was 48 MB.

The other gap is the cloud bucket credentials, which are in the vault but also needed to reach the cloud copy. I wrote the retrieval steps in the runbook.

I have not tested the whole runbook in sequence. That is a task for a quiet weekend, and I will measure the Home Assistant restore then.

summary: Started pinning Docker image versions after a latest-tag update changed a service unannounced; listed every image on the three Docker VMs and which ones float.
body:
The trigger was the Caddy VM, where a routine pull last week brought in a newer image than I had tested, and nothing in the repository said which version was meant to run. Today I went through the compose files for all three Docker VMs and listed every image with its tag. Of 23 images, 11 use latest or a bare name, 7 use a major-only tag, and only 5 carry a full version.

I then ran docker image ls and docker inspect on each VM to find the version that is actually running. Some containers print their version in the log, and others needed the image label. Two images, the restic REST container and the speedtest exporter, had no version label at all, so I took the digest and matched it against the registry tag list.

The result is a table in docs/images.md with the image, the current tag in compose, the running version and the digest. It is not yet used by any playbook. Three images are running versions that are no longer the newest, and I did not touch them, because pinning must first record what runs and not change it.

I also checked how the update script handles tags. It calls docker compose pull and then up -d for every stack, so a floating tag is replaced the moment upstream publishes. That is the real cause of the surprise on the Caddy VM, and pinning alone will make the script harmless for those images.

The plan has three steps. First, one vars file in Ansible that holds all image versions. Second, compose templates that read from it. Third, a deploy that must change nothing on the VMs. I will begin with Uptime Kuma and Caddy, because they are the services where a silent change hurts most.

Nothing was deployed in this session. The only change committed is the documentation table and a short note in the README about the pinning rule. The remaining open point is how to be told when a pinned image has a security fix, and I will think about that after the pins are in place.

summary: Moved image versions into a single Ansible vars file and pinned Uptime Kuma and the Caddy image to the running versions; a deploy changed nothing on the VMs.
body:
I created group_vars/docker/images.yml with one variable per image and switched the compose templates for Uptime Kuma and Caddy to use them. Both values are the versions that were already running, read from the containers yesterday.

I ran the playbook with --check --diff first. The only diff was the image line in the two templates, which is the expected change from latest to a fixed tag. Then I ran it for real against the monitoring VM and the Caddy VM.

Both containers stayed up and their IDs did not change, so docker did not recreate them. Kuma showed no gap in its heartbeat chart, and Caddy answered on IPv4 and IPv6 as before.

Seven more images were left in the nine, and I put them in the vars file already but did not use them in templates. Next I will do Pi-hole and Jellyfin, because those need a look at release notes first.

summary: Looked into why the update script reported success after a Caddy image pull failed on a rate limit; the pull error was swallowed, so the run looked green.
body:
A scheduled update on the Caddy VM last night ended with the usual green push to Uptime Kuma, yet the log showed one stack had not changed. I read the script line by line to see why. The pull for the Caddy stack failed with the registry message 'toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit', and the script went on to the next stack.

The cause is in the loop. It runs docker compose pull inside a command substitution that is piped into tee, and the exit code seen by the loop is that of tee, not of compose. Because of this every failure of the pull looked like success. The same pattern wraps the up -d call, so a failed recreate would also be hidden.

I reproduced it on the test VM by pointing one compose file at an image tag that does not exist. The script printed the error into the log and still exited with 0. That confirmed that the problem is the pipe and not something special about the rate limit.

I have not changed the script yet. First I wrote down what it should do. Each stack is handled on its own, and an error in one stack does not stop the others. The exit code of pull and of up is checked directly, and with pipefail set. The name of every failed stack goes into the log and into the final message to Kuma, and the push status is down if any stack failed.

I also looked at the rate limit itself. The three VMs share one public address, and the pulls all start at the same minute, so together they use up the anonymous limit quickly. Two fixes are possible: a login with a free account, or a stagger of the start times. I prefer the stagger first, since it needs no new secret in the vault.

I added two items to the TODO file in the repository: the exit code fix and the staggered timer. The next session will do the fix on the test VM first and then roll it out to the others. The Caddy stack still runs the older image, which is fine for now, and the log of this run is saved next to the notes.

summary: The update script silently ignored a failed recreate; it now checks the exit code, logs which container failed, and pushes a failure to Uptime Kuma.
body:
The Jellyfin finding from earlier today pointed at a real gap in update-all.sh. The pull and the up -d were chained with a semicolon, so a failed recreate did not change the exit status of the script.

I changed it to run per project in a loop and record the exit code of docker compose up -d for each. A failed project is added to a list, and at the end the script prints the list and exits with 1 if it is not empty.

I also added a curl to the Kuma push URL for the update job. On success it sends status up with the number of projects updated, on failure it sends status down with the names of the failed ones in the message.

To test it I made a copy of a compose file with a wrong image tag and pointed the script at it. The script reported that one project failed, kept going with the others, exited with 1, and Kuma turned red with the project name in the message. I removed the broken copy after that.

The real run on the Docker VMs showed no failures. Still open: the script should skip pinned images when pulling, which I will do together with the remaining pins.

summary: Pinned the remaining five images, including Home Assistant and the restic REST container, and deployed them with no container recreated.
body:
The last five images were Home Assistant, the Mosquitto broker, the restic helper container, a small speedtest exporter and the Samba test container. I read each running version with docker inspect and set the variable in images.yml.

For the exporter and the Samba container only a digest was visible, so I pinned them by digest. Home Assistant and Mosquitto have proper version tags.

Check mode showed only image line changes. After the real run, docker ps showed the same container IDs and uptimes as before, which is what I wanted: pinning to the running version must not restart anything.

No image uses latest any more according to a grep over the repository. I added that grep as a check in the lint script so a new service with latest fails it. The script still pulls whatever the compose says, so the pins now take effect there as well.

summary: Upgraded Jellyfin from the pinned older version to the next minor release on purpose, read the release notes first, and the library scan and playback worked afterwards.
body:
With the pins in place I did the Jellyfin upgrade that the failed recreate had hidden. I read the release notes for the versions in between. One note mentioned a database migration at first start, so I ran a restic snapshot of the config path before changing anything.

I changed the one variable, ran the playbook for the Jellyfin VM, and watched the logs. The migration took about 40 seconds and finished without errors.

Afterwards I checked a library scan, which took the usual 11 minutes, and played an episode on the TV with the bitrate cap from before. Transcoding was not needed. The Kuma monitor on /health stayed green throughout.

The README now has the correct version, and I added a line to it saying versions are read from images.yml, not written by hand. If a problem shows up in the next days I can roll back with the old tag and the snapshot.

summary: Question from the user: why does the nightly restic run still take 20 minutes with almost no changed data; found it re-reads the whole Jellyfin cache folder, which needs no backup.
body:
The user asked why the nightly restic run takes about 20 minutes even on quiet nights. I looked at the last week of logs on the NAS. The snapshot step reported few new bytes, but scanning took most of the time.

Using restic stats and a du over the backup paths, I found the Jellyfin VM backs up the whole /var/lib/jellyfin directory. That includes a cache folder and transcode temp files, 14 GB in total with thousands of small thumbnail files.

Those are rebuilt by Jellyfin on its own, so they have no value in a restore. The metadata and the database in the same tree do.

I wrote an exclude list for the cache and transcodes folders and put it in the repository next to the backup script, with a comment for each line. I tested with restic backup --dry-run -v and the file count dropped from 212,000 to 31,000.

I have not applied it to the real job yet, because I want to check first that the database and the metadata folder are not matched by any pattern. Next session: apply it and compare run times.

summary: Applied the restic exclude list for Jellyfin cache; the nightly run fell from 20 to 7 minutes and a test restore still opened the database.
body:
I checked the patterns against the list of paths from the dry run one more time. Only cache and transcodes matched, the library.db and the metadata folder did not.

Then I deployed the exclude file through Ansible and let the job run by itself overnight settings, starting it by hand once to see the time. It took 7 minutes 10 seconds, compared with about 20 before.

To be sure, I restored the newest snapshot of the Jellyfin config into a temp folder and opened the database with sqlite3. An integrity_check returned ok and the library tables had the expected row counts.

The cloud copy will pick up the smaller set tomorrow. Old snapshots still contain the cache, and they will drop out with the normal prune.

summary: The cloud bucket bill and size were checked: 410 GB stored, 90 GB of it from old snapshots of a deleted VM, which a forget with a fixed host filter removed.
body:
While looking at restic's cloud side I listed the bucket size and snapshots. The repository was 410 GB, more than the data I expected.

restic snapshots grouped by host showed a host name that belongs to an old Jellyfin VM which I deleted last spring. It had 38 snapshots and no new ones, so the normal forget policy, which groups by host and path, never touched them.

I ran restic forget with --host for that name and --keep-last 1 first as a dry run, which listed 37 snapshots to remove. I kept the last one in case something from that VM is still wanted.

The prune that followed ran 52 minutes and the repository went to 318 GB. That is 92 GB freed.

I added a note to the runbook that deleting a VM means also forgetting its snapshots. Next I might add a check that lists hosts with no snapshot in 30 days.

summary: Wrote a small script that reports restic hosts without a recent snapshot and pushes the result to Uptime Kuma, then caught a real stale one: the Samba test container.
body:
Following the bucket cleanup, I wrote check-restic-hosts.sh. It runs restic snapshots --json, takes the newest snapshot time per host and compares it with the current time.

Any host older than 30 hours counts as stale. The script prints the names and sends a push to a new Kuma monitor, up when none are stale and down with the names otherwise.

I tested it by lowering the threshold to 1 hour, which flagged everything, and then restored 30 hours. On the first real run it flagged one host: the Samba test container, whose backup job had been failing since the pin deploy.

I looked at the log. The job started the container by name, and the digest pin changed how its compose project was named, so the backup script could not find it. A one-line fix in the script variable made the name match again.

After a manual run the host had a fresh snapshot and the monitor turned green. The monitor is on a daily push with a 26-hour heartbeat limit.

Two lessons: the pin change had a side effect I had not tested, and the checks are useful. I also added the project name to the lint script so it flags a mismatch. Nothing else is open on this topic.

summary: Started looking at the second DNS server idea: listed what breaks when the Pi-hole VM is down for a reboot, and measured that clients stall about 8 seconds.
body:
For a while I have wanted a second DNS server so a reboot of the Pi-hole VM does not stop the whole house. Today I only measured the current state.

I stopped the Pi-hole container for one minute in the evening and tested from the laptop. Lookups took about 8 seconds each before falling back to the router, which hands out Pi-hole as the only DNS. Names under home.lan did not resolve at all through the fallback.

So a second server has two jobs: answer both ad blocking and the local names, and be on different hardware. The Raspberry Pi is the obvious candidate, because it is separate from Proxmox and the UPS covers it.

What I need to decide is how to keep the two Pi-holes in sync for local records and blocklists. Options I wrote down: nebula-sync, a small rsync of gravity.db and custom.list, or generating the records from Ansible on both.

I prefer Ansible, because the local names already come from a variable file and that avoids another tool. Blocklists are the rest, which can be set in the same role.

Nothing was changed except the notes in docs/dns-second.md. Next: check the Pi's current load and OS version.

summary: Checked the Raspberry Pi as second DNS host: it runs an old OS release with 1 GB free on the SD card, so it needs an upgrade before taking on Pi-hole.
body:
I logged into the Pi over SSH and looked at its state. It runs an OS release two versions old, uptime 94 days, load near zero.

The SD card has 1.1 GB free of 16 GB, mostly logs. The Pi only runs a small script for the sensor readings at the moment.

Pi-hole and Unbound together would fit, but a nearly full SD card is a risk, and journald was writing a lot. I set the journal limit to 100 MB and cleared old logs, which gave 3.4 GB free.

I decided to reinstall the OS cleanly rather than upgrade across two releases, and to use Ansible for everything on it. The sensor script has to be saved first, so I copied it into the repository.

summary: Reinstalled the Raspberry Pi with the current OS release, added it to the Ansible inventory, and moved the sensor script into a role; it reads sensors again.
body:
I flashed a new card with the current lite release, set a fixed address, enabled SSH with my key and booted it. The old card is kept as it is, in case something is missing.

The Pi is now in the inventory under its own group. A base role handles the user, the SSH hardening, unattended upgrades and journald limits, the same as on the VMs, with one extra task for the log-to-RAM setting to spare the card.

The sensor script became a small role with a systemd timer. After the run, the readings arrived in Home Assistant again within a minute.

The first run failed once because the apt cache was empty and the role assumed it was filled; I added update_cache to the task. The second run was clean and a third run showed zero changes, so the role is idempotent.

Next time I install Docker on it and prepare the Pi-hole role for a second instance.

summary: Deployed a second Pi-hole with Unbound on the Raspberry Pi through the existing role, with local records generated from the same variable file as the main one.
body:
The Pi-hole role already takes a host group, so I added the Pi to it with a different address and hostname. Docker was installed by the base docker role.

The local records for home.lan are rendered from group_vars into custom.list on both servers, so they cannot differ. The same is true for the blocklist file, which the role loads with pihole -g after the first start.

After the run I tested with dig against the Pi directly: nas.home.lan answered with its A and AAAA records, an ad domain returned 0.0.0.0, and an uncached external name resolved through Unbound in 38 ms on the first try, which is slower than on the VM but fine for a Pi.

I did not change the DHCP settings yet. The Pi's query log is empty, as expected.

One difference showed up: the Pi image is arm64 and the pinned Pi-hole digest from the vars file is for amd64 only. I had to pin by version tag instead, which is multi-arch, and the role now takes the pin per group.

Next step is the router: give out both servers via DHCP and test a failover.

summary: Switched the router's DHCP to hand out both DNS servers, then tested failover by stopping the main Pi-hole: lookups continued with no visible delay on renewed clients.
body:
I set the router DHCP to give the Pi-hole VM as the first DNS and the Pi as the second. Clients only pick this up at renewal, so I forced a renewal on the laptop and the phone.

Both showed two servers afterwards. I also checked the IPv6 router advertisement, which carries its own DNS option. I added the Pi's ULA address there as well, after giving the Pi a fixed ULA.

The failover test went like this: stopped the Pi-hole container on the VM, then ran a loop of dig against the system resolver every second for a minute. The first lookup took about 2 seconds, then every one was fast, because the OS marks the first server as down for a while.

That is better than the 8 seconds measured before, but not perfect. Some clients, like the TV, only use the first server and showed errors for a few seconds, but recovered.

I started the container again and checked that the query logs match what I expected: nearly all queries on the VM, a few on the Pi from the test.

Two open points. The blocklist update on the Pi runs at a different time than the VM's, and I want a Kuma monitor for the Pi instance. I will do the monitor first.

summary: Added Kuma DNS monitors for both Pi-hole servers and a check that the Pi answers local names, and a mismatch alert if the two servers give different answers.
body:
There were monitors for the Pi-hole VM already, a DNS type query for a local name. I copied the pattern for the Pi, pointing the resolver address at it.

Then I wrote a small script, dns-compare.sh, that asks both servers for five names: three local ones, one blocked ad domain and one external name. It compares the answers and prints any difference.

For the external name the addresses can differ legitimately, so the script only compares whether the result is empty or not. For the others it needs an exact match.

The script runs every 15 minutes from a systemd timer on the monitoring VM and pushes to Kuma. At first it reported a mismatch for the blocked domain: the Pi had not finished the gravity update, so it still returned a real address. After the update it matched.

I aligned the blocklist update time with a cron at 03:30 on both through the role. The monitor has been green for the afternoon.

summary: Looked into a disk showing SMART errors in the NAS: reallocated sector count rose from 0 to 8 on bay 3, so ordered a spare and set up a longer SMART test schedule.
body:
Synology sent a notice that a disk in bay 3 had a warning. I checked the SMART details over SSH on the NAS with smartctl.

The reallocated sector count was 8, where it was 0 at the last check, and the pending sector count was 0. The disk is about four years old. The volume is healthy, with redundancy intact, and no data errors showed up in the last scrub.

I started an extended SMART test on that disk, which takes around 9 hours, and the result will come later tonight. In the meantime I wrote down the serial and the hours, 31,800.

The decision is to order a spare drive of the same size now, and not to replace the disk until the count rises further or the extended test fails. The restic backup of the NAS data is current and checked, so the risk is acceptable.

I also changed the schedule: a short test every week and an extended test on the first of each month, through the Synology task scheduler. I noted the steps in the runbook for a disk swap.

summary: The extended SMART test on the NAS bay 3 disk completed without errors, but the count stayed at 8; the spare disk is ordered and the plan is to watch weekly.
body:
The extended test finished overnight with status completed without error. The reallocated count is still 8, so it did not grow during the test.

That suggests a small surface defect that was remapped and stopped. I will not swap the disk now.

I added a check script that reads the count through smartctl and pushes to Kuma, going down if the number is above 8. So any further growth alerts me quickly.

The spare is ordered and arrives next week.

summary: Spare disk arrived; ran a full badblocks-free burn-in using a long SMART test and a write check, then left it in the drawer since the bay 3 count has not moved.
body:
The spare drive arrived. Before putting it aside as a ready replacement, I tested it in a USB dock on the laptop, because a spare that is dead on arrival is useless.

I ran smartctl -t long, which took about 9 hours and passed. Then I wrote a 200 GB random file to it and read it back with a checksum comparison, which matched.

The SMART attributes of the new disk are clean: zero reallocated, zero pending, 3 power-on hours before my test.

The bay 3 disk has stayed at 8 for two weeks now, according to the Kuma check. The weekly short test passed each time.

So I labeled the spare and stored it with the swap steps from the runbook printed on a card. If the count passes 8 or the volume degrades, the swap procedure is: hot-remove the bay 3 disk, insert the spare, repair the pool from the DSM storage manager, which should take about a day for rebuild.

I did not rehearse the rebuild because it would put the pool at risk without a reason. The NAS monitor now includes the volume status too, which reports the pool state through SNMP. That ran green after the first poll.

summary: The weekly restic prune on the NAS repository started failing with a lock left behind by a killed job; removed the stale lock and made the script clean up on exit.
body:
Kuma showed the weekly prune job red. The log said: unable to create lock in backend, repository is already locked by PID of a process on the Docker VM.

The cause was last night's restic run, which was killed when the VM rebooted for a kernel update, so it never removed its lock. The unattended upgrades reboot at 03:00, which overlaps the backup window.

I checked with restic list locks that only one lock existed and that the process was really gone, then ran restic unlock. The prune started normally and ended after 14 minutes.

To prevent a repeat I did two things. The backup script now has a trap on EXIT that runs restic unlock for its own lock only, which is safe because restic unlock without --remove-all only removes stale ones. And I moved the reboot window of unattended upgrades to 05:00, after the backup.

I will watch the next two nights to see if the window change holds.

summary: Planned and did the first part of a Home Assistant upgrade after a skipped release train: backup, read breaking changes, and a test restore of the snapshot into a throwaway VM.
body:
Home Assistant was pinned at a version five months old. Several releases lay between it and the current one, so I did not want to jump blindly.

I first read the breaking changes of each release in between. Three affected me: a change to the MQTT discovery for sensors, the removal of an old YAML option I use for the template sensors, and a change in the recorder database schema.

Then I made a full backup from the HA UI and also took the restic snapshot of the config path. The backup is 380 MB as before.

Instead of upgrading in place, I created a throwaway VM from a template with Docker and restored the backup into it, using the same pinned old version at first. That worked, and the dashboards loaded with the same entities, except those depending on USB devices, which is expected on a VM without them.

Then I raised the version in the test VM step by step: first to the middle release, then to the newest one. The schema migration took 3 minutes on the 10-day recorder database.

The errors in the log after the last step were two. One was the template sensor option, which showed a deprecation that became an error: 'platform: template' under sensor is no longer valid in my old format. The other was a custom integration for the UPS that failed to load because it was outdated.

I fixed the first by rewriting the template sensors in the new syntax in the test copy and saved the diff as a patch. For the second, the NUT integration is built in now, so the custom one can go.

Nothing was touched on the real instance. The next session applies the patch to the real config and does the upgrade with the same steps, with a short rollback plan: old tag plus the backup.

summary: Upgraded the real Home Assistant to the newest release using the tested steps; migration took 4 minutes, the template sensor patch applied, and all automations ran again.
body:
I started with a new backup from the UI and a restic snapshot, and noted the old tag in the commit message for a rollback.

Then I applied the template sensor patch from the test VM to the real configuration. There were 11 template sensors in the old syntax and I rewrote them in the new format under template:. I ran the config check from the HA container before restarting, and it passed.

I removed the outdated custom UPS integration from the custom_components folder and checked that the built-in NUT integration still provides the battery charge and load entities. The entity names stayed the same, so the phone notification automation is unchanged.

I changed the image variable in images.yml and ran the playbook. The container was recreated and the schema migration ran for about 4 minutes, with the web page unavailable during it. Kuma showed a short red, and I had set a maintenance window for 15 minutes first.

Afterwards I went through the checks. All 38 automations show their last triggered times updating over the next hour. The Mosquitto devices reconnected, but two sensors needed a restart of the sensor script on the Pi, because discovery messages were retained with the old format. I cleared the retained messages with mosquitto_pub -r -n for those two topics, and they came back with the new format.

One warning remained in the log: a deprecation about a REST sensor I use for the speedtest exporter, which still works and will be removed in a later release. I noted it in docs/todo.md.

The backup size after the upgrade was 390 MB, the same as before. The upgrade is finished. A rollback would not have been needed, so I left the old backup in place for a week.

summary: Fixed the deprecated REST sensor for the speedtest exporter by moving it to the new configuration style, so the Home Assistant log has no warnings left.
body:
The warning from last week's upgrade said the REST sensor platform syntax is going away. The speedtest exporter sensors used it for download, upload and ping.

I rewrote them under the new rest: key with three sensors under one resource, so the exporter is only polled once every 30 minutes instead of three times. This was a nice side effect, since each poll of the exporter triggers nothing, but the exporter had been timing out now and then.

I ran the config check and then reloaded the REST entities with the developer tools, without a full restart. The three entities kept their names and history, and new values came in within a minute.

The log is clean after the reload. I deleted the todo line for this in docs/todo.md.

Next check is whether the upgraded instance behaves over the whole week, especially the recorder size, which should stay near 10 days of data.

summary: Checked the unattended-upgrade reboot window change after three weeks: no killed backups, no stale restic locks, and the weekly prune ran clean each time.
body:
Three weeks ago I moved the reboot window of the Docker VMs to 05:00 and added the unlock trap to the backup script. Today I checked whether that really solved the problem.

I went through the Kuma history of the backup and prune monitors. All push monitors stayed green for 21 nights. Restic list locks on both repositories showed no locks.

I also grepped the apt logs on the three VMs for reboots. Two kernel updates caused reboots, both after 05:00 and after the nightly restic run, which on average ends at about 03:20 now.

The cloud copy ran in 6 to 8 minutes each night. The Jellyfin exclude list works still, and the repository size is stable at about 320 GB.

So I closed the topic in docs/todo.md. A remaining idea is to make the reboot depend on the backup being finished, but the margin of nearly two hours seems enough for now.

summary: Looked at the Docker VMs' disk and memory trends after three quiet weeks and found the Jellyfin VM's swap use creeping up, so its memory was raised from 4 to 6 GB.
body:
The check started from a Kuma graph that showed the Jellyfin VM's swap climbing slowly. I logged in over SSH and ran free -m and vmstat 5 during a library scan. Swap used was 1.1 GB while the VM had only 4 GB of RAM. Top showed the Jellyfin process at 2.3 GB resident and the image-extraction helper adding another 600 MB during scans.

I looked at whether this was a leak. The resident size dropped after a restart and grew only while scans ran, so it looked like normal cache growth and not a leak. Playback stalled twice in the last two weeks according to the user, which fits the swapping.

I changed the memory value in the Ansible vars for the VM from 4096 to 6144 and ran the Proxmox play with --check first. The check showed only the memory line changing. After the real run the VM needed a reboot, which I did at a quiet time of day.

Afterwards I ran a full library scan again. Swap stayed under 80 MB and the scan finished about three minutes faster. The Proxmox host still has 9 GB free, so the margin is fine. I added a Kuma memory push check for the VM that alerts when swap goes above 500 MB. Next I will watch the graph for a week before touching the other VMs.

summary: Started the UPS purchase research: measured the real power draw of the Proxmox host, NAS and router at 71 W and sized the unit to give about 15 minutes of runtime.
body:
Before buying a UPS I wanted real numbers instead of guesses. The user had a plug-in power meter, so I asked for readings at idle and under load and logged them in the repository notes. Idle draw of the Proxmox host, NAS, router and switch together was 58 W. During the nightly backup it rose to 71 W.

I compared those numbers with the runtime tables of three small line-interactive models. A 700 VA unit rated for 390 W gave an estimated 18 minutes at 58 W, but battery tables are optimistic. I assumed about 70 percent of that, so roughly 12 to 15 minutes in practice. That is enough for a clean shutdown, which takes about 4 minutes in my estimate.

I also checked what the UPS must offer. It needs a USB port that NUT supports, because the Proxmox host will run the NUT server. I looked at the NUT hardware compatibility list and two of the three models were listed as fully supported. The third was only marked as partly working, so I dropped it.

The Raspberry Pi and the Pi-hole second server will stay on a separate plug at first, since their draw is only 4 W. I may move them to the UPS later so DNS survives a short outage. A pure-sine-wave output matters little for this hardware, so I did not weigh it.

The result is a short list of two models with price and runtime. I wrote the numbers and the NUT notes into docs/ups.md. The next step is the user's choice of unit, then a written plan for the shutdown order.

summary: Added NUT client configuration through Ansible on the NAS and the Pi, and found the Synology needs its UPS server address entered in its own control panel format.
body:
With the NUT server running on the Proxmox host, the next step was to make the other devices listen to it. I wrote an Ansible role named nut_client for the Raspberry Pi that installs the package and writes upsmon.conf with the server address and a monitor user. The password comes from the vault file like the other secrets.

The Pi part worked at once. Running upsc on it returned the battery charge and status from the Proxmox host. I then pulled the plug briefly for one second to see the status change, and the Pi logged the on-battery event and the return to line power.

The Synology was different. It cannot take a normal upsmon.conf, because its UPS settings live in the control panel under hardware and power. There I could enter the address of a network UPS server, but the first attempt failed with a connection refused message in the log.

The cause was that upsd on the Proxmox host listened only on localhost. I changed LISTEN in upsd.conf to the host's LAN address and added a firewall rule that allows port 3493 from the NAS and the Pi only. After that the NAS showed the UPS as connected with the right model name.

I also noted that the Synology shows a different battery percentage rounding than upsc, which is harmless. Both the listen address and the firewall rule are now in Ansible, not edited by hand. I ran the play a second time and it reported no changes. The shutdown order is still to be written, and I will do the test after that.

summary: Wrote the NUT shutdown script that stops the VMs first, then the NAS, then the host, and tested it in dry-run mode with the real commands printed but not run.
body:
The shutdown order had to be fixed in a script, since NUT alone only shuts down the machine it runs on. I wrote scripts/ups-shutdown.sh on the Proxmox host. It is called by upsmon when the battery goes low.

The order is the Docker VMs first, then the Home Assistant VM, then the Pi-hole VM last so name lookups keep working while others stop. After that it tells the NAS to shut down over SSH with a key limited to that command. The host itself powers off last through the normal NUT path.

Each step has a timeout of 90 seconds. If a guest does not stop in time, the script uses qm stop and logs that it did. I wanted the log written to a file on the host because the NAS will be down at the end.

I added a DRY_RUN variable that prints each command instead of executing it. Running it that way showed the right order and the total waiting time. One mistake showed up: the script looked for guests by name, and one VM had a name with a space, which broke the loop. I switched to VM IDs from a list in the vars file.

The real test comes next, with the plug pulled. Before that I will check the battery has charged fully.

summary: Tuned the NUT low-battery threshold after reading the measured shutdown time, and set it to start shutdown at 40 percent charge so there is margin.
body:
After the first test the user asked how I chose the point at which the shutdown begins. Until then it was the default of the UPS, a low battery flag at around 20 percent. I checked the log of the test for the facts.

The shutdown of everything took 4 minutes 40 seconds from the first command to the host powering off. The battery went from 100 to 71 percent in 11 minutes under the load measured earlier. That means about 2.6 percent per minute.

From this I calculated that 4 minutes 40 seconds costs about 12 percent. A threshold of 20 percent would leave only a thin margin, especially as an older battery gives less. I chose 40 percent, which leaves room for a battery at 60 percent of its capacity.

The value is set with an override in ups.conf, ignorelb and the lowbatt setting, written through Ansible. I also added a second rule that starts the shutdown when the power has been out longer than 10 minutes, whatever the percentage. A short outage of a minute or two should not trigger it, and it did not in a simulated check.

I documented the numbers in docs/ups.md so the threshold can be recomputed when the battery is replaced. A retest is planned after three months.

summary: Added a Kuma push monitor and a mail notice for UPS events so a power failure is reported even though the network may be down soon after.
body:
After the power test I noticed that nothing told the user a failure had happened, unless they looked at the logs afterwards. I wanted two things: an alert when the UPS is on battery and one when the shutdown starts. I wrote a small NUT notify script and hooked it into upsmon with NOTIFYCMD.

The script handles the events ONBATT, ONLINE and LOWBATT. For ONBATT it pushes a down status to a Kuma push monitor with the message text, and sends a mail through the existing local relay. For ONLINE it pushes up again.

There was a problem with the Kuma side: Kuma runs on a VM that is itself shut down early. So the push for the shutdown can fail. I made the script try the push for 5 seconds and then carry on, so the shutdown does not wait for it.

I also changed the order so the Kuma VM is stopped late, right before the Pi-hole VM. That gives the alert time to go out. The mail goes to the user's phone and works even when Kuma is gone.

I tested by pulling the plug for 30 seconds. The mail arrived after about 8 seconds and Kuma showed the monitor down, then up on return. The notify script and its config are in the Ansible role. Left to do is the IPv6 work and I will look at that soon.

summary: Added the missing piece to the runbook: the order of Ansible plays for a full rebuild and the time each play took in the scratch test.
body:
After the scratch rebuild of Kuma I updated the recovery runbook. It now lists the playbook tags in order: base, docker, caddy, dns, then the application roles. Each has the measured time.

The base play takes 3 minutes, docker 4, and the services between 1 and 2 each. The slowest part is image pulls, which depend on the rate limit; I noted that logging in to the registry avoids it.

I also noted the things not covered by Ansible: the Proxmox host itself and the NAS settings. Those are the next candidates for documentation.

summary: Wrote a UPS plan: a small unit on the Proxmox host, NUT server on it, and clean shutdown of the VMs and the NAS in order when the battery drops below a threshold.
body:
Power cuts have happened twice this month and the NAS came back with a check run each time. I looked into a UPS. A line-interactive unit with USB should carry the Proxmox host, the NAS, the router and the switch for about 15 minutes at the measured 62 W draw.

Plan: NUT runs in server mode on the Proxmox host, which has the USB link. The NAS and the Raspberry Pi act as NUT clients over the network. Shutdown order: first the VMs and containers via the Proxmox shutdown, then the NAS, since the VMs mount its shares, and the host last.

I measured the actual draw with a plug meter: host 38 W, NAS 18 W, router and switch 6 W. The Synology has built-in UPS support that can act as a client, so no extra software is needed there.

Open question: how long the VMs need for a clean stop. I will time it before choosing the battery threshold. The unit is ordered.

summary: Set up a stable IPv6 address for the Pi-hole VM with a static ULA and a fixed suffix, so it no longer changes when the prefix does.
body:
The earlier look at IPv6 had shown that the Pi-hole VM had no stable address. The provider prefix can change, so a global address is a poor choice for DNS. I decided to give the VM a unique local address in addition to the global one.

I generated a ULA /64 following the usual random method and wrote it into the vars file. The router can advertise it as a second prefix, which it supports in its IPv6 settings. For the VM I set a static address with a fixed suffix in the netplan template of the Ansible role.

After deployment the VM showed both the ULA and a global address. I tested with ping -6 from the laptop to the ULA address and it answered. Pinging after a router reboot gave the same result, which was the point.

Then I told the router to hand out the ULA of the Pi-hole as the IPv6 DNS server. Clients picked it up after a renewal. One Android phone ignored it, which is a known limit and I left it.

The Pi-hole itself listens on all interfaces, so no change was needed there. I checked with dig AAAA over the IPv6 address and got answers. The second DNS server on the Raspberry Pi still needs the same treatment, which is next.

summary: Gave the Raspberry Pi second Pi-hole the same kind of stable ULA address and tested IPv6 failover; lookups continued when the main Pi-hole was stopped.
body:
Today I did the same on the Raspberry Pi that I did for the main Pi-hole yesterday. A ULA with a fixed suffix was added to the Pi's network role, using the same prefix from the vars file. The Pi runs a current OS with NetworkManager, so I used a small connection profile instead of netplan.

After the Ansible run the Pi had its ULA and answered dig AAAA for a local name. I added the address to the router's IPv6 DNS list as the second entry. Now both servers are handed out over router advertisements.

For the failover test I stopped the main Pi-hole VM and ran lookups from the laptop over IPv6 only. I forced that by disabling IPv4 on the interface for the test. The lookups were answered by the Pi after a delay of about 1 second on the first query, then fast.

That first delay is the client trying the dead server before it moves on, similar to what I saw in the IPv4 test. The Kuma checks for the second server alert only on the IPv4 address, so I added an IPv6 DNS monitor for each of the two. I also extended the mismatch alert to compare answers over IPv6.

All of this is in the repository and a second deploy changed nothing. The remaining work is firewall rules for IPv6 on the VMs.

summary: Ran the first controlled power-failure test by pulling the UPS plug: shutdown started at the threshold and everything stopped in order.
body:
Pulled the mains plug in the evening. The UPS switched to battery and upsmon logged the event. I had temporarily raised the threshold so the test would not take 35 minutes.

The guests stopped first, then the NAS shut down, then the host powered off. Total time from threshold to power off was 3 minutes 10 seconds. After plugging back in, the UPS turned the outlets on again, but the host did not boot by itself because the BIOS setting was on last state. I changed it to power on.

The threshold is back to 5 minutes.

summary: After the power test, the services all came back in order, but the Pi-hole VM started before the router had a link; added a start delay.
body:
Checked the boot after the test. All VMs were up. The Pi-hole VM had logged upstream resolution failures at the start because the router was not ready. I added a 60 second up delay after the NAS in the start order, and the Pi as second DNS covered the gap anyway.

Kuma raised a short alert for the DNS monitors that cleared by itself.

summary: Wrote IPv6 firewall rules for the Docker VMs after finding that published container ports were reachable from the internet through the global address.
body:
A scan from outside showed something I did not like. Port 8096 of Jellyfin answered over the global IPv6 address of its VM. With IPv4 the router's NAT hides this, but IPv6 has no NAT and the router's firewall allowed inbound traffic for that prefix.

I first fixed the router's rule to block inbound new connections to the LAN prefix by default. That is the main fix. The router uses a stateful firewall, so replies to outgoing traffic continued.

As a second layer I added nftables rules on the Docker VMs through Ansible. They accept established traffic, ICMPv6 which IPv6 needs, SSH from the LAN and ULA, and the service ports from the LAN only. Everything else is dropped on the global address.

Docker adds its own rules and I took care they do not conflict. I put my rules in the input chain, and Docker's published ports go through forward, so I also restricted the port binding in compose to the LAN address where it was easy. I ran the outside scan again and all ports were closed. Local access, including the Caddy proxy, worked as before.

summary: Looked at IPv6 on the network: the provider hands out a /56 prefix, the router distributes a /64, and the Pi-hole VM lacks a stable address.
body:
Started the IPv6 topic. The provider delegates a /56 prefix. The router uses one /64 for the LAN and announces it with router advertisements. All clients already have addresses.

Problem: the prefix can change after a reconnect. I therefore want ULA addresses for internal use as well. I chose an fd prefix from a random generator and planned a static ULA for the DNS servers and the Proxmox host.

Checked what already works: ping6 to the router and to the NAS works. The Pi-hole VM has only a SLAAC privacy address, which changes. I noted it. Next: static ULA on the DNS servers, AAAA local records, and checking that Caddy listens on IPv6.

summary: Checked the IPv6 changes after a week: no problems seen in Kuma, and the one Android phone still ignores the IPv6 DNS server, which is accepted.
body:
A week after the IPv6 work I looked at the logs to see whether anything had gone wrong. Kuma showed no outages for the new IPv6 DNS monitors. The router's prefix did not change in that time, so the ULA address was not yet tested by a real renumbering.

The Pi-hole query log showed about 22 percent of the queries coming in over IPv6. That means the clients use it. The Android phone still sends all its queries over IPv4, as I expected.

The firewall rules on the VMs dropped a few hundred packets from outside, mostly scanners, and nothing from the LAN. I looked for ICMPv6 problems and found none. I decided no more changes were needed for now.

summary: Looked into a Caddy certificate renewal that failed with a rate-limit error and found that two Caddy instances were requesting certificates for the same names.
body:
Kuma's certificate-expiry monitor warned that one of the certificates had only 12 days left. That should not happen, as renewals start at 30 days. I looked at the Caddy log on the proxy VM.

The log showed repeated errors from the ACME server about too many failed validations. The renewal tried every hour and failed with a DNS challenge error each time. So the rate limit was a result and not the cause.

The DNS challenge writes a TXT record through the DNS provider's API. I checked the API token and it was valid. Then I noticed that a second Caddy container had been left running on the test VM from an earlier experiment, with the same domain names and its own copy of the config.

The two instances overwrote each other's TXT records, so validation failed for both. I stopped and removed the test container and its volume. Then I waited for the rate limit to expire, as the error message said a retry was allowed after about one hour.

After that the renewal on the real Caddy worked on the next try, and the certificate showed 89 days left. I added a check to the Ansible play that makes sure no Caddy container exists on any VM except the proxy one. I also wrote the cause into the notes.

summary: Added a Kuma check on the certificate age for each public name and a rule in the Ansible docs that experiments must use a staging ACME URL.
body:
Following the failed renewal of earlier today, I wanted two safeguards. The first is a check that warns earlier and for every name. Before, only one certificate had an expiry monitor.

I created a Kuma monitor of type HTTP with the certificate expiry notice turned on for each of the six names. The warning limit is 21 days. Because Caddy renews at 30 days, an alert at 21 means a renewal has failed for more than a week, and that is a real problem.

The second safeguard is for experiments. The test Caddy container had used the production ACME endpoint, which is how it reached the rate limit. I changed the Caddy template in Ansible so that a variable acme_staging can be set. If true, the global options use the staging URL.

The test VM group now sets this variable to true. I deployed to a test VM and Caddy took a staging certificate, which browsers reject, as expected. The production proxy kept its normal settings and nothing was reloaded there.

I wrote a short note in docs about this and about the earlier cause. The note says to check docker ps on all VMs when a renewal fails. After the run, Kuma showed all six monitors green.

summary: Reviewed the whole Ansible setup after the move: found three drifted settings on the VMs, removed the old update script's duplicate pull logic, and listed what is not yet managed.
body:
Ran the full playbook in check mode against every host to see how much drift exists after the move. Three items showed up: a different sysctl value on the Jellyfin VM, a missing cron entry for log cleanup on the monitoring VM, and an old docker daemon.json on the Pi.

I fixed each one in the roles, not on the hosts. The sysctl value turned out to be set by hand months ago for a Samba test and no longer needed, so I dropped it.

The update script still pulls images by itself. Now that image versions are pinned in the vars file, the script should only be a thin wrapper around the playbook. I changed it to call ansible-playbook with the docker tag, and removed 60 lines of pull logic. The failure reporting to Kuma stays.

Not yet managed: the Proxmox host's network config, the NAS settings, and the router. I put them in a list in the runbook with notes on how each is exported or documented.

A full real run took 7 minutes and changed only the three items. I will repeat the check run weekly with a timer and a Kuma push so drift shows up as an alert.

summary: Started the Proxmox upgrade planning: read the release notes of the next major version, listed the guests and their dependencies, and decided on a test on a spare machine first.
body:
The Proxmox host runs a version that will soon lose security updates, so I started planning the move to the next major version. I read the upgrade guide and the release notes. The guide has a script named pve7to8 style, a checker that reports problems before the upgrade, and I ran the matching one on the host.

The checker gave two warnings and no failures. One was about a systemd-boot package that is not needed on this ZFS-less setup. The other was a note that LXC containers with old cgroup settings may need changes.

I listed all guests: five VMs and two LXC containers. The WireGuard container is the one with a special setup, since it uses a tun device. I checked its config for the cgroup lines and found one older line that needs the new syntax.

I decided against upgrading the real host first. There is a spare laptop that could run a fresh install of the old version, restore a few vzdump backups and then upgrade. That tests the steps and shows how long the upgrade takes.

I also noted the things to do before the real day. Take a fresh vzdump of all guests, copy the /etc/pve folder, and tell the user that DNS goes down for a while, since the Pi will carry it. A date for the work has not been set. The first step is the laptop install, which the user will do on the weekend.

summary: Ran the upgrade on the spare laptop with restored backups: it took 32 minutes, and the WireGuard container needed the cgroup line changed to start.
body:
The user had installed the old Proxmox version on the spare laptop, so I could test the upgrade path. I restored three vzdump backups to it: the Pi-hole VM, a Docker VM and the WireGuard container. That gave a realistic base without waiting for all guests.

I followed the upgrade guide step by step: updated to the last point release, ran the checker, changed the apt sources to the new release, and ran apt dist-upgrade. The download took 9 minutes and the install 17. The reboot added another 4 minutes, so the total was about 32.

After the reboot, the VMs started without trouble. The WireGuard container did not start, and the log said an invalid key in the config. It was the old cgroup device line that I had found in the planning. I replaced it with the cgroup2 form and the container started.

Inside it, the tun device worked and wg show listed the interface. I also tested the peers from the laptop's LAN side with the path-test script, and all five paths passed.

I looked at the web interface for deprecated settings. There was a notice that one storage definition used an old option, which I removed. The backup job definitions were kept as they were.

I wrote the steps with the actual times into the runbook, including the container fix. The real upgrade can follow the same list. The remaining question is the right moment, as the family uses Jellyfin in the evening.

summary: A Jellyfin update test: tried the newest release on a clone VM first, found that the hardware transcoding failed with a changed device permission, and held back the real upgrade.
body:
A new Jellyfin release came out and I wanted to test it before touching the live VM. I cloned the VM in Proxmox, changed the image tag on the clone only, and started it with a different IP.

The library loaded and direct play worked. But the transcode test of a high-bitrate file failed. The log said that ffmpeg could not open /dev/dri/renderD128 with a permission error. In the new image the user inside runs with a different group id.

I checked the render group id on the VM: 104. The container needed group_add with that number. I added it as a variable in the role, tried again on the clone, and the transcode worked, using about 12% CPU instead of 90%.

I did not upgrade the live VM yet. I want to read the release notes about a database migration first, which may not be reversible. A restic snapshot of the live data is the fallback.

Summary of the state: the role has a render group variable, the clone VM is still there, and the live version is unchanged. I will delete the clone after the real upgrade.

summary: Upgraded the real Proxmox host to the next major version in a morning window, with all guests backed up first; the host was down for 38 minutes and everything came back.
body:
Today was the real upgrade, using the list tested on the laptop. I started by taking fresh vzdump backups of all seven guests, which took 21 minutes, and copying /etc/pve and the network config to the NAS. I then checked that the restic job had finished and that the NAS held the copies.

I told the user that Jellyfin and Home Assistant would be off for about 45 minutes. Before shutting down guests I confirmed the Raspberry Pi Pi-hole was answering, since it would carry DNS. The test lookup returned local names correctly.

I ran the checker once more on the real host. It gave the same two warnings as before and no failure. Then I changed the apt sources and ran the dist-upgrade over SSH inside a tmux session, to survive a lost connection.

The download and install took 24 minutes, a little slower than on the laptop because of more packages. During the install a prompt asked about the sshd config being changed. I kept the local version, as the laptop test had taught me to do. The reboot took 5 minutes, since the host does a longer memory check.

After the host was up, the guests with onboot set started in the order configured, with the delay for Pi-hole added earlier. The WireGuard container had the cgroup fix applied before the upgrade, so it started cleanly. I checked each service: Jellyfin played a video, Home Assistant showed its dashboard, and Caddy served all names.

The NUT server also kept working, and upsc showed the UPS status. One thing that broke was the Proxmox backup storage entry, with a changed option name for the NAS share. I fixed it in the storage config and a test vzdump of one guest succeeded.

Total host downtime was 38 minutes. I updated the runbook with the real times and the storage fix. I will check the logs again tomorrow and the next backup run.

summary: Checked the logs after the Proxmox upgrade and found the nightly vzdump had run fine, but the Ansible Proxmox play failed because a module option had been renamed.
body:
The morning after the upgrade I went through the logs. The nightly vzdump for the critical guests took 15 minutes as before and finished before the restic job. Both Kuma push monitors for the backups were green.

I also looked at the kernel log and the journal of the host for errors after the boot. There were no new warnings except one about a deprecated cgroup setting, which comes from an LXC container config. I noted it as harmless but to be cleaned later.

Then I ran the Ansible play for the Proxmox host with --check to see whether the setup was still in line. The play failed at a task that sets VM options, with an error that an unsupported parameter was given. The upgraded API had renamed the option for the CPU flags.

I looked at the module documentation for the installed collection version. The collection was old, and an update fixed the parameter handling. I updated the version in requirements.yml and ran ansible-galaxy to install it. After that the check passed with no changes.

I ran the real play as well and nothing changed on the host. That shows that the manual fixes made yesterday, like the storage option, matched the declared state. I added the storage change to the vars file anyway, since it had only been done by hand.

The remaining item is to remove the deprecated cgroup line in the second LXC container. I will do this with the next small change.

summary: Replaced the manual WireGuard peer list with data in the vars file and a template, and checked each existing peer kept its key and address after deployment.
body:
The WireGuard config on the LXC was still edited by hand. I moved the peers into a list in the vars file with name, public key and allowed address, and wrote a template for wg0.conf. Private keys stay in the vault.

The check run showed only whitespace differences. I applied it and used wg syncconf instead of a restart so existing sessions stay. Handshakes from the phone and the laptop continued without drop.

I ran the path test script from earlier, and all paths passed, including the duplicate address check, which now fails the template build if two peers share an address.

summary: Cleaned up the last deprecated cgroup setting in the second LXC container and checked that the Proxmox journal has no warnings left after the upgrade.
body:
This was the small clean-up left over from the Proxmox upgrade. The journal had one warning about a cgroup device setting in an LXC container config. It belonged to the Samba test container, which is rarely used.

I looked at the config file under /etc/pve/lxc and found an old lxc.cgroup.devices.allow line that was not needed anymore. The container does not use any special device. I removed the line and restarted the container.

It came up normally and the Samba share could be mounted from the laptop. I also checked that the container still got its restic snapshot in the stale-host report, as that had caught it once before.

Then I read the journal for the host since the last boot with journalctl -p warning. It showed nothing that was new, only the known message about the UPS driver reconnecting once at boot. I accepted that one.

The change is in the Ansible role for LXC containers, so the line cannot return. A final run of the play showed no differences. This closes the upgrade work.

summary: Wrote a restic restore drill script that restores a random sample of files from the NAS repository and compares checksums, so restore tests no longer depend on memory.
body:
The restore test from long ago was a manual list of steps, and after the Proxmox upgrade I wanted something repeatable. The new script, scripts/restore-drill.sh, picks 40 random files from the latest snapshot with restic ls, restores them into a temp directory and compares sha256 sums against the live files.

Files changed since the snapshot are expected to differ, so the script skips anything with a newer mtime than the snapshot time. On the first run 40 files were checked and 3 were skipped for that reason, with no mismatches.

The script exits non-zero on any mismatch and prints the snapshot id. It also removes the temp directory on exit, using the same trap pattern as the prune script. Next step is to run it weekly from a systemd timer and send the result to a Kuma push monitor.
