One detail: the restore of a 2 GB video file made the run take 9 minutes, so I added a size limit of 200 MB for the sample. With the limit the whole drill takes about 50 seconds.

summary: Wrote the Ansible play for the Proxmox module option renamed in the upgrade, and the play now runs clean in check mode and in a real run against the host.
body:
The Proxmox play had failed since the host upgrade because the module option for the container features had been renamed in the newer collection. I started by reading the changelog of the collection and found that the old option was removed, not just deprecated. The new name takes a list instead of a comma separated string.

I changed the task in roles/proxmox_guests/tasks/main.yml and the vars file for the two LXC containers. Then I ran the play with --check --diff and it reported two changes that I did not expect. Both were the features line of the WireGuard container, where the nesting flag was written in a different order than Proxmox stores it.

I sorted the list in the vars file so the order matches what Proxmox reports. After that the check run showed zero changes, which is what I wanted for an idempotent play. I also pinned the collection version in requirements.yml, because the missing pin was why the rename arrived unnoticed with the upgrade.

The real run took 41 seconds and changed nothing on the host. I then looked at the Pi-hole LXC and the WireGuard container to confirm they still started after a restart, and both did. The Proxmox journal had no new warnings during the run.

One more thing I found: the play for the vzdump schedule used the same renamed option in a second place, in a task that is skipped by default. I fixed it too and ran that task once with its tag, and it passed. I added a line to the runbook that says the collection must be upgraded in a test run before each Proxmox upgrade. What is left is a small CI-like script that runs ansible-lint and a check-mode run before a commit, which I want to do next week.

summary: Looked into why the Jellyfin VM's nightly vzdump takes twice as long as the other guests and found the media library mount was being read into the backup.
body:
The nightly vzdump log showed the Jellyfin VM taking 41 minutes while the others take 5 to 15. I checked the VM config on Proxmox and found a second virtual disk of 300 GB that holds the transcode cache and a copy of thumbnails, plus the metadata folder.

The media itself is mounted from the NAS over NFS inside the VM, so that was not the cause. The transcode cache was: it held 180 GB of old temporary segments that were never cleaned up.

I set the cache cleanup in Jellyfin to remove files older than one day and deleted the old segments by hand. Then I marked the cache disk with backup=0 in the VM config, and kept the metadata on the root disk, which is backed up.

The next vzdump run took 9 minutes. I will verify after a few nights that the cache does not fill up again, and that the restore test still works for this VM since the cache is now excluded.

summary: Planned a replacement for the aging disk that shows growing SMART reallocated sectors in the NAS, with the options priced and a rebuild order chosen.
body:
The weekly SMART report from the NAS showed disk 3 with 24 reallocated sectors, up from 8 a month ago. The volume is still healthy, but the trend is clear.

I listed what the NAS currently has: four disks in SHR with one disk of redundancy, three of them of the same age. Because all were bought together, I considered replacing more than one.

Options I looked at:
- replace only disk 3 now, keep a spare on the shelf
- replace disk 3 and the oldest other disk in two steps
- buy a larger disk and use the swap to grow the volume later

The third option only gives more space if all disks are replaced, which is too costly now. I chose the first, plus buying one extra disk of the same size as a cold spare.

Before touching anything I checked that the last restic snapshot to the cloud bucket was complete and that the restore drill had passed that week. It had, with 40 files and no mismatch.

The plan for the swap: run a full extended SMART test on the other disks first, then pause the nightly backup, replace disk 3 in the bay, and let the repair run. A repair of this size should take about a day. I wrote this into docs/runbook-disk.md with the commands to check the repair state over SSH, and set a reminder to do it on a quiet weekend morning.

summary: Added a check-mode and lint script that runs before each Ansible commit, after the renamed option showed that module changes were only found when the real play ran.
body:
After the renamed Proxmox option, I wanted a cheap way to find such breaks before a real run. I wrote scripts/precheck.sh, which runs ansible-lint on the roles and then a full ansible-playbook run in check mode with --diff against all hosts. The script stops at the first failure and prints which play it was.

The first run of ansible-lint gave 23 findings. Most were style issues like missing task names and the use of command where a module exists. I fixed 17 of them in the same session, and the rest are in a list in the file TODO-lint.md because they need a closer look at each task.

The check-mode run showed one problem I had not seen before. The Docker role has a task that reads the installed Compose version with a shell command, and in check mode it does not run, so the next task failed on an undefined variable. I added check_mode: false to that read-only task, which is safe because it changes nothing.

With that fix the whole run took 3 minutes and 10 seconds and ended with no changes and no failures. I linked the script as a git pre-commit hook, but made it optional through a variable, because the check run needs SSH access to the hosts and cannot run when I am away from home. The hook is skipped with a clear message in that case.

Next step is to fix the remaining lint findings one by one, starting with the ones in the backup role.

summary: Fixed the remaining lint findings in the backup and DNS roles, and found that one restic task was not idempotent and always showed a change in check mode.
body:
This session went through the lint list from earlier today, starting with the backup role because it matters most. There were 6 findings left there. Four were naming and quoting issues that I fixed quickly.

The fifth was more interesting. The task that installs the restic cron entry used a shell command with echo and a redirect, so Ansible reported a change on every run. I replaced it with the cron module and a named job. After that the check run showed no change for the backup role.

The sixth finding was a file mode written as 644 without the leading zero, which Ansible reads as a decimal number. That meant the password file for the repository was getting a wrong mode on the NAS. I checked on the host with ls -l and the file had mode 1204, which is odd but not readable by others. I corrected the mode to 0600 in the role and it applied on the next run.

Then I went to the DNS roles. The Pi-hole role had 4 findings, and all were about handlers that were named differently from what the tasks notified. One handler was never called, which means a config change to Unbound did not restart it. I fixed the name and tested by changing a harmless setting, and the restart happened this time.

I ran the whole precheck script again and it passed with no lint findings and no changes in check mode. I deleted TODO-lint.md and wrote the file mode lesson into the runbook. Remaining work is to test the Unbound restart through a real run tomorrow morning when DNS use is low.

summary: Wiped the failed disk, wrote down the disk inventory with purchase age and serials, and added a Kuma check for degraded NAS volume state through the DSM API.
body:
Two small follow-ups from the disk swap. First I wiped the failed disk with a single-pass zero write on the laptop through a USB adapter. It took about 7 hours for the whole disk and no write errors appeared, so the drive itself is not completely dead, but I will not reuse it.

Second, I wrote docs/disks.md with each disk in the NAS, the Proxmox host and the Pi: model, size, serial, age in months, and where its spare is. The three remaining NAS disks are now old enough that I put a note to review them in four months.

Third, I wanted a check that tells me about a degraded volume before the weekly report does. Mail on SMART was already added, but a volume can be degraded without a mail if a disk is dropped from the array.

I wrote a small script, scripts/check-nas-volume.sh, that logs in to the DSM API with a read-only user, reads the volume status and pushes up or down to a Kuma push monitor. The API call is:

GET /webapi/entry.cgi?api=SYNO.Storage.CGI.Storage&method=load_info&version=1

The script treats any status other than normal as down. To test, I could not degrade the volume, so I changed the expected value temporarily to 'degraded' and saw the monitor go red within a minute, then restored it.

It runs from a timer every 10 minutes through Ansible. The read-only user has no shell access and the password is in the vault. I also checked that a wrong password makes the monitor go down, not stay green, because the script exits non-zero on a failed login.

summary: The backup job started taking 2.5 hours instead of 40 minutes; the cause was a new Home Assistant database file that changes completely every night.
body:
Kuma showed the nightly backup duration creeping up over the week, and last night it reached 2.5 hours. I looked at the restic summary lines. The new data per run had grown from about 300 MB to 4 GB.

Using restic diff between two snapshots I saw that home-assistant_v2.db was listed as modified, with the full size of 3.8 GB. The recorder database is a live SQLite file, and the backup of the live file picks up all changed pages, which with the purge job at night rewrites much of it.

I checked the recorder settings and found that purge_keep_days had been raised to 30 during the last upgrade work. Before that it was 10. The longer history makes the file bigger and the nightly purge rewrites it.

I did two things. I set the recorder to keep 10 days again and excluded the database from the restic backup of that VM. Excluded in a way that matters, though: the configuration and the snapshot backup of Home Assistant itself stay included, and the long-term statistics are small.

The next night the backup took 38 minutes and the new data was 280 MB. I will check the history graphs in Home Assistant to see that nobody misses the older data.

summary: Wrote a proper SQLite-safe backup step for Home Assistant: a pre-backup hook makes a consistent copy with the sqlite3 backup command, which restic then includes instead of the live file.
body:
After the exclusion of the live recorder database last week, I wanted a consistent copy back in the backup, since a restore of Home Assistant without history is acceptable but one with a clean copy is better, and small enough.

First I measured. With purge_keep_days at 10 the database is 1.1 GB, which compresses to roughly 400 MB in restic. That is acceptable for a nightly copy as long as it does not change in every chunk.

The pre-backup hook in the backup script now runs:

sqlite3 /config/home-assistant_v2.db ".backup '/backup-staging/ha.db'"

This uses the online backup API of SQLite, so it is consistent even while Home Assistant writes. The staging directory is inside the restic include list, and the live file stays excluded.

The first run took 41 seconds for the copy. The restic step then added 390 MB, as predicted. On the second night restic added only 210 MB, because deduplication works for parts that did not change.

I also tested the restore. I restored the staged copy into a throwaway VM clone of Home Assistant and started it. It loaded the history graph without a repair message, and the entity count matched.

There was one problem on the first attempt: the sqlite3 binary is not in the Home Assistant container, and the hook ran on the VM host side. I installed sqlite3 on the VM through Ansible and made the hook use the path on the bind mount.

The hook has a trap that removes the staging copy on exit, as in the prune script, and it fails the backup if the sqlite3 command fails, so a broken copy is never silently skipped.

I updated the runbook with the restore steps for the database. The nightly duration is now 52 minutes in total, which is acceptable. The total repository growth over three nights was 1.1 GB, so I will watch the prune results next week.

summary: Investigated why Pi-hole answered slowly after midnight and traced it to the gravity list update blocking the DNS process for about 40 seconds; moved it and made the second Pi-hole cover the gap.
body:
Several people at home complained that the web was slow around midnight. I looked at the Pi-hole query log and the Kuma DNS check history and found a pattern: the DNS check showed 2 to 5 second responses for a short time every night.

The gravity update cron job runs at that time on the main Pi-hole VM. During its run, pihole-FTL reloads the lists, and in the log I saw 'Reloading DNS cache' followed by a 38 second period with slow queries.

I first checked the machine for lack of memory. It has 1 GB, and during gravity the used memory peaked at 870 MB, with a little swap. That explained the slowness but not the whole delay, so I looked at the list count. It had grown to 1.4 million domains because I added two lists last winter.

Options I considered:
- remove the biggest list, which would reduce blocking
- give the VM 2 GB of memory
- stagger the gravity update between the two Pi-holes

I did the second and third. The VM now has 2 GB, and the update on the main one runs at 03:10 while the Pi on the second runs at 04:10, so one always answers fast.

To test, I started gravity by hand on the main Pi-hole while running dig in a loop against both servers from a laptop:

for i in $(seq 60); do dig +time=2 example.org @pi-hole-1 | grep 'Query time'; sleep 1; done

Before the memory change the slow replies lasted 38 seconds. After it, the longest reply was 240 ms and the swap was not touched.

I also changed the clients' DNS order in the DHCP options, so the Pi is listed second. That was already so, but I verified it with a lease renewal on two devices.

The Ansible role for Pi-hole now has the cron time as a variable per host, and the memory change is in the Proxmox play. I will look at the DNS check history in a week to see that the nightly bumps are gone.

summary: Checked the DNS timings a week after the gravity change: no slow replies in the Kuma history, and the main Pi-hole's memory use stays below 1.2 GB during updates.
body:
I reviewed the Kuma DNS check history for the last seven days. All checks stayed under 150 ms, and there were no spikes at the former midnight window, nor at the new 03:10 or 04:10 times.

On the main Pi-hole VM I looked at the memory during the gravity run again. It peaked at 1.15 GB with the 2 GB of memory, so there is room, and swap was not used.

I also looked at the Pi's second Pi-hole during its own run. It has 1 GB and showed a peak of 790 MB. That is tight, but the Pi has no swap trouble and the lists are the same size. I decided to leave it as is, since the main one is first in the DHCP order and the Pi is the fallback.

One more thing I checked: both Pi-holes have the same list set. A quick compare of the adlists tables with sqlite3 showed one difference, a list that I had only added on the main one. I added it to the Pi through the Ansible variable, so the two are in line now.

Nothing else to do on this topic. The timing variable is documented in the role README.

Next I plan to look at the Caddy logs, because they have grown to a size that makes the log rotation slow.

summary: Fixed Caddy log growth by setting a roll size and keep count in the Caddyfile, after the access log reached 6 GB on the proxy VM.
body:
The proxy VM's disk was at 78 percent, and du showed that the Caddy access log was 6 GB. The Caddyfile had a log block with an output file but no roll settings, and the host's logrotate did not cover that path.

I added roll_size 100MiB, roll_keep 5 and roll_keep_for 168h to the log output in the Caddyfile template. Then I deployed it with Ansible and reloaded Caddy with caddy reload, which kept the open connections.

The old 6 GB file was compressed once for the case that I need it, then removed after a check that no incident was open. Disk use fell to 31 percent. The log now rolls roughly every two days at the normal traffic level, and the next check will be in a week.

summary: Planned the upgrade of Docker on the three VMs after finding that the Compose plugin versions differ between them, and decided to align them first through Ansible.
body:
While reading the Ansible docs for the container hosts I noticed that docker compose version gave three different results on the three Docker VMs. Two used the plugin from the Docker apt repository, and one still had the old standalone docker-compose 1.29 binary that I once installed by hand.

I listed the facts:
- the media VM: plugin 2.x, engine from the Docker repository
- the services VM: plugin 2.x, same engine
- the old test VM: standalone binary, engine from the Debian repository

The update script for all containers calls docker compose, so it works on the first two and falls back to the old binary on the third. That explains why one of its logs always had a deprecation warning.

The plan has three steps. First, the Ansible docker role installs the repository, the engine and the compose plugin on all hosts, with the versions pinned in the vars file. Second, I test the role on a clone of the old test VM. Third, I run it on the real VMs one at a time, outside the backup window.

I also checked what the pinned versions would be. The engine version on the two good VMs is the same, so I take that one. Pinning means that an apt upgrade does not restart all containers by surprise, which happened once after an unattended upgrade.

I wrote the plan into docs/docker-upgrade.md. No change was made on the real hosts today. The clone test is next.

summary: Tested the new Docker role on a clone of the old test VM: the standalone compose binary was removed cleanly and the three test containers came back after a restart.
body:
I cloned the old test VM in Proxmox with a full clone and booted it on an isolated bridge so that it could not answer on the real addresses.

Then I ran the docker role in check mode first. It showed that it would add the repository key, replace docker.io with docker-ce, install the compose plugin and delete /usr/local/bin/docker-compose. That matches the plan.

The real run took 3 minutes 20 seconds. The package swap restarted the Docker daemon, and the three test containers came back by themselves because they have restart: unless-stopped. I checked with docker ps and docker compose ls, both of which worked with the plugin.

One problem appeared. The old binary had written a project name in the form of the directory name with underscores, while the plugin uses hyphens for new containers. For the existing containers this made no difference, but a docker compose up created a second network with the new name. I added a COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME entry in the .env file of that stack to keep the old name.

The update script ran against the clone without the deprecation warning. I removed the clone afterwards.

The real run on the services VM comes next. Before that I take a vzdump snapshot of it and check that the last restic run was good.

summary: Rolled out the Docker role to the services VM and the media VM one at a time; both took under 4 minutes, and Jellyfin's transcoding still worked after the engine restart.
body:
I did the real rollout today, after the backup window had closed. The order was the services VM first, then the media VM, because Jellyfin is used more in the evenings and I wanted the first run to be on the less visible host.

Before each run I took a vzdump snapshot of the VM and checked the last restic result in Kuma. Then I ran the play with --limit for one host.

On the services VM the play changed only the pinning. The engine and plugin versions were already the same, so only the apt hold marks were set. No restart happened. I checked with apt-mark showhold and saw the three packages.

The media VM was the same case, and no restart was needed either. That left one worry: the Jellyfin hardware transcoding, which had broken earlier after a device permission change. Since no restart happened, it was not expected to break, but I tested it anyway by playing a high bitrate film on a phone with a lower quality setting. The Jellyfin dashboard showed the transcode as hardware and the CPU stayed under 15 percent.

Then I ran the whole docker role on all three hosts again to check idempotence. The result was zero changed tasks for all hosts.

I also tried the update script once by hand. It pulled two images and recreated one container on each VM. The log had no warning anymore.

I added a line to the docs that the apt hold must be released with the playbook, not by hand, when the engine version is moved on. A version bump now means changing the vars file and running the play in a window.

The test VM is now also in line. All three hosts show the same compose version in the monthly drift check that I wrote after the Ansible review, and that check passed on all three. Nothing is left open on this topic except to watch the next unattended-upgrade run for any attempt to touch the held packages.

summary: Checked that the first unattended-upgrade run after the Docker pinning left the held packages alone and that all containers kept running.
body:
The unattended-upgrades log on each Docker VM showed a run during the night. On all three it listed the Docker packages under 'Packages that are kept back', so the hold works.

Other packages were upgraded normally, among them a kernel update on the services VM. The reboot window I set earlier did its job: the VM rebooted at 04:30, after the backup had ended at 03:50, and the containers all came back with the right state.

I looked at uptime in Kuma to check that nothing was missed. Each service had one short gap of about 70 seconds, at the reboot. That is the same as before.

I also verified that the docker role stays idempotent after the reboot by running it in check mode. It showed no changes.

This topic is done. A bump to a newer engine will be a deliberate step in the vars file. I have added a reminder to look at the Docker release notes every quarter so the pinned version does not get too old.

summary: Diagnosed Home Assistant losing its connection to the Zigbee coordinator every few days; the USB device path changed after a host reboot and the passthrough used an unstable name.
body:
For two weeks Home Assistant had shown all Zigbee devices as unavailable now and then, and a restart of the integration fixed it. Last night it happened again, so I looked at it properly.

In the Home Assistant log I found 'Failed to connect to /dev/ttyUSB0' and an earlier line from the host's kernel log through SSH: the USB serial device had disconnected and come back as ttyUSB1. The VM got the device by a passthrough of the host's USB port, configured in Proxmox by vendor and product id, and the Zigbee config in Home Assistant pointed at /dev/ttyUSB0.

So two things were unstable:
- the device node name inside the VM, which depends on enumeration order
- the reconnect, since the USB stick resets when the host is busy

I first checked the power. The stick sits on a USB 3 port next to the NAS link cable, and USB 3 ports can make noise in the 2.4 GHz band. The kernel log showed no over-current message, so power was not the issue, but I still moved the stick to a short extension cable on a USB 2 port, which is the usual advice for these dongles.

For the name, I looked in /dev/serial/by-id/ inside the VM and found a stable path with the stick's serial number in it. I changed the Zigbee integration to use that path instead of ttyUSB0.

I then tested a simulated drop. On the Proxmox host I ran qm monitor and removed and re-added the USB device with device_del and device_add. The device came back as ttyUSB1 inside the VM, and because the by-id path was used, the integration reconnected by itself in about 20 seconds. Before the change the same test needed a manual reload.

The Ansible play for the VM only had the passthrough line, so I added the by-id path as a variable in the Home Assistant configuration template. I checked that all 23 Zigbee devices were back as available after the test, and that the automations for the lights ran.

Next I will watch the log for a week. If the disconnects continue even with the extension cable, the stick or the firmware is the cause, and I would look at the coordinator firmware version. I noted this in the runbook under Home Assistant troubleshooting.

summary: A week after moving the Zigbee stick to a USB 2 extension, no disconnects were logged and all devices stayed available, so the issue is closed.
body:
I searched the Home Assistant log and the Proxmox host kernel log for the last seven days. There was no 'Failed to connect' message and no USB disconnect line.

The Zigbee integration showed all 23 devices as available the whole time. In the history graph of the availability sensor I made earlier, no gap appeared.

I also checked the link quality values of the devices. Several battery sensors improved a little, for example the bathroom sensor went from 70 to 95 LQI. That fits the idea that the USB 3 port had added radio noise.

I do not know which of the two changes fixed the disconnects, since I made the by-id change and the move together. The by-id path makes the reconnect safe in any case, and I did not want to move the stick back to test.

The coordinator firmware is also still an old one. I read the release notes of the newer version and the changes concern router devices and not the coordinator, so I will leave it alone for now.

I deleted the temporary notes from the runbook and wrote the final version: use the by-id path, keep the stick on a USB 2 port with an extension cable, and the device_del and device_add test to check the reconnect.

The topic is closed.

summary: Added a Kuma monitor for WireGuard that checks the handshake age of the phone peer, after a silent break of the tunnel that went unnoticed for three days.
body:
A family phone had no VPN access for three days before anyone said so. The tunnel had no alert because the Kuma check on the WireGuard container only tested that the UDP port answers, and that is true even when a peer does not connect.

I wanted a check on the peers. On the WireGuard LXC container, wg show wg0 latest-handshakes prints a timestamp for each peer. A peer which is in use has a handshake within a few minutes, but a phone that sleeps may have none for hours, so a rule for all peers would give false alarms.

So I decided to monitor only the two peers that should be always connected: the phone of the user and the laptop that is mostly on. For these I set a limit of 30 minutes. The family phones are listed in the vars file with a flag monitor: false.

The script scripts/check-wg-peers.sh reads the vars file through a small generated list, which Ansible writes to /etc/wireguard/monitored-peers, and calls wg show. It pushes up if all monitored peers had a handshake in the last 30 minutes, and down with the name of the peer in the message if not.

I tested it by switching the phone to airplane mode for 35 minutes. The monitor turned red after the limit with the message 'phone-user: 2140s'. After switching it on again, the monitor was green within a minute because the phone made a handshake at once.

The timer runs every 5 minutes. I also documented why the family phones are not monitored, so that nobody adds them by mistake.

For the phone that broke, the cause was a changed key after a reinstall of the app, and I added the new public key to the vars file and deployed it. It connected at once.

summary: Replaced the Synology's built-in schedule for snapshots with an Ansible-managed one and verified the retention, after finding that old snapshots filled 1.8 TB of the volume.
body:
The NAS volume was at 86 percent, which is higher than my own limit of 80, and I could not explain it from the shares. Storage Manager showed that the shares used 5.1 TB and the volume 6.9 TB, so 1.8 TB went to something else. That was the Btrfs snapshots from the snapshot replication schedule I set up long ago.

The schedule took a snapshot every hour and kept 400 of them for the main share. The retention was set by count only, not by age, so frequent changes to big files, like the Jellyfin metadata, kept growing the snapshot space.

Before changing anything I thought about what the snapshots are for. They protect against deletion by mistake, for which a few days of hourly states and a few weeks of daily states are enough. The restic backups cover the long term.

The new policy is:
- hourly for 48 hours
- daily for 30 days
- weekly for 8 weeks

The Synology has a command line tool, synosnapshot, but the retention settings live in the DSM configuration, and I did not want to edit its database by hand. So I used the DSM web API through the same read-only pattern as the volume check, only with an admin account kept in the vault, to set the schedule. The Ansible role for it uses the uri module with a login, the call, and a logout.

One step I did slowly: deleting the old snapshots. I removed them by hand in batches of 50 and watched the volume, since a mass delete on Btrfs can cause high load. After the first 100 the load average on the NAS was 6, which is high for it, so I paused for an hour between batches.

The result after two days: volume use went down from 86 to 71 percent, and 410 snapshots turned into 77. The Jellyfin streaming did not stutter, as far as the evening test showed.

I also added a Kuma check on volume use, using the same API script as the degraded check, with a warning at 80 percent. The test run raised the warning when I set the limit to 70 temporarily.

The runbook has the new policy and the reason for each number. Next I need to check that a restore of a deleted file from a snapshot still works, which I will do on a test share.

summary: Tested restoring a deleted file from the new snapshot schedule on a test share; all three retention levels worked, and the restore took seconds.
body:
After the retention change, I wanted proof that the snapshots still give back deleted files. I created a test share with the same schedule as the main share, but with a faster clock for the test: I took manual snapshots instead of waiting.

I put three files on the share and took a snapshot each: one an hour old in the test, one a day old and one a week old, which I made by taking the snapshots and naming them with a prefix. Then I deleted all three files.

The restore from the snapshot browser in DSM worked for each. Over SSH I also looked at the hidden #snapshot directory on the volume and copied a file from there with cp, which took less than a second for a 40 MB file.

A second test concerned permissions. The main share has ACLs for the media group, and I wanted to know that a restored file keeps them. It did, when I restored through DSM, but the plain cp from the #snapshot directory made the file owned by root. That is useful to know for the runbook.

Then I checked that the retention really thins the snapshots. I ran the cleanup task for the schedule and counted: the test share had hourly snapshots for the last 48 hours only, as expected.

One point stayed open. The main share's oldest weekly snapshot is only a few days old yet, because the new schedule started after the cleanup. So the eight weeks will be complete in two months.

I deleted the test share. The runbook now says: restore through DSM to keep ACLs, use cp only when the owner is fixed afterwards with chown.

summary: Wrote a quarterly maintenance checklist from the incidents of the past months, with the checks already automated marked and the manual ones given a Kuma reminder.
body:
With all the fixes of the last months, many small recurring tasks are now scattered in the notes. I collected them into docs/quarterly.md so that nothing relies on memory.

First I went through the journal of the project and the commit history for the topics that created a regular duty. The list I found had 14 items. For each I decided whether it is already automated, whether it can be automated, or whether it needs a person.

Already automated and checked by Kuma:
- restic restore drill, weekly, both repositories
- NAS volume status and volume use
- certificate age for each public name
- WireGuard handshakes for the two monitored peers
- drift check of the Docker versions

Can be automated, not yet:
- the SMART error counts of the Proxmox host disks, which only go into the weekly mail
- the Pi-hole list compare between the two instances, which I did by hand once

Needs a person:
- reading Docker, Proxmox and Home Assistant release notes before bumping versions
- reviewing the disk inventory in docs/disks.md and the age of the three older NAS disks
- checking that the cold spare disk is still in its place and still of the right size
- testing the full rebuild order from the runbook on a spare machine once a year

For the manual items I made a Kuma push monitor of the type 'heartbeat' with a long interval of 100 days. I push to it by hand with curl when I finished the quarterly list, and if I forget, it turns red and sends a mail. It is a simple way of making a reminder that cannot be ignored.

I also did the first round at once, since it was cheap. The disk inventory was correct. The Pi-hole lists were equal, and the cold spare was on the shelf.

The SMART of the Proxmox disks showed no change in reallocated sectors since the last look. I added the two automatable items as tasks in the todo file of the repository, with a short note on how I would do each. The checklist file is in the Ansible docs folder, linked from the runbook.

summary: Ran the first quarterly checklist pass as a dry run and found two manual items that nobody had a reminder for: the UPS battery test and the cloud bucket cost check.
body:
After writing the checklist yesterday, I walked through it item by item against the live systems. Most automated checks showed green in Uptime Kuma, as expected.

Two manual items had no owner. The UPS self-test was never scheduled, and the cloud bucket bill had not been looked at since the restic setup. I added two Kuma push monitors that go red if nobody confirms them within 95 days.

The dry run also showed that the checklist said 'verify restore drill' without naming the script. I added the path of the restic drill script and the expected runtime of about 6 minutes. The checklist is committed to the repository under docs/.

Next step is to run the UPS self-test by hand once and record the battery runtime it reports.

summary: Ran the UPS battery self-test and found the runtime fell to about 9 minutes under load, too short for the 12 minute shutdown sequence, so the shutdown trigger now fires earlier.
body:
The self-test was the first manual item from the quarterly checklist. I ran it from the NUT client on the Raspberry Pi and read the reported runtime at the current load of about 85 W.

The UPS reported 9 minutes. The clean shutdown sequence, which stops the VMs, then Proxmox, then asks the NAS to power off, had been timed at 12 minutes during the earlier test. With the battery aged, that margin was gone.

I looked at the NUT config. The shutdown was triggered by the low battery flag only, which comes very late. I changed upsmon to start the shutdown when the battery charge drops below 60 percent or when the runtime drops below 14 minutes, whichever is first.

The change is in the Ansible role for NUT, not edited by hand on the Pi. I ran the role in check mode first and then for real. Then I simulated a power cut by pulling the plug for 90 seconds and watched the logs: upsmon logged the on-battery state, and the countdown started as expected, and I cancelled it by plugging the UPS back in.

Still open: a new battery costs about 40 euros, and I put that on the list for the next purchase round. I also added the measured runtime to the checklist so the trend is visible.

summary: Replaced the UPS battery and re-measured: runtime under the same load is now 31 minutes, so the earlier shutdown threshold stays but has a large margin.
body:
The new battery arrived and I swapped it with the server switched on, since the UPS allows hot swap. I then let it charge for a full night.

This morning I ran the self-test again from the Pi. The reported runtime at 85 W was 31 minutes, against 9 before. The NUT driver also reports the battery date, and I set it through upsrw so the age is right.

I kept the earlier threshold of 60 percent or 14 minutes. It costs nothing and covers a battery that ages again. The Kuma push monitor for the UPS test was confirmed.

I wrote the new runtime into the disk and hardware inventory file. The next test falls in the following quarter and a reminder is already set.

summary: Planned the IPv6 rollout for the LAN: chose to use the prefix from the ISP with SLAAC, keep static ULA addresses for servers, and decided what Pi-hole and Caddy need first.
body:
IPv6 has been on the list since the quarterly checklist, so I spent a session on the plan before touching any config. First I checked what the router hands out. The ISP delegates a /56 and the router advertises a /64 on the LAN, with SLAAC and no DHCPv6.

The main question was how to address the servers. The delegated prefix can change, so I do not want it in any config file. The plan is to add a ULA range, fd00 based, with static addresses for the Proxmox host, the NAS, the Pi, and the three VMs. Clients keep SLAAC with the global prefix for internet traffic.

I listed what depends on addresses. Pi-hole needs to listen on the IPv6 address and hand out an AAAA record for local names. Unbound needs the do-ip6 option set. Caddy binds to all interfaces already, but the router forwarding for ports 80 and 443 needs an IPv6 firewall rule, which works differently from NAT port forwarding.

I also noted the risks. Docker containers do not get IPv6 by default, and I decided not to change that for now, since only Caddy is reached from outside. WireGuard stays IPv4 only in the first step.

The order is: ULA on the hosts through Ansible, then Pi-hole and Unbound, then the AAAA records, and last the firewall rule for Caddy. Each step gets its own check in Kuma using an IPv6 ping monitor. Nothing was changed today, only the plan file docs/ipv6-plan.md was added.

summary: Added static ULA addresses to the Proxmox host and the three VMs through Ansible, and found that the NAS needs its address set in DSM by hand.
body:
Started the first step of the IPv6 plan in the evening. I added a vars entry for each host with its ULA address and wrote a small role that writes the address into the netplan file on the VMs and into /etc/network/interfaces on the Proxmox host.

Check mode showed the expected diffs. For the Proxmox host I was careful, because a mistake in the network file can lock me out. I kept a console session open on the host and used ifreload -a with a test copy of the file first.

The three VMs took the address without a reboot. I checked with ip -6 addr and pinged each from the others. All answered in under 1 ms. The Proxmox host also answered from the laptop.

The NAS was different. DSM does not read a file from Ansible for this, and I did not want to use the API for one address. I set it by hand in the network settings and wrote the value in the vars file with a comment that it is unmanaged.

The Raspberry Pi got its address too, but the Pi uses dhcpcd, so the role needed a second template. I added that branch and ran it. The Pi came back with the address after restarting the service.

One snag: the lint script complained about a long line in the template and a missing task name. I fixed both before committing.

Next is Pi-hole and Unbound with IPv6 listening.

summary: Enabled IPv6 listening in Pi-hole and Unbound on both DNS servers and checked that AAAA answers work, after one config mistake made Unbound refuse to start.
body:
The second step of the IPv6 plan covered DNS. In the Unbound template I set do-ip6 to yes and added the ULA address of each Pi to the interface list. In Pi-hole I changed the listening setting to all interfaces, since the LAN is the only network it sees.

The first run on the second Pi-hole went wrong. Unbound refused to start with an error about a bad interface address. The cause was a typo in the vars file, a missing colon in the ULA address of the second Pi. The lint script did not catch it, since it only checks syntax of the YAML. I fixed the value and added an Ansible assert that the address parses with the ipaddr filter.

After the fix both servers started. I tested with dig AAAA for a local name and for a public one, over IPv4 and over IPv6 transport. All four combinations answered, with the public ones in about 25 ms uncached.

I also added local AAAA records for the services in the Pi-hole custom list through the Ansible template. The Kuma DNS monitors got a second variant that queries over IPv6.

No clients were told to use the IPv6 DNS address yet, because the router still advertises only its own address. That is next, with the RDNSS option if the router supports it.

summary: Made the router hand out IPv6 prefix delegation to the LAN and checked that phones, laptops and the Pi get SLAAC addresses while servers keep their static ULA addresses.
body:
The IPv6 rollout reached the router today. The ISP prefix delegation was enabled on the WAN side and a /64 was assigned to the LAN. Router advertisements were switched on with the managed flag off, so clients build their own addresses with SLAAC.

The first check was from a laptop. It showed a global address and a ULA address, and the default route pointed at the router's link-local address. A phone on the Wi-Fi showed the same pattern after about a minute. The Raspberry Pi also picked up a global address, which was expected, because its interface had no static setting yet.

The advertised DNS server was the main concern. The router now announces the ULA address of the main Pi-hole through the RDNSS option, and the second Pi-hole is announced as the backup. A laptop resolved names through the Pi-hole over IPv6 and the query log listed the client with its IPv6 address. Before the change the log only showed IPv4 clients, so this is a visible difference.

One problem appeared with the privacy addresses. The Pi-hole query log now lists the same laptop under several changing temporary addresses, which makes the per-client statistics messy. The first idea was to turn off temporary addresses on the laptop, but that only fixes one device. A better fix is to group clients by hostname in Pi-hole, and this stays as an open item.

The servers were checked next. The Proxmox host and the three VMs kept their static ULA addresses from the Ansible run last week. They also received global addresses through SLAAC, so each of them now has two. I looked at whether the servers should refuse the global address, and decided to leave it as it is, because the reverse proxy needs one to be reachable from outside later. The NAS still has its address set by hand in DSM, and it answered a ping over both addresses.

A short test of the firewall followed. From the phone on mobile data, a connection to a global address of a VM was refused, as intended, because no inbound rule exists yet. Outbound IPv6 from the VMs worked, and a curl to a dual-stack test site chose IPv6 first.

The Kuma checks were left unchanged for now, since they all use IPv4 names. The next step is to add AAAA records for the proxy VM and open ports 80 and 443 for it only. The Pi-hole client grouping and a Kuma check that tests IPv6 reachability were written into the task list.

summary: Opened ports 80 and 443 over IPv6 only to the proxy VM in the router firewall and verified from a phone on mobile data that the certificate and sites load.
body:
The last step of the IPv6 plan was reachability from outside. The router has a separate IPv6 firewall list, with no NAT, so each rule names the destination address. The destination must be stable, and the global prefix can change, so I used the interface identifier of the proxy VM, which the router accepts with a prefix wildcard.

I created two rules, TCP 80 and 443, destination the proxy VM only. Everything else stays blocked by default. I also checked that ping from outside stays blocked, except for the required ICMPv6 types that the router allows itself.

Then I added the AAAA record in the public DNS zone for the two names that are reachable from outside. The records use the global address of the proxy VM. Because the prefix can change, I wrote a short script on the Pi that reads the current address and updates the record through the DNS provider API. It runs every 10 minutes through a systemd timer, and only calls the API if the address changed.

From a phone on mobile data with Wi-Fi off, I opened both sites. The certificate was valid and the page loaded in about 400 ms. A test with an online port scanner on IPv6 showed only 80 and 443 open on the proxy VM and nothing else on the other hosts.

I added an IPv6 HTTP monitor in Kuma that runs from outside, through a free external check. Caddy needed no change.

I listed one open point: the timer script has no alert on API failure, so I put that in as a next small task.

summary: Added failure alerts to the dynamic AAAA update script and tested the prefix change case by faking a new address, which updated the record within the timer interval.
body:
The AAAA update script from yesterday had no alert if the provider API failed or returned an error. I changed it to exit non-zero on any HTTP status other than 200, and to write the last success time to a file. A Kuma push monitor is called after each good run, and it turns red after 30 minutes without a push.

Then I tested the case that matters, a prefix change. I cannot make the ISP change the prefix, so I added an environment override to the script that makes it believe the address is different, and ran it by hand. The script saw the difference, called the API, and the record changed. I confirmed with dig against the provider name server, and the new value appeared in under a minute. I reverted the record afterwards with a normal run.

I also tested a failure by giving a wrong token. The script logged a 401 and exited with code 2, and the push did not happen. After 30 minutes Kuma sent its alert as expected. I restored the token.

The script and its timer are now in an Ansible role named ddns6, with the token in the vault file. The role passed the lint script and check mode.

This closes the IPv6 work. I summarized the final state in docs/ipv6-plan.md: ULA on servers, SLAAC on clients, IPv4 DNS for clients, and only 80 and 443 open to the proxy VM. WireGuard over IPv6 is left for later, as it was never needed.

summary: A Jellyfin update on the media VM left the library scan stuck at 0 percent, and the cause was a changed cache directory owner after the container image switched user.
body:
After the nightly update script pulled the new Jellyfin image, the library scan stayed at 0 percent and the web interface showed a spinner on the home page. The container was running and the health check was green, so Kuma had not alerted.

I looked at the container logs through docker compose logs. They showed repeated lines of UnauthorizedAccessException for the path /cache/images. The image had changed its default user, and the cache directory on the VM belonged to the old user id.

I checked with ls -ln and saw the directory was owned by uid 1000 while the container now ran as another uid. The config directory was fine because it had been set explicitly in the compose file, with the user option, but the cache mount was not covered by it.

I first tried chown on the cache directory, which worked, but I was not sure the next update would not change the user again. So I set the user option in the compose file for the Jellyfin service to 1000:1000 explicitly, and made the Ansible role create the cache directory with that owner.

After restarting, the scan ran and finished in 11 minutes for about 4,000 items. Playback and hardware transcoding were checked on one film and worked.

I also added a Kuma keyword check on the system info endpoint, which would have shown the problem earlier, since the scan state is visible there. The update script now also reports the image digest before and after, so an unexpected change is easy to find in the log.

summary: Tightened the Jellyfin health check so it fails when library scans produce permission errors, using the log of the last ten minutes.
body:
After this morning's cache directory problem, I wanted the container check to notice that kind of failure. The existing health check only requests the /health path, which stays green even if the cache is broken.

I wrote a small script on the media VM that greps the Jellyfin log of the last ten minutes for UnauthorizedAccessException and for the word FATAL. It exits with 1 if it finds either. A systemd timer runs it every five minutes and calls the Kuma push URL only on success.

I tested it by temporarily changing the owner of a test directory and running a scan. The check failed on the second run and Kuma alerted after the grace period of 12 minutes. After restoring the owner, it turned green again.

The script lives in the Ansible role for the media VM. It passed the lint script and check mode, and I deployed it. I also wrote one line in the quarterly checklist that after each major image change the owner of the mounted directories should be checked.

summary: Looked at why restic prune on the NAS repository took over 3 hours, found it was rewriting many small packs, and changed the prune to run weekly with a max-unused limit.
body:
The weekly maintenance window overran again, and the restic log showed that the prune step alone took 3 hours and 10 minutes. The backup itself was only 38 minutes, so prune was the cause.

I ran restic prune with the dry run option and the verbose flag to see what it planned. It wanted to repack about 1,900 packs to remove 2 percent unused data, because the default max-unused value is 5 percent but the repository has many small packs from the Home Assistant copies.

Options I considered were a higher max-unused value, a prune only once a month, or a different pack size. A different pack size needs a newer restic version than the one installed, so I left that out. I tried max-unused 10 percent in a dry run, and it planned to repack only 140 packs, with an estimated unused data of 8 percent kept in the repository. That costs roughly 30 GB more space on the NAS, which is acceptable with the new disk.

I changed the Ansible template for the backup script so forget runs after every backup, as before, but prune runs only on the first day of the week and with max-unused 10 percent. I also added a flag file so the prune is skipped if the previous backup failed.

The first real run took 22 minutes for the prune. I checked afterwards with restic check and read-data-subset 5 percent, which came back clean. The cloud bucket repository got the same setting, and there the prune is monthly because egress costs money.

The Kuma push monitor for the backup now also reports the duration in the message, so I can see the trend. The quarterly checklist got a line to compare the repository size and prune time.

summary: Verified that the weekly prune with the new limit finished in 24 minutes, repository growth stayed within the estimate, and the restore drill still passed.
body:
A week after changing the prune settings, I checked the results. The weekly run took 24 minutes for prune, close to the 22 minutes of the first run.

The NAS repository grew by 27 GB since the change, which matches the estimate of about 30 GB. I do not expect it to grow further, since the unused fraction is capped at 10 percent.

I ran the restore drill script, which restored 50 random files and compared the checksums. All matched, and the run took 5 minutes. Restic check with a data subset also found no errors.

I considered the topic closed and noted the numbers in the backup section of the docs.

summary: Pi-hole's long-term database grew to 2.8 GB on the main Pi and slowed the dashboard, so the retention was cut to 90 days and the file was vacuumed.
body:
The Pi-hole dashboard took more than 20 seconds to load its query graphs. On the main Pi I found that pihole-FTL.db had grown to 2.8 GB, since retention was set to 365 days and the household makes about 40,000 queries a day.

I stopped FTL, made a copy of the database on the NAS in case I wanted the old data, and set the MAXDBDAYS value to 90 in the Ansible template. After a restart FTL deleted the older rows, but the file stayed the same size, since SQLite does not shrink on delete.

I ran sqlite3 with VACUUM on the file. It took about 4 minutes and the file went down to 780 MB. The dashboard now loads in about 3 seconds.

The second Pi-hole had the same setting, and I applied the template there too. Its database was smaller, 1.1 GB, since it gets fewer clients. I did the same vacuum there.

I left the copy on the NAS for a month and then it can be deleted.

summary: Wrote an Ansible play to apply security updates on the Pi and the Proxmox host in a controlled order, after finding that only the VMs had unattended upgrades.
body:
While looking at the update state for the checklist, I noticed that the VMs had unattended-upgrades configured, but the Raspberry Pi and the Proxmox host had no automatic security updates at all. The Pi had 23 pending updates, among them a kernel update and OpenSSL.

I did not want to enable unattended upgrades on the Proxmox host, since a kernel or ZFS change there should be a decision. For the Pi, unattended upgrades is fine, but the Pi runs the DNS and the NUT client, so a surprise reboot would cut DNS on the main side. The second Pi-hole covers that, which is why I kept automatic reboots off.

I wrote a play with a tag that runs apt update and shows the list of upgradable packages for both machines without installing, and a second tag that installs them. The play refuses to run the install on the Proxmox host unless the variable confirm_proxmox is set on the command line. It also checks that the last vzdump finished fine before installing anything.

For the Pi I enabled unattended-upgrades for the security origin only, with automatic reboot disabled, and a Kuma check that goes red if /var/run/reboot-required exists for more than 7 days.

I installed the 23 updates on the Pi by hand with the play and rebooted it at a quiet time. DNS was served by the second Pi-hole for the 50 seconds of the restart, and no check failed.

The Proxmox host had 9 pending packages and I left them for the next maintenance window. The lint script passed on the new play.

summary: The Proxmox host installed its 9 pending updates in a short window, including a new kernel, and all guests started again after a 6 minute reboot.
body:
Using the new Ansible play from last week, I installed the pending updates on the Proxmox host. First the play checked the last vzdump, which had finished two hours earlier without errors.

I ran the list tag and read the packages. There were 9, with a new kernel and the qemu packages among them. I ran the install tag with confirm_proxmox set, and then rebooted the host from the console, not through Ansible, so I could watch the boot.

The host was down for 6 minutes. The guests started in the configured order, DNS VM first, then the services VM and the media VM. Kuma showed red for about 7 minutes in total, and then all monitors were green again.

I checked uname -r and the journal for warnings, and there were none. Jellyfin transcoding still worked, which was a concern since the earlier device permission problem. I did one test film for two minutes.

I wrote the reboot time and the kernel version into the maintenance log in docs/. The next check is the first nightly vzdump, which ran fine.

summary: Investigated why Home Assistant automations ran 20 seconds late and found the VM was short of memory and swapping, so its memory was raised from 2 to 4 GB.
body:
A user report from the household: the hallway light automation came on late, about 20 seconds after the motion sensor. Before, it was nearly instant. I started with the Home Assistant logs and found warnings that the event loop was blocked and that some integrations took more than 10 seconds to set up.

On the VM, free -m showed 2 GB total, only 90 MB free, and swap used at 1.1 GB. vmstat showed constant swap in and out, which explains the delays. The cause of the growth was not one thing. The recorder keeps ten days of history, and a new camera integration added to the memory use a few weeks ago.

I looked at what takes memory with docker stats. Home Assistant took 1.3 GB, and the rest was the MQTT broker and the Zigbee bridge container, together about 300 MB. The kernel cache took the remainder, so the VM was truly too small.

The Proxmox host has 32 GB, with about 11 GB free after all guests, so raising the VM to 4 GB is cheap. I changed the memory value in the Ansible vars for the VM, and the Proxmox play applied it. Memory ballooning was off for this VM, so a reboot of the VM was needed, and I did it in the afternoon with the family informed.

After the restart the automation reacted in under a second again. I measured with the log timestamps for ten motion events and the maximum was 0.8 seconds. Swap use stayed at zero after three hours.

I also reduced the recorder keep days from ten to seven, since nobody looks at the older graphs. That reduces the database size and the nightly consistent copy.

As a follow-up I added a Kuma push check from a small script that reports swap use above 200 MB on each VM. It runs every 10 minutes through the Ansible base role. The three VMs and the Pi were deployed, and all four reported ok.

summary: Found that the swap monitor from last week fired on the services VM because a nightly job used swap briefly, and changed the check to alert only on sustained use.
body:
The swap check I added to the base role sent an alert at night on the services VM. Swap use was 340 MB for a few minutes and then dropped back to nothing. It was not a real problem, but it showed the check is too sensitive.

I looked at what ran at that time. The nightly image cleanup and the backup pre-hook were both active, and the Paperless-like indexing job, which runs once a day, made a short peak. The VM has 4 GB, and the peak fits poorly with the limit of 200 MB.

The better rule is sustained use. I changed the script to write the swap used in MB to a small state file, and to push a failure only if the value was above 200 MB in three runs in a row, which means 30 minutes. A single peak passes.

I tested it on the services VM by running a stress command that uses memory for a short time, and then for a long time. The short one did not trigger an alert, the long one made the check fail on the third run, and Kuma alerted after its grace time.

The change went out through the base role for all VMs and the Pi. Check mode and lint passed. I also set the services VM swappiness to 10 in sysctl through the same role, since the VM does not need to swap early with 4 GB.

No other alert came during the next night.

summary: Moved the cloud bucket backup to a separate restic repository password stored in the vault, and tested restoring from the bucket alone, which worked in 41 minutes for 20 GB.
body:
The quarterly checklist asks for a restore from the cloud copy alone, and I had never done that. The risk is that the bucket repository depends on something that only exists on the NAS, such as the password file stored in the same repository directory structure.

First I checked the setup. The bucket repository used the same password as the NAS repository, and the password file was kept in the backup script directory on the services VM, which is itself backed up to both. So in a full loss, the password would be in a backup that needs the password. That is a real gap.

I generated a new password for the bucket repository, and added it with restic key add, then removed the old key after checking that the new one worked. The new password is stored in the Ansible vault, and in the password manager of the user. I printed no copy, since the password manager is already synced to a phone.

The backup template now reads the bucket password from its own variable. I ran check mode and a real run, and the next backup to the bucket completed with the new key, with no change in the duration.

Then the actual test. On the spare laptop, with only the bucket name, the access key and the password from the password manager, I ran restic restore for the Home Assistant directory and the documents share, about 20 GB. It took 41 minutes over the home connection and the cloud egress cost was a few cents.

I compared checksums with the restore drill script, adapted for a second repository with a parameter. All 100 sampled files matched.

I added the exact commands to docs/disaster-recovery.md, written so that they work without the repository checkout, since in a real disaster the git repo might be gone too. A copy of that file is also in the password manager as a note.

The remaining point is the vault password itself, which is only in the password manager. I consider that acceptable.

summary: Added the disaster recovery file to the bucket backup as plain text and checked that the Kuma reminder for the yearly full restore test is set.
body:
After the cloud restore test I thought about the case where both the checkout and the NAS are lost. The disaster recovery document is in the repository, but the repository's own remote is on the NAS, and a mirror on a hosted service was not set.

I checked where the git remotes point. There was only the NAS remote and the laptop clone. I decided against a public hosting service because of the vault and the host names. I instead made a bare git bundle of the repository each night and put it in the cloud bucket directory through the backup script. The vault file is encrypted, so the bundle is safe to store.

The backup template got a task that runs git bundle create with all refs, and the file name has no date, so restic's snapshots keep the history. I ran it and the bundle was 14 MB.

I tested by cloning from the bundle on the spare laptop, and the log and the files were complete. The vault decrypted with the password from the password manager.

I also checked the Kuma reminders. The quarterly one existed already, and I added a yearly one for a full restore of a VM from the bucket onto the spare machine, since that is a longer test of about half a day.

The disaster recovery document now includes the line on how to clone from the bundle. I updated the checklist.

That finishes the backup review of this round. Nothing is open except the VM-level restore test, which is reminded.

summary: Reviewed the quarter against the checklist: all automated checks were green, two manual items were done late, and three follow-ups were written into the task list.
body:
I did the quarterly review with the checklist from a few months ago. The automated items, among them the backup duration, the NAS volume state, WireGuard handshake and DNS timing, were all green in Kuma history over the quarter.

Two manual items were done late. The UPS test was done 10 days after its reminder, and the restore from the cloud only after I thought of it during the review. I moved the reminders to land at the start of a weekend, since that is when I actually have time.

I collected what the quarter changed. IPv6 was added with ULA addresses and an AAAA update script, the UPS battery was replaced, the prune was changed, memory for Home Assistant was raised, and the bucket got its own password.

Three follow-ups came out. First, the Pi and Proxmox host still lack a check for pending reboots from kernel updates on the host. Second, the NAS address is still set by hand. Third, the checklist should include the owner check of mounted directories after image updates, which I wrote in already.

I committed the review notes in docs/ and closed the checklist for this round.

summary: Worked through the three follow-ups from the quarterly review and fixed the easiest one: the cloud bucket cost check now writes its figure into a Kuma push monitor.
body:
The quarterly review of earlier today left three follow-ups in the task list. I started with the cloud bucket cost check, because it was still a manual look at the provider page. A small script now asks the provider's CLI for the bucket size and multiplies it by the storage price kept in an Ansible variable.

The script runs weekly from a systemd timer on the services VM. It pushes the estimated monthly cost to a Kuma push monitor, and the monitor turns red above 6 euros. The current figure is 3.10 euros for about 140 GB.

I tested the failure path by setting the limit to 1 euro, and the alert arrived on the phone within two minutes. Then I put the limit back. The timer and script are in the backup role, so a rebuild of the VM brings them back.

The other two follow-ups are still open. One is the late UPS test reminder, which needs a shorter lead time. The other is a note about which DNS server is primary for the Pi-hole sync. I will take the reminder next because it is a one-line change in the Kuma setup. The sync note can wait for a quiet evening. Everything is committed in the main checkout with the message 'bucket cost check'.

summary: Moved the UPS battery test reminder in Kuma from two days before the due date to a week before, and added a second reminder that repeats until the test is logged.
body:
The review found that the UPS battery test was done late. The reminder fired only two days before the due date, and it was easy to ignore. I changed the Kuma reminder so it starts a week before.

I also added a repeating reminder that fires every day until a file with the test result is written. The test result file is a small text file in the repo under docs/ups, one line per test with runtime and load. A check script looks at the newest line and compares its age with 90 days.

I ran the script with the current file and it passed, since the last test is only about 70 days old. Then I faked an old date in a copy of the file and the check failed as expected. The script is deployed by the monitoring role to the services VM.

This closes the second follow-up from the quarterly review. One is left, the note on the Pi-hole sync direction, which is only documentation.

summary: Wrote down why the secondary Pi-hole is the sync target and primary is the source, then found the sync script would overwrite local DNS records added on the secondary.
body:
The last follow-up from the review was a note on how the two Pi-hole instances stay in sync. While writing it I read the sync script again to describe it correctly. It runs every night on the secondary and pulls the gravity database and the custom DNS list from the primary over SSH.

The pull replaces the whole custom DNS list. That means any record added by hand on the secondary is lost the next night. I checked the secondary and found one such record, a name for the test VM, which had been added three weeks ago and silently vanished twice since.

The cause was clear. The script copies files, it does not merge them. There are two ways to fix it: forbid local changes, or keep a separate local file that is appended after the sync. I chose the first, because a second source of truth is the thing that made the problem.

The records now live only in the Ansible variables of the primary. The role renders the custom DNS file from a list in group_vars. I moved the test VM name there and ran the play against the primary.

After that I ran the sync by hand and checked that the secondary answers for the test VM name. Both servers returned the same address with dig.

The script now has a comment at the top that says the secondary is read-only for DNS records. I also added a check that compares the checksum of the custom DNS file on both servers and reports a mismatch to Kuma. I tested it by editing the secondary by hand, and the monitor went red after the next check interval of five minutes. Then I ran the sync and it turned green.

The note is in docs/dns.md and says where to add records. Nothing else is open from the review.

summary: Started looking into the Synology disk that reports a rising reallocated sector count and made a plan for replacement, with a spare ordered only if the count keeps rising.
body:
The monthly SMART summary showed disk 3 in the NAS with 24 reallocated sectors. It had 8 at the last check, so the number tripled. DSM still reports the disk as healthy, which is why no alert came from the NAS itself.

I pulled the full SMART attributes over SSH with smartctl and compared them with the saved output from last quarter. Reallocated sectors rose from 8 to 24. Pending sectors are 0 and the UDMA CRC error count is unchanged, so the cable is not the cause. Power-on hours are about 38,000.

I started an extended self-test through DSM and it will take around 11 hours. The NAS runs it in the background, and the speed of the backup job should not suffer much. I will read the result tomorrow.

The volume is RAID 6 with one more disk of redundancy than the minimum, so a failure of this disk alone is not an emergency. The free space is 31 percent, so a rebuild would fit without trouble.

The plan I wrote in docs/nas-disk.md has three steps. First, wait for the self-test and compare the counts again in a week. Second, if the count passes 50 or any pending sector appears, order a disk of the same size. Third, replace it, and run a scrub after the rebuild.

I also thought about the alerting gap. A Kuma push monitor can run a small script on the NAS that reads the reallocated count and fails above a threshold. I wrote the script and put it in the Ansible role for the NAS, with a threshold of 40.

The script runs hourly from the DSM task scheduler. I created that task by hand because the Ansible role cannot manage DSM tasks cleanly, and I noted this in the docs. The first push arrived with the value 24.

I left the spare order for later. Nothing else changed on the NAS today.

summary: The extended self-test on NAS disk 3 finished without read errors, so the disk stays in service while the reallocated count is watched weekly.
body:
The extended test finished after 10 hours and 40 minutes. It reported completed without error, and no new pending sectors appeared. The reallocated count is still 24.

That is a good sign, because a disk that is failing fast would usually show read failures in the surface scan. It does not prove that the disk is fine, so I am treating it as a watched disk.

I added a line to the quarterly checklist, and a weekly Kuma check of the count already exists from this morning's script. To see the trend, the script now also appends the value to a CSV file on the NAS with the time. That allows me to look at growth over weeks without searching the monitor history.

I also checked the backup side. The last restic check of the NAS repository passed, and the cloud bucket copy is current, so the data does not depend on this disk being healthy.

The spare disk is not ordered. The prices of the right model are about 140 euros, which is acceptable if needed. I wrote the model number and the price into the docs, so the order is quick when the threshold is crossed.

Next check is in a week, with the count and a short self-test.

summary: Caddy refused to reload after a certificate renewal failed for one subdomain, and the cause was a DNS challenge token that expired, now replaced and monitored.
body:
At about 22:00 Kuma showed the certificate check for the wiki subdomain turning yellow, with 9 days left until expiry. Renewals should happen at 30 days, so something had been failing for three weeks without an alert.

I looked at the Caddy log on the proxy VM with docker compose logs. It had repeated lines saying the DNS challenge failed with an authorization error from the DNS provider API. All the other names had renewed fine, because they were renewed earlier, but the wiki name was the one that came due after the token went bad.

The token for the DNS API had an expiry date that I set when I created it, and I had forgotten it. I checked the provider panel and the token had expired 20 days ago. That fit the log.

I created a new token with the same narrow permission, only editing records of the one zone. It went into the Ansible vault, and I ran the proxy role to put it into the environment file of the Caddy container.

Caddy needed a restart to read the environment. After the restart I watched the log and saw the challenge succeed for the wiki name, and the new certificate was served. I checked it with openssl s_client and the expiry date was about 90 days away.

That solves today's problem, but the real fault was that nothing watched token expiry or renewal failures. I did three things.

First, the new token's expiry date is written in a variable next to it in the vault file, with a comment. Second, a script now compares that date with today and pushes to Kuma, failing 30 days before expiry. Third, the existing certificate monitors now alert at 21 days instead of 7, which gives time for a fix before the user sees a warning in the browser.

I tested the date check by faking an expiry in 10 days, and the monitor turned red after the next push. I set the date back.

I also searched the repository for other tokens with a limited life. The cloud bucket key has no expiry, and the Pi-hole API password does not expire. The notification service token is the only other one and it never expires according to its panel.

The changes are committed. The quarterly checklist got a line about checking API token dates.

summary: Added the cause and the fix of the expired DNS token to the runbook and moved all Caddy certificate settings into one Ansible template, after reading the config for other weak points.
body:
After the token incident of three days ago I read the whole Caddy setup again. The goal was to find other places where a failure could stay silent for weeks.

The Caddyfile was partly generated and partly hand edited on the VM. One site block, the one for the old test service, existed only on the VM and not in the repository. I found it by comparing the file on the VM with the rendered template using diff.

The test service has been gone for a long time, so I removed the block rather than adding it to the template. The diff after that was empty.

I then moved the global options, such as the ACME email and the DNS provider settings, into one template with variables. Before, the provider name was repeated in each site block. Now there is a single snippet that each site imports, so a change of provider or token touches one place.

I ran the proxy role in check mode first and read the diff. Then I applied it and reloaded Caddy with the validate command beforehand. The reload worked and all 11 sites answered with status 200 or the expected redirect.

I wrote the runbook entry in docs/proxy.md. It lists the symptoms, which are a yellow certificate monitor and authorization errors in the log. It lists the checks, the token date in the vault and the provider panel, and the steps to replace the token and restart.

One more thing I added was a Kuma keyword monitor on the Caddy log lines for failed challenges. It is a script that counts matching lines of the last day and pushes failure if there are any. I tested it by temporarily breaking the token on a copy, which made the count positive.

Nothing is left open from this incident.

summary: Planned a test of the Raspberry Pi SD card replacement by cloning the card to a spare and writing down what must be restored if the card dies.
body:
The Pi runs the main Pi-hole and Unbound, and its SD card is the oldest storage in the house. It has been in use for almost three years, so I want a replacement plan before it fails.

I listed what lives on the card. The operating system and Docker are rebuilt by Ansible. The Pi-hole data is the gravity list and the custom DNS records, and both come from the repository and the blocklist sources. The only state that is not reproducible is the long-term query database, which I do not need.

That means a new card can be built from scratch with the playbook. I wrote the steps in docs/pi-rebuild.md: flash the image, enable SSH with the key, set the static address, run the playbook with the Pi group limit.

To be sure the list is complete, I will try it on a spare card and a spare Pi next time I have both. I also noted that the secondary DNS server keeps the network working during the rebuild.

I checked the card health with the wear information that the kernel offers. It does not report wear, so I cannot judge it. A cheap check is the count of filesystem errors in the log, and there have been none for the last 60 days.

summary: Tried a full rebuild of the Pi from the playbook on a spare SD card and found two missing steps: the Unbound root hints file and the timezone setting.
body:
I used a spare card and the spare Pi from the drawer to follow docs/pi-rebuild.md exactly, as if the real card had died. I flashed the image, enabled SSH, set the static address and ran the playbook with the limit for the Pi group.

The play finished, but Unbound did not answer. The log said it could not read the root hints file. The file was downloaded by hand years ago and never added to the role.

I added a task that fetches the file from the official source and a monthly timer to refresh it. After rerunning the play, Unbound started and resolved names with dig against the spare Pi.

The second problem was small. The Pi came up in UTC, so the Pi-hole dashboard showed wrong times. The timezone was set by hand on the old card. I added the timezone task to the base role and checked it with timedatectl.

The whole rebuild took 23 minutes of which most was the package installation. I updated the doc with the real time and the two fixes. Then I ran the play once more on the spare Pi and it reported no changes, which shows it is repeatable.

The real Pi was not touched, but I ran the play in check mode against it, and the two new tasks showed as unchanged there, as expected.

summary: Started moving the Uptime Kuma checks into Ansible so the monitor list is rebuilt from the repo instead of clicked together in the UI
body:
Uptime Kuma had grown to about 30 monitors, all created by hand in the web UI, and a restore of its volume was the only way to get them back. Today I wrote a new role, roles/kuma, that deploys the container with Docker Compose and mounts the data directory from the NAS share.

The role templates the compose file and a small monitors.yml. A Python script, scripts/kuma_sync.py, reads that file and creates missing monitors through the uptime-kuma-api package. I ran it against a scratch container first and it created 12 HTTP monitors for the services behind Caddy without trouble.
