Ping monitors for the Proxmox host, the NAS and the Pi worked as well. The DNS monitors did not: the script sent the resolver field as a string, and Kuma answered with a validation error. I fixed that by passing the Pi-hole address as a list entry.

The script is idempotent by monitor name, so a second run changed nothing. It does not delete monitors that are missing from the file, on purpose, because I do not want a typo to wipe the live set.

Still open: notification settings, which still live only in the UI, and the status page. Next session I will export the notification config and see whether the API can set it.

summary: Imported the 30 existing Uptime Kuma monitors into monitors.yml and found the sync script duplicated two that had trailing spaces in their names
body:
After the first step this morning I needed the real monitor list in the repo. I wrote scripts/kuma_dump.py, which reads all monitors from the running instance and writes them to YAML in the same shape the sync script reads.

The dump gave 31 entries. I trimmed the fields that are only runtime state, such as the id and the last heartbeat, and kept type, url, interval, retries and the accepted status codes.

A dry run of kuma_sync.py against the live instance then wanted to create two monitors that already existed. The cause was trailing spaces in the names of 'Jellyfin ' and 'Grafana ' in the UI. Matching by name failed for exactly those two. I renamed them in the UI and added a strip() in the script so it cannot happen again.

I also looked at the intervals. Most checks ran every 60 seconds, but the restic heartbeat monitor was a push type with a 60 second window, although the backup runs once a night. That is why it had been flapping now and then. I set the window to 26 hours in the file.

The notification channel is a Telegram bot. The API can create it, but the token would have to sit in the repo. I put the token in an Ansible vault variable and let the role pass it to the script as an environment variable.

After a full run, the diff between the dump and the file was empty. I committed the role, both scripts and the monitor list.

The status page is still manual. It is low priority, because only the user looks at it.

summary: Checked why the UPS reported 38 minutes of runtime but the NAS shut down after 9, and found the NUT low-battery threshold was set far too high
body:
The user noticed during a short power cut that the NAS shut itself down far earlier than expected. The UPS had advertised about 38 minutes at the current load.

I logged in to the Pi, which runs the NUT server, and ran upsc on the UPS. battery.charge was 100 and runtime was 2280 seconds, so the numbers matched the claim. The setting that decided the shutdown was battery.charge.low, which was 95 percent. The UPS raised the low-battery flag almost immediately after the mains dropped, and the NUT clients obeyed.

I tried to change it with upsrw, but this model only lets the runtime threshold be set, not the charge threshold. battery.runtime.low was 600 seconds. The shutdown after 9 minutes fits that.

I changed the value to 300 seconds, which still leaves enough time for the NAS to power down, which takes about 90 seconds, and for Proxmox to stop the VMs in order. The Ansible role for NUT now sets it through a handler that calls upsrw after the service starts.

I did not pull the plug to test it. I used upsmon -c fsd on a dry configuration instead, and the shutdown order on Proxmox looked right in the log. A real test is planned for a day when the user is at home.

summary: Ran the planned UPS pull-the-plug test and the whole chain shut down cleanly, with the NAS last and the Pi staying up long enough to log it
body:
With the user at home, we pulled the UPS from the wall at about nine in the evening. I watched the NUT log on the Pi over SSH.

After 4 minutes of battery the runtime fell to the new 300 second threshold and the Pi sent the shutdown signal. Proxmox stopped the VMs and containers in about 70 seconds and then powered off. The NAS followed and was off after roughly 85 seconds.

We put the power back on and everything came up by itself within 6 minutes. Pi-hole answered DNS again after 2 minutes, which is fine. The only open point is that Jellyfin needed a manual start of its container, because it came up before the NAS media share was mounted. I will add a mount dependency next.

summary: Fixed the Jellyfin start-up order after power loss by making the compose service wait for the NAS mount, and added a check to Ansible so it is verified
body:
After the UPS test the Jellyfin container started before the NFS share with the media was mounted, so the libraries looked empty and I had to restart it. This is the same problem that probably hit other services without anyone noticing.

On the Proxmox side the media share is mounted by an fstab entry with the _netdev option. Docker, however, starts at boot with no knowledge of that mount. The container saw an empty directory on the host and ran happily with it.

I first tried depends_on, but that only works inside Compose. The cleaner fix was a systemd drop-in for docker.service with RequiresMountsFor=/mnt/media /mnt/backup. I wrote it as a template in roles/docker and added a handler that does a daemon-reload.

Then I tested it. I disabled the mount, rebooted the VM, and Docker did not start until I mounted the share again. That is the intended result, but it also means that if the NAS is down, all Docker services on that VM stay down. For this VM that is acceptable, because it only hosts media related services.

The Home Assistant VM is a different case. It does not use the NAS at all, so I left it alone.

I also added a small guard to the Jellyfin compose file: the media volume is mounted read-only, and a healthcheck runs test -e /media/.mounted, a marker file I created on the share. If the marker is not there, the container reports unhealthy, and Uptime Kuma sees it through the Docker monitor.

I ran the Ansible playbook with --check first, then for real. It changed 3 things, as expected. A second run changed nothing.

Left to do: a reboot of the whole box under the UPS, to see the full ordering once more. I will do that when the next kernel update arrives.

summary: Pi-hole gravity update was failing silently for weeks because of a full /tmp on the Pi, now cleaned up and monitored
body:
The user asked why a known ad domain was not blocked. I checked pihole -g on the Pi and it ended with 'Not enough space' while building the list. The gravity database was therefore still the version from about five weeks ago.

The Pi has a small tmpfs for /tmp, 100 MB, and the combined lists had grown past that. I did not want to shrink the lists. Instead I set TMPDIR for the weekly gravity cron job to a directory on the SD card, which has 9 GB free.

I ran pihole -g by hand afterwards. It finished in 40 seconds and the domain count rose from 812,000 to 1.1 million. The test domain is now blocked.

The reason nobody saw this is that the cron job writes only to a log. I added a push monitor to Uptime Kuma, and the job calls it with curl only on success. The window is 8 days.

I put the change into the pihole role in Ansible and ran it against the Pi. One thing to watch is the SD card wear, but a weekly write of a few hundred MB is no problem.

summary: Planned the IPv6 rollout: the ISP gives a /56 prefix that changes, so the LAN will use ULA addresses plus the delegated prefix with Pi-hole serving AAAA
body:
The user wants IPv6 for the home network. I spent the session reading the router settings and making a plan, with no changes to the live network yet.

The router receives a /56 through prefix delegation. The prefix is not guaranteed to be stable, and it did change once after a router restart according to the user. Because of that, no service config should contain the global address.

The plan has three parts. First, a ULA prefix, fd-something /48 which I generated with a random generator, for stable internal addresses of the servers. Second, the delegated prefix for SLAAC on the client VLAN so devices can reach the internet. Third, the DNS: Pi-hole answers AAAA records for the internal names with the ULA address, and Caddy listens on both families.

I checked what is affected. Proxmox needs the bridge to accept router advertisements, but I want a static ULA on it, so I will set accept_ra to 2 on vmbr0 and add the address in /etc/network/interfaces. Docker ignores IPv6 unless the daemon is configured with ipv6 and a fixed-cidr-v6, and I will leave that off for now, because the containers sit behind Caddy on the host anyway.

The NAS supports IPv6 in its network settings, so it only needs the ULA address as a static entry. WireGuard is the most delicate part. The tunnel carries IPv4 only today, and adding an IPv6 address pair to the config means changes on every client.

Order of work: the Proxmox host first, then Pi-hole, then Caddy, then the NAS, and last WireGuard. After each step I check with ping -6 and a curl -6 from a laptop.

A risk is the firewall. The router firewall for IPv6 inbound is open by default for delegated prefixes on this model, so I must verify that nothing is reachable from outside before we turn on global addresses at all. I wrote the plan into docs/ipv6.md.

summary: Gave the Proxmox host and the Pi static ULA addresses and confirmed they answer on IPv6 from the laptop, while global SLAAC stays off the servers
body:
First step of the IPv6 plan. I added the ULA prefix as a variable in group_vars/all.yml, along with a per-host suffix for each machine.

On Proxmox I edited the network template: vmbr0 got an inet6 static stanza with the ULA address and a /64 mask, and accept_ra 2 so that the default route from the router still arrives. Without the route the host would only reach the local prefix. I applied it with ifreload -a rather than a reboot. The SSH session survived.

On the Pi I used dhcpcd, which already had an ipv6 section. I set a static ip6_address there and told it not to use SLAAC for the global address, because I do not want a changing address on the Pi. The Pi has the ULA only and still gets the router as the default gateway.

I tested from the laptop with ping -6 to both addresses, and ssh -6 worked. A traceroute showed one hop, as expected.

One surprise was that the Proxmox web interface did not answer on the IPv6 address at first. pveproxy listens on both families by default, but the firewall rules I had written for the datacenter only allowed the IPv4 range. I added the ULA prefix to the management IP set in /etc/pve/firewall/cluster.fw and the page loaded.

I have not touched the VMs yet. They are the next step, after Pi-hole serves AAAA records.

The Ansible changes are committed. The role for the network now has an ipv6 flag per host, set to true for these two.

summary: Pi-hole now answers AAAA for internal names with ULA addresses, and Caddy listens on IPv6, so the services open over IPv6 from the laptop
body:
Next step of the IPv6 work. In Pi-hole I added AAAA entries through the custom DNS file that the Ansible role writes, using the ULA suffixes from group_vars. Names like jellyfin.home and ha.home now have both an A and an AAAA record.

The Caddy VM got a static ULA address in the same way as the host. Caddy itself needed no change, because it binds to all interfaces, but the Docker published ports are IPv4 only unless the daemon proxies them. Caddy runs with host networking, so it listens on both. I checked with ss -tlnp and saw [::]:443.

From the laptop, curl -6 https://jellyfin.home/ returned the expected redirect and the certificate was valid. Home Assistant over IPv6 failed with a 400. Its config has trusted_proxies with only the IPv4 address of Caddy, so the request from the ULA address was rejected. I added the ULA /128 of the Caddy VM and restarted Home Assistant.

After that all 11 names opened over IPv6. Unbound still answers with the AAAA records that Pi-hole holds, and I saw no change in lookup times. The NAS and WireGuard are left.

summary: Added the NAS to IPv6 with a static ULA address and found its backup share mounts still worked, since restic goes through the IPv4 name
body:
I set a static ULA address on the NAS in the Synology network settings and added the AAAA record to Pi-hole through the usual Ansible variable. The NAS accepted the address without a reboot.

Then I checked what could break. The restic repository is on an SFTP path that uses the host name nas.home. With both records now existing, the client may choose IPv6. I ran a restic snapshots against the repository from the Proxmox host and it worked over either family. I forced each with ssh -4 and ssh -6 to make sure.

The NFS mounts are written with the IPv4 address in fstab, so they did not change. I left them like that on purpose; mixing in IPv6 there brings little benefit.

One problem: the DSM firewall had no rule for the ULA range, so SMB from the laptop over IPv6 timed out while IPv4 worked. I added an allow rule for the ULA /48 on the shares ports, and it opened at once.

WireGuard is the last open piece and I will do it in a separate session.

summary: Looked at adding IPv6 to WireGuard and decided on a ULA-only tunnel, because the global prefix changes and would break every client config
body:
I reviewed how to give the VPN an IPv6 address pair. The server config on the Pi has Address = 10.8.0.1/24 and each peer has a /32 in AllowedIPs.

The idea is to add a second ULA subnet, a /64 carved from the home ULA prefix, with the server at ::1 and the peers numbered like their IPv4 ones. The peers would then reach the internal services through the tunnel with the same names as at home.

I decided against routing the global IPv6 through the tunnel. The delegated prefix can change, and there is no need for the phone to send all its traffic home. So the clients keep AllowedIPs limited to the internal ULA /48 and the IPv4 ranges.

I wrote the template change in the wireguard role but did not apply it. The peers have to get new configs, and I want to do that together with the user, since two of the devices are theirs only. A second concern is ip6tables: the forwarding rules on the Pi are IPv4 only, so I will mirror them before enabling anything.

summary: Applied the WireGuard IPv6 change and mirrored the forwarding rules, and the phone reached Jellyfin over the tunnel by its internal name
body:
Following the plan from earlier, I rolled out the ULA subnet on the WireGuard server. The template now writes two Address entries, and the PostUp and PostDown lines contain the ip6tables equivalents of the IPv4 forwarding and masquerade rules. Masquerade is not needed for ULA, since the servers know the route back, so I only added the forward accept rules and left NAT out.

I enabled net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding on the Pi with a sysctl file from Ansible. Note that with forwarding on, the Pi stops accepting router advertisements unless accept_ra is 2 for the interface. I set that for eth0 to keep the default route, and verified with ip -6 route.

I restarted wg-quick@wg0. The first start failed with 'RTNETLINK answers: Permission denied' for the ULA address. The cause was a leftover line in the config from my first test, which gave the same address twice. After removing the duplicate it started.

The phone config got the new Address and the ULA range in AllowedIPs. I regenerated the QR code and the user scanned it. Over mobile data the phone opened jellyfin.home by name. Pi-hole is the DNS server in the tunnel config, and it answered with both record types.

The laptop peer worked on the first try. The tablet is still on the old config, and it keeps working on IPv4 only, so nothing broke.

I checked from outside, with a scan from a rented host, that no IPv6 ports were open on the global prefix: all filtered. The WireGuard UDP port is open on IPv4 only, which is how the router is set.

The IPv6 project is done except for the tablet. I updated docs/ipv6.md with what was actually done.

summary: Ran the second restic restore test of the year: a full restore of the Home Assistant VM backup took 41 minutes and booted, but exposed that the vault password was only in one place
body:
The user wanted proof that backups still work after the many changes. I picked the Home Assistant VM, because losing it hurts most, and restored it onto a spare ID on Proxmox.

The backup of that VM is a vzdump file stored in the restic repository on the NAS. I listed the snapshots, picked the one from the night before, and restored the single file with restic restore --include. The file was 14 GB and the transfer took 29 minutes over the gigabit link.

Then I ran qmrestore to create the VM with ID 910, without starting the network. It needed another 12 minutes to write to the local storage. In sum 41 minutes, which is acceptable for this size.

I started the VM with its network interface disconnected, so that it would not fight with the live one for the address. It booted to the login, and the Home Assistant core came up after about 90 seconds. I checked the entities through the console log and the database loaded, with the history of the last night present.

The problem showed up before all this. To access the repository from a clean shell, I needed the restic password. It is in the Ansible vault, and the vault password is stored in my password manager on the laptop only. If the laptop dies together with the house, the backups are unreadable. This was noted as a risk in the first restore test and I had not fixed it.

The user agreed to print the vault password and the restic password on paper and store it with a relative. I wrote a short docs/recovery.md that lists exactly which secrets are needed and where each one is. It contains no secrets itself.

I also noted that the cloud bucket copy uses a separate key, and I tested listing it with the credentials from the file, which worked.

After the test I destroyed VM 910 and deleted the restored file from the scratch directory. A timing line went into the recovery doc: about 45 minutes for the Home Assistant VM, not counting the time to find the passwords.

Next: do the same for the Pi-hole container, which is much smaller.

summary: Restored the Pi-hole LXC backup to a spare ID in 4 minutes and confirmed that DNS answers from it, so the small-service restore path is proven too
body:
This was the follow-up to the Home Assistant restore. The Pi-hole container backup is about 600 MB, so I expected a fast test.

I pulled the file from restic and ran pct restore with ID 911 and a different static address in the same subnet, to avoid a clash. The restore took 4 minutes in total.

I started it and queried it with dig @ on its test address. It answered both blocked and normal names, and the gravity database had the current domain count of 1.1 million. Unbound inside the container resolved recursively as well.

One detail came up: the container config had the old MAC address in it, and the router showed two entries with the same MAC for a moment before I changed it. For a real recovery that does not matter, since the original would be gone.

I destroyed container 911 afterwards. The recovery notes now have the Pi-hole figure of 4 minutes.

summary: Weekly container update script pulled a new Home Assistant image that failed to start, so I pinned the tag and made the script stop on unhealthy containers
body:
This morning Uptime Kuma alerted that Home Assistant was down. The update script had run overnight and pulled a new image. The container was restarting in a loop, and docker logs showed an error about a custom integration, which no longer loaded with the new core version.

I rolled back by setting the image to the previous tag in the compose file and running docker compose up -d. It was back after 50 seconds. The integration was an unofficial one installed through HACS, and its author has not released a fix.

The real problem was the update script. It used the latest tag and moved on regardless of the result. I changed two things. The compose files for Home Assistant, Jellyfin and Caddy now use explicit version tags, set in a variable file that the user can raise on purpose. For the other services, the script now waits 30 seconds after the update, checks docker inspect for the health state, and if a container is not running or not healthy, it stops the loop, writes a message to the log and calls the Kuma push URL with a failure status.

I tested by giving the script a bad tag for a throwaway container, and it stopped as intended and the Kuma monitor went red.

The integration question stays open: I will ask the user whether they still use it.

summary: Checked SMART errors on a NAS disk that reported 8 reallocated sectors, compared with last month, and ordered a replacement as a precaution
body:
DSM sent a warning mail about bay 3. I connected to the NAS over SSH and ran smartctl -a on that disk. Reallocated_Sector_Ct was 8, and Current_Pending_Sector was 0.

I looked for the earlier values. The weekly SMART summary that a script on the Pi writes to a text file in the repo directory had 2 reallocated sectors a month ago, and 0 before that. So the number is rising, which is more worrying than a flat small value.

The disk is 4 years old with about 31,000 power-on hours. Its model is the same as that of the other three, bought together, so their failure is likely to come close.

The volume is SHR with one disk of redundancy, and the status is healthy. A rebuild of a 8 TB disk takes about 14 hours on this NAS, during which a second failure would lose the data, but the restic backups in the cloud bucket give a fallback.

I ran an extended SMART test on bay 3. It will take around 11 hours. I also checked the backup job: the last cloud run was good yesterday.

I told the user my recommendation, which is to buy a replacement drive now instead of waiting. They agreed, and a drive of the same size, but from another batch, is on order.

I also changed the SMART script so that it sends a Kuma push when the reallocated count grows between two weeks. Before, it only logged.

The next entry will be the result of the long test and the swap plan.

summary: Replaced the failing NAS disk in bay 3 and the SHR rebuild finished in 15 hours with no data errors, after the extended test had found read errors
body:
The extended SMART test from yesterday ended with a read failure at 71 percent, so the decision to replace was right. The new drive arrived this morning.

Before touching anything I started a fresh restic backup to the cloud bucket and waited until it finished, which took 40 minutes because there was little change. I also ran a data scrub on the volume to be sure of its current state. The scrub is the long part, and I let it run through the early afternoon. It reported no inconsistencies.

In DSM I used the deactivate drive function for bay 3 and then pulled it out. The NAS beeped, as it should for a degraded volume. I put in the new drive, and DSM offered to repair the storage pool. I chose the new disk in the dialog.

The rebuild started at about 14:00 and it was slow at first, around 60 MB/s, because Jellyfin was streaming from the NAS. I asked the user not to watch anything during the night. After that it ran at about 150 MB/s.

I checked the progress over SSH with cat /proc/mdstat. It showed the rebuild at 38 percent after 5 hours, and I left it.

The nightly restic job started in the middle of the rebuild. I let it run, but it slowed the rebuild and extended the job to 3 hours. I should have paused it, and I note that for the next time.

This morning the pool was healthy again. The total rebuild time came out at about 15 hours. I ran smartctl on the new drive and it shows 0 for all error counters.

I wrote the old drive's serial number and its error history into docs/hardware.md, and the user will dispose of the drive after wiping it. The SMART script was updated for the new serial.

Finally, I started a second scrub, to confirm that the data on the rebuilt array is consistent. It will run during the next hours.

The other three drives are the same age as the failed one. I proposed to replace one more drive in a few months, when the price goes down. The user wants to wait and see.

summary: The nightly restic job started running past 6 in the morning, so I measured where the time goes and found the new Jellyfin metadata directory adds 400k small files
body:
Uptime Kuma reported the backup heartbeat late twice this week. I looked at the restic log on the Proxmox host: the job used to take 35 minutes and now takes between 2 and 3 hours.

The summary at the end of the log shows 'Files: 412,000 new' on most nights, though little data changes. Those are tiny files. I traced them to the Jellyfin volume, where the metadata and trickplay images folder grew after a library rescan. Jellyfin generates thumbnails for scrubbing, and each video gets thousands of them.

I measured the directory. It has 380,000 files and about 22 GB. The files are rewritten whenever Jellyfin regenerates them, so restic sees new modification times, and has to hash the content again.

The cache in restic is not the issue: I checked that the cache directory exists and has a recent state. The time goes to scanning and reading the files.

The options were to exclude the trickplay folder, or to turn the thumbnail generation off. The thumbnails can be recreated by Jellyfin at any time, so there is no reason to keep them in a backup. I added an exclude line for the trickplay and cache directories to the exclude file in the repo, which the Ansible role copies to the host.

I ran the job by hand with the new exclude. It finished in 38 minutes. The repository does still contain the old copies of those files in earlier snapshots, and restic forget with prune will drop them over time with the retention policy.

I also moved the job start from 02:00 to 03:30. It had collided with the Jellyfin library scan that runs at 02:00, and the two together slowed each other down.

One more thing: the cloud copy runs after the local backup in the same script, so a long local run pushed it far into the day. With the short local run it should be done by 05:00 again.

I will check the duration for a week. If it stays under an hour, the problem is closed.

summary: Ran restic forget and prune to drop the old trickplay snapshots, which freed 61 GB on the NAS repository after a long prune
body:
Following the exclude change this morning, the old snapshots still hold the thumbnails. I wanted the space back and a smaller repository to check.

First I ran restic forget --dry-run with the current policy, 7 daily, 4 weekly, 12 monthly. It listed 9 snapshots to remove. The oldest snapshots that hold the trickplay data are the monthly ones, so some of the space will only come back after months. That is expected.

Then I ran the real forget with --prune. It took 1 hour 50 minutes, since restic had to rewrite many packs to remove the small files. The output said it would delete 61 GB and rewrite 18 packs, and the repository went from 1.42 TB to 1.36 TB.

I ran restic check afterwards, with the default structure check, and it reported no errors. I did not run the full read-data check, since it needs many hours, but I put it on the list for the weekend.

The prune also ran while the cloud sync was idle, so I did it on the local repository only. The bucket repository is separate and gets its own prune from the weekly script, which I did not change.

One point to fix: the weekly script runs prune for both repositories in a row, and the local one used to take 10 minutes. It will be longer for now but go back to normal.

I updated the retention note in docs/backup.md with the exclude list, and the reason for it.

summary: Second DNS server: set up Pi-hole and Unbound in a Debian LXC on Proxmox and synced its blocklists and custom records from the Pi with a small script
body:
The Pi is the only DNS server, and when it reboots, the whole network loses name resolution. The user asked for a second one.

I created an LXC container with ID 120 on Proxmox, Debian 12, 512 MB of memory, and a static address with ULA suffix as well. I wrote a role, pihole, that already existed for the Pi, and just added the container to the inventory. Applying it installed Pi-hole and Unbound with the same config files as on the Pi, including the Unbound options for the local zone.

Unbound answered on port 5335 and Pi-hole forwards to it, as on the Pi. dig for a test domain returned in 40 ms for the first query and 1 ms for the second.

The issue is keeping both in sync. Blocklists and the whitelist are in the repo, so the role handles those. The local DNS records are also written from Ansible variables, so they are the same on both. What is not in Ansible is the group of clients and the manual allow entries that the user adds through the web page. I looked at tools such as gravity-sync, but I prefer something simpler.

I wrote scripts/pihole_sync.sh, which uses the Pi-hole teleporter export on the primary, copies the archive to the second server over SSH, and imports it. It runs every night at 04:30 from a systemd timer on the Pi. I ran it by hand and the group configuration showed up on the second server.

The next step is to hand out both addresses. The router DHCP server gives DNS addresses to clients, and I put the new container as secondary. I changed it on the router and renewed the lease on the laptop, where resolvectl showed both servers.

A test: I stopped pihole-FTL on the Pi for a minute, and browsing from the laptop continued after a delay of a few seconds on the first lookup. Clients mostly switch quickly, but some devices stick to the first server for longer. The TV did that, so the delay is a client matter.

A Kuma DNS monitor for the new server was added in monitors.yml. The WireGuard config still gives only the Pi as DNS, which I will change next.

summary: Added the second DNS server to the WireGuard client configs and found that Pi-hole on the container logged all queries as coming from one address
body:
This session continued the second DNS server work. First the simple part: the wireguard role template now writes DNS = the Pi, the new container, for every peer. I regenerated the configs for the phone and the laptop. The user imported them, and a lookup through the tunnel worked against both servers.

Then I opened the query log of the new Pi-hole to see traffic and noticed that nearly all queries came from the router address. On the Pi the log shows the real clients. The difference showed up quickly: the router forwards DNS for the clients that still have it as their resolver, and the router asks the first server only.

I checked the DHCP leases on the router. Some devices, mostly the older ones, had the router address as their DNS because they had received the lease before I changed the settings. With a renew they got both servers. Others had a hard-coded address on the device.

The case where the router forwards is more important. The router has its own upstream setting, with the Pi as the only entry. I added the new container as the second upstream. That makes the router fall back correctly when the Pi is down.

After the change, I stopped Pi-hole on the Pi again for a few minutes and counted what stopped working. The smart plugs and the TV kept resolving through the router. Home Assistant uses its own DNS setting in the VM, so I added the second server there as well, in the network config of the VM, with the ULA address.

I also tested the sync direction in an unexpected way: I added a test entry on the second server, and the next sync from the Pi wiped it. That is the intended one-way behavior. I wrote it in the doc so that nobody edits the secondary by hand.

One more item to improve. The sync timer fails silently if SSH to the container breaks. I added a Kuma push call at the end of the script with a 26 hour window.

All DNS clients now have two servers. I did not touch the IPv6 router advertisements for DNS, which still only list the Pi. It is a point for the next session.

summary: Added the second DNS server to the IPv6 router advertisements and verified a client keeps resolving when the Pi is off, closing the DNS redundancy work
body:
The remaining gap from the last session was the RDNSS option in the router advertisements. The router only announced the Pi's ULA address, so IPv6-only lookups on devices that use RDNSS had no fallback.

In the router settings, there is a field for IPv6 DNS servers with two slots. I put the Pi in the first slot and the new container's ULA address in the second. The router did not need a restart. I checked on the laptop with resolvectl status and the link showed two IPv6 DNS servers after a few minutes, when the next advertisement came.

For the test I shut down the Pi's Pi-hole again and disabled IPv4 DNS on the laptop's interface, so that only the IPv6 servers were left. A dig for a name returned an answer from the container. The first query had a 2 second delay, then it was fast.

The Android phone ignored the RDNSS entries and used the DHCP ones, which is a known limit of the system. It is fine, because DHCP gives both.

I looked at the Kuma monitors for the whole thing: both DNS servers are checked every minute, and the sync push is green. I changed the monitor group so that an alert is only sent when both DNS servers fail in the same minute, and a single failure is a warning in the UI only. That seemed to the user the right level to avoid the night alerts.

The documentation in docs/dns.md now describes the two servers, the sync direction and the router settings, and the order in which to update them: the secondary first, then the primary, so there is always one server running.

With this the second DNS server is finished. What remains is the question about the HACS integration for Home Assistant from the update problem, which the user has not answered yet.

summary: Pi-hole on the new LXC logged every query as coming from the Proxmox bridge address, so per-client stats were useless; fixed by changing the listening mode and the DNS forwarding rule
body:
Followed up on the oddity found yesterday with the second DNS server: all queries in the Pi-hole log showed one client address. The cause was the LXC sitting behind the NAT rule that the WireGuard clients use, so the source was rewritten before it reached the container.

I looked at the nftables ruleset on the Proxmox host and found a masquerade rule that matched the whole 10.0.0.0/8 range instead of only the tunnel subnet. That rule was copied from the old WireGuard notes. I narrowed it to the tunnel subnet in the Ansible template and applied it.

After the change I ran dig from the laptop and from the phone over the tunnel and checked the Pi-hole query log. The laptop showed its own address and the phone showed its tunnel address. Per-client groups now work on the second server as well.

I also set the Pi-hole listening mode to allow all origins only on the tunnel interface, because the previous setting was why it had accepted queries it should have dropped. The old Pi still has the stricter setting, so I left it alone.

One leftover: the sync script copies custom records but not client group assignments. I noted that in the repo TODO and will look at it after the weekend. Nothing else changed today.

summary: Extended the Pi-hole sync script to copy client groups and group assignments, so both DNS servers filter the same way
body:
The sync script from last week only copied blocklists and custom DNS records. Today it also copies the groups, clients and adlist assignments, using the gravity database on the Pi.

I first tried copying the whole gravity.db file. That worked but overwrote the query-related tables and restarted FTL at a bad moment, so I dropped the idea. Instead the script now dumps the group, client and assignment tables with sqlite3 and loads them on the second server.

I tested it by creating a test group on the Pi and a client entry for the laptop. After the script ran, the second server showed the same group. Then I removed both and ran the script again to check that deletions propagate; they did.

The script runs from a systemd timer every night at 03:30 on the Pi. I added it to the Ansible role so a rebuilt Pi gets the timer back. The run takes about 4 seconds and logs to the journal.

Uptime Kuma has a push monitor for it now, which goes red if the timer misses a run for 26 hours.

summary: Reviewed the Caddy certificate renewal setup after a renewal warning in the log and moved the DNS challenge token out of the compose file into a secrets file
body:
Caddy logged a warning that a certificate would expire in 29 days and was still retrying a renewal. The renewal had not failed, but the warning made me check how the DNS challenge is configured.

The API token for the DNS provider was written directly in docker-compose.yml, and that file is in git. I checked the history and the token had been committed since the first setup. I rotated the token at the provider first, which was the important step.

Then I moved the new token into an env file, caddy.env, that is encrypted with ansible-vault and templated onto the host at deploy time. The compose file now only references env_file. I added caddy.env to .gitignore for the plain copy on the host.

The old token still exists in git history. I decided not to rewrite history, since it is revoked and the repo is private.

After redeploying I forced a renewal with caddy reload and watched the log. The challenge succeeded and the certificate now shows 89 days left. I also checked the renewal on the Uptime Kuma certificate expiry monitor, which turned green.

The token now has a narrower scope: it can only edit TXT records for the one zone. The earlier token could edit the whole account. That was the bigger problem and is now closed.

summary: Found why the weekly update script skipped the Jellyfin container for a month: a stale label excluded it, and removed the label after checking the new image
body:
While reading the update log I noticed the Jellyfin image was a month older than all the others. The script skips any container with the label update.skip=true. That label was added when a Jellyfin release broke hardware transcoding, and nobody removed it.

Before removing it I read the release notes for the versions since then. The transcoding regression was fixed two releases ago. I pulled the newest image on the Proxmox VM only, ran it next to the current container on another port with a copy of the config, and played a 4K file with transcoding to a phone.

The transcode used the GPU and the CPU stayed low, around 12 percent. The log showed no VAAPI errors. I then removed the label and ran the update script by hand.

The script pulled the image, restarted the container and waited for it to become healthy, which took 40 seconds. That is the new health check from the Home Assistant incident, and it worked as intended.

I added a line to the script output that lists skipped containers with the reason, so a forgotten label shows up in the log every week. That would have caught this.

summary: Wrote an Ansible role for Pi-hole and Unbound so both DNS servers are built from the repo, and tested it by rebuilding the LXC from scratch
body:
Both DNS servers had been set up by hand, with notes. Today I turned the notes into an Ansible role called dns, used for the Pi and for the LXC.

The role installs Unbound, writes unbound-pihole.conf, installs Pi-hole unattended with a setupVars.conf template, and sets the listening interface and upstream. The upstream is the local Unbound on port 5335. It also installs the sync timer, but only on the Pi, through a variable.

The first run on the LXC failed because the Pi-hole installer asked for a static address confirmation. Adding the unattended flag and the IPV4_ADDRESS value in the template fixed that. The second failure was Unbound not starting, since the root hints file path differed on Debian and Raspberry Pi OS. I made the path a variable.

To prove it, I destroyed the test LXC, created a fresh one with the same ID and ran the playbook. It took 6 minutes to a working resolver. I checked with dig for a blocked domain, an internal name, and a DNSSEC test domain; all gave the expected answers.

Then I ran the role in check mode against the Pi and the LXC and both showed no changes except a comment line in the Unbound config. I accepted that difference by updating the template.

Next step is adding the role to the main site playbook and a tag, so a single command rebuilds DNS.

summary: Asked whether the cloud restic bucket was really getting nightly snapshots; it was, but the last check of its integrity was never run
body:
The question came up while reading the backup notes: does the cloud copy get written every night, and has anyone verified that it is readable? I listed the snapshots in the bucket with restic snapshots and found one per night, the newest from this morning.

The integrity check had never been run against the bucket. A full restic check with --read-data would download everything and cost egress fees, so I ran a partial one with --read-data-subset=5%. It finished in 22 minutes and reported no errors.

I added a monthly job that checks a different 5 percent each time, using a subset like 3/20 that rotates by month number. Over 20 months this covers the whole repository. The result goes to Uptime Kuma as a push monitor.

The NAS repository gets the same check weekly, since local reads are free. Its last full check passed after the disk replacement.

Nothing was wrong, but now there is evidence instead of an assumption.

summary: Home Assistant VM ran out of disk because the recorder database grew to 18 GB; trimmed the retention and excluded noisy sensors, which cut it to 2 GB
body:
Home Assistant stopped saving history and the log said the disk was full. The VM has a 32 GB disk, and home-assistant_v2.db was 18 GB.

I first looked at which entities wrote the most. A query on the states table grouped by entity showed that the power meter sensors and the Pi temperature probe produced about 70 percent of the rows, each with an update every two seconds.

I set recorder purge_keep_days to 10 instead of the default that had been overridden to 60 some time ago. I also added an exclude list for the five noisiest entities and the energy sensors that already have long-term statistics.

The database does not shrink on its own after a purge. I stopped Home Assistant, ran a manual purge with repack through the service call, and then restarted. The file went from 18 GB to 2.1 GB and the repack took about 11 minutes.

Before doing that I took a Proxmox snapshot of the VM and a restic backup, since the VM was nearly full and a repack needs free space. The temporary space need turned out to be about 3 GB, which fit after I deleted old logs.

The history graphs for the excluded sensors will have a gap from now, but the statistics for energy remain. I checked the energy dashboard and it still shows the whole past year.

I added a disk usage sensor for the VM and an Uptime Kuma threshold check at 80 percent. That would have warned weeks ago. The VM backup is also faster now, because the image is mostly compressed text, so tonight's run is a good test.

summary: Night backup after the Home Assistant cleanup finished 25 minutes faster, and the disk usage alert fired once as a test and then cleared
body:
Checked the restic log from last night. The VM backup of Home Assistant took 7 minutes instead of 32, and the whole job ended at 04:50, which is the earliest since the Jellyfin metadata growth.

The repository on the NAS grew by only 600 MB, because the database was repacked and the changed blocks were small. The cloud upload finished at the same time as before, since it is limited by the uplink.

I tested the new disk usage monitor by temporarily lowering the threshold to 5 percent. Uptime Kuma showed the monitor red within a minute and sent the notification to the phone. After restoring 80 percent it went green.

I also looked at the notification text. It said only that the monitor was down. I changed the message template to include the host and the usage in percent, which is much more useful at 3 in the morning.

The template change was added to monitors.yml, so the sync script applies it everywhere. One monitor did not take the message because its type has a different field name. I fixed that one by hand in the file.

The backup duration monitor from earlier now has a stricter limit of 90 minutes. That reflects the actual duration and will catch a regression early.

Nothing else was needed today.

summary: Planned the replacement of the old Pi SD card with a USB SSD after seeing write errors in dmesg, and listed the steps for a safe migration
body:
Saw EXT4 and mmc write error lines in dmesg on the Pi during a routine check. The card is more than three years old and the Pi runs Pi-hole, NUT and the sync timer, so a failure would hurt the UPS shutdown chain.

I wrote the plan in the repo as docs/pi-ssd.md. First, take a full image of the card with dd to the NAS, since it still works. Second, check that the Pi firmware boots from USB, which needs the bootloader EEPROM to be recent; I checked with rpi-eeprom-update and it is current.

Third, install a fresh OS on the SSD and run the Ansible roles instead of cloning the card. This tests that the repo really rebuilds the Pi, and avoids copying the bad blocks. Fourth, restore the few state files: the NUT config comes from the repo, and Pi-hole state is synced from the other server.

The second DNS server means clients keep resolving during the swap, which makes this safe to do in the evening. NUT is the one thing with a gap: the NAS will not get the shutdown signal while the Pi is down, so I will do it when power is stable.

I ordered a 120 GB SSD and a USB adapter. Image of the card taken tonight: 29 GB read in 14 minutes, checksum saved next to it.

summary: Booted the Pi from the new USB SSD after a clean Ansible build, and DNS and NUT both came up without manual steps
body:
The SSD arrived and I did the migration this morning. I flashed the OS to the SSD from the laptop, enabled SSH with the key, and set the boot order to USB first.

After the first boot I ran the site playbook against the Pi. It failed once on the NUT role because the udev rule for the UPS USB device was missing in the repo. I had made that rule by hand years ago. I added it to the role and ran again.

The second run completed with 3 changed tasks at the end. Pi-hole came up empty, and the sync script filled it from the other server within a minute. Unbound answered, and dig for a DNSSEC test domain returned the ad flag.

NUT saw the UPS and upsc showed battery charge and runtime. I did not pull the plug, but I ran the shutdown test in dry mode, upsmon -c fsd with the NAS client disabled, and the logs showed the right sequence.

Boot time is 19 seconds instead of 48, and the Pi feels much faster over SSH. The old card is labeled and kept as a rollback for two weeks.

I updated the docs with the real time it took, about 50 minutes from start to working.

summary: Weekly update broke Pi-hole on the LXC after a Pi-hole major release changed the config file layout, so I pinned the version and wrote down the upgrade path
body:
This morning the second DNS server stopped answering. Uptime Kuma showed the DNS check red for that host only, and the Pi was fine, so clients kept resolving.

On the LXC, pihole-FTL was in a restart loop. The log said it could not read the config, and a new file pihole.toml had appeared. A Pi-hole major release moves most settings from setupVars.conf into one TOML file, and the update on the LXC had run automatically through unattended upgrades.

The Pi had not updated yet because the SSD migration reset its apt state and the timer had not fired. That is luck, not design.

I first tried pihole -r repair. It reached the migration but left the upstream pointing at the public resolver instead of Unbound. I fixed that in the TOML by hand and the service came up, but the setting differed from the Ansible template.

The real fix was in the role. The template now writes pihole.toml, with the upstream as 127.0.0.1#5335 and the listening mode, and the old setupVars template is only used for versions before the change. I selected between them with a variable for the major version.

The sync script was also affected. The groups and adlists tables kept their layout, so that part still worked, but the custom DNS records moved from a file into the TOML. I changed the script to use the pihole-FTL config command for records.

I tested by rebuilding the LXC from zero with the new role, which took 7 minutes, then ran the sync from the Pi. Custom records arrived, and the internal AAAA names also resolved.

Afterwards I disabled unattended upgrades for the pihole packages with an apt pin on both hosts. Updates for Pi-hole will happen by hand, one host after the other, with the Pi first only when the LXC proved fine.

The Pi is still on the old version and will be upgraded tomorrow using the same steps.

summary: Upgraded the Pi to the new Pi-hole release using the tested role and confirmed that both DNS servers now give identical answers
body:
Did the Pi upgrade tonight, after yesterday's LXC repair. I took a copy of /etc/pihole and the gravity database to the NAS first.

I ran the role with the new major version variable. The install migrated the old settings into pihole.toml, and the role then overwrote it with the template. I compared the migrated file with the template and found two differences: a rate limit value and the webserver port. I kept the template values.

The sync timer was restarted and ran once. The LXC received the custom records and group assignments with no error in the journal.

To compare the two servers, I queried 200 names from the Pi-hole top domains list on both and diffed the answers. There were no differences for blocked or allowed domains, and the internal names matched too.

Uptime Kuma stayed green throughout, because the LXC answered while the Pi restarted.

I removed the leftover setupVars.conf template path from the role comments, but kept the version switch for old hosts.

summary: Looked at why Jellyfin library scans take two hours since the metadata move and found the scan runs over an NFS mount with attribute caching switched off
body:
Library scans in Jellyfin had grown from 25 minutes to about two hours. I suspected the new metadata directory, but the earlier backup work showed that was a file count problem, not a scan one.

I checked the mount options of the media share inside the VM with findmnt. It used NFS with noac, which disables attribute caching. That option was added months ago when a rename on the NAS was not visible for a while, and it stayed.

With noac every stat call goes to the NAS, and a scan does hundreds of thousands of them. I measured with a find over the movies folder: 3 minutes 40 seconds with noac, and 41 seconds with the default caching.

I replaced noac with actimeo=30 in the Ansible mount definition, remounted, and restarted the Jellyfin container. The mount-wait check from the power loss work still passed.

A full scan after the change took 31 minutes. Metadata and cache folders are on local disk, so only the media reads use the share.

The delay for new files is now up to 30 seconds, which is fine, since Jellyfin watches for changes with a delay of its own. I added a comment to the mount task that explains why noac was removed, so nobody puts it back.

I will leave it a week and check whether any file shows up late.

summary: Wrote a restore runbook that covers each service with the actual commands and timings from the three restore tests, and put the vault password location in it
body:
The restore tests this year proved the paths, but the knowledge was spread over journal notes. Today I collected it in docs/restore.md in the repo.

The runbook has one section per case: a single file from the NAS repository, the Pi-hole LXC, the Home Assistant VM, and the whole Proxmox host. Each section lists the restic command with the repository path, the expected time from the tests, and the checks to run afterwards.

The timings come from the real runs: 4 minutes for the LXC and 41 minutes for the VM. The Proxmox host case has no measured time, so I marked it as untested and listed what it depends on.

The vault password problem from the earlier test is addressed in a first section. The password now lives in the password manager, a sealed paper copy at a relative's house, and an encrypted file on the NAS. I verified that each of the three opens the repository by doing a restic snapshots with it.

I also noted that the cloud bucket uses a separate key and where it is stored, since it is needed if the NAS is lost.

The last part is a list of what is not backed up on purpose, such as the media files themselves and the Jellyfin transcode cache.

summary: Tested restoring the Proxmox host configuration into a spare VM and found that the backup lacked /etc/pve for nested storage definitions, then added it
body:
The runbook marked the Proxmox host restore as untested, so I tried it today. A real host cannot be wiped, so I built a nested Proxmox in a VM on the same host and restored the backed up host files into it.

The backup job already covers /etc, but on Proxmox the cluster file system in /etc/pve is a FUSE mount from a database file. The restic job read it fine while running, so the files were there, but I found the storage.cfg and the VM definitions were present only as that snapshot of the mount.

First problem: restoring the files over the nested host's /etc/pve is not possible when pve-cluster is running. I stopped pve-cluster and pmxcfs, and then restored the database file /var/lib/pve-cluster/config.db instead. That file was not in the backup at all.

I added /var/lib/pve-cluster to the backup includes and ran a one-off backup. The database is small, 280 KB, and sqlite handles a copy while running, but to be safe the job now makes a dump with sqlite3 .backup into a staging directory first and backs up that.

Second problem: after restoring, the nested host showed VMs but their disks were missing. That is expected, since the disk images are backed up separately through vzdump. The storage definitions pointed at the NAS, and they worked once the NAS share was reachable from the nested VM.

Third: the network config in /etc/network/interfaces named the physical NIC of the real host, so the bridge had no port. I noted the NIC rename step in the runbook.

After fixing these, I started a restored LXC from the vzdump archive on the nested host. It booted and ran Pi-hole, which answered a test query.

Total time for the host config part was about 25 minutes, plus the time of the restore of the disks which I did not repeat. I updated the runbook with the real steps and changed the status from untested to tested with the three caveats.

The nested VM is deleted again. The next thing is to make the backup staging step part of the Ansible role, which I did at the end, and I ran the role once to confirm it creates the dump directory.

summary: The nightly backup alerted because the new staging dump step failed once on a full /tmp, so I moved the staging directory to the data disk
body:
The Uptime Kuma push for the backup was missing this morning. The log showed the sqlite dump step failing with no space left on device, in the staging directory under /tmp.

The /tmp on the Proxmox host is a small tmpfs, and a leftover file from a test had filled most of it. It is the same type of problem as the Pi-hole one earlier in the year, which I should have remembered.

I moved the staging directory to /var/backup-staging on the root disk and made the job clean it at the end with a trap, so a failed run does not leave files. I also removed the leftover test file.

The job was run by hand and finished in 38 minutes, with the push sent. Tonight's run will confirm the change.

summary: Checked the IPv6 delegated prefix after the ISP router rebooted and found the Pi-hole AAAA records for global addresses were stale, while ULA ones kept working
body:
The ISP router restarted overnight and the delegated /56 prefix changed. Clients with global addresses lost some internal names for a while.

The ULA design from the IPv6 rollout held: internal names answer with ULA addresses, so most things kept working. The stale ones were three custom AAAA records that I had put in with global addresses for external access testing.

I removed those records and replaced them with ULA addresses, in the same Ansible variable that generates the others. The sync script copied the change to the second server.

I also checked that the servers themselves did not take global addresses, since SLAAC is off for them. That was the case, and the laptop got a new global address from the new prefix as expected.

WireGuard used only ULA, so the tunnel was not affected. The phone connected and opened Jellyfin by name.

I added a note in the IPv6 docs: never put a global address in an internal record.

summary: Uptime Kuma update changed the monitor import format and the Ansible sync script failed with a schema error, so I adapted it and pinned the image
body:
After the weekly container update, the monitor sync script failed with a validation error on the field accepted_statuscodes. The new Uptime Kuma major version changed some field names in its API.

The monitors in the UI were intact, since the database migrated fine. Only the push from the repo broke, so the monitor list in git could no longer be applied.

I read the changelog and found two renames and one new required field for the notification list. I changed the template that builds each monitor and the sync script. A dry run showed no differences for 30 monitors, which means the state read back matches the repo.

The script also had a bug that I noticed while in there: it did not remove monitors that were deleted from monitors.yml. I added a prune option, off by default, and a log line that lists what would be removed.

I pinned the Uptime Kuma tag in the compose file like the Home Assistant one. The update script now prints when a pinned image has a newer tag, so I see it without applying it.

The lesson is the same as before: a major version should be read before it runs.

summary: Investigated slow Samba transfers from the laptop to the NAS, found a duplex mismatch on a switch port after a cable swap, and fixed it by replacing the cable
body:
Copying large files from the laptop to the NAS had dropped to about 12 MB/s, where it used to be 110. The laptop on Wi-Fi was not the cause, since the wired dock showed the same.

First I ran iperf3 between the laptop and the Proxmox host, which gave 940 Mbit/s, so the laptop side was fine. Then iperf3 to the NAS gave only 95 Mbit/s. That pointed at the NAS link.

On the NAS, ethtool is limited, but the DSM network page said the link was at 100 Mbps full duplex. The port should negotiate 1 Gbps. The switch's own page agreed with 100 Mbps for that port.

I remembered that I swapped the cable when moving the NAS next to the UPS. The new cable was an old one from a drawer. Cat5 cables can work at 1 Gbps, but a damaged one drops to 100 when a pair is bad.

I replaced it with a Cat6 cable, and the port came up at 1 Gbps at once. iperf3 then showed 935 Mbit/s and a copy of a 20 GB file ran at 108 MB/s.

There were also CRC errors on the switch port counter, 4,300 before the swap. I cleared the counters and will look tomorrow to see whether they stay at zero.

I wrote a small check script that reads the link speed from the Proxmox host's view of the NAS port through the switch's SNMP, and added it to Uptime Kuma as a push monitor. It goes red if any server port is below 1000 Mbps.

The backup job also ran over this slow link for days. The recent runs were slower, and I only saw it as noise, since the job still finished before morning.

summary: Planned a monthly maintenance routine as an Ansible playbook that checks SMART, restic integrity, certificate expiry, pending updates and link speeds, and wrote its first half
body:
The small checks had grown across many places: SMART, backup integrity, certificates, link speed, updates. I decided to make one monthly playbook that runs them all and prints a report.

The design is simple. Each check is a role with a result variable: ok, warn or fail, plus a text line. The playbook ends with a task that prints a table and exits non-zero if any check failed. It runs from the laptop, because the laptop can reach every host.

Today I wrote the first four roles. The SMART role runs smartctl on the Proxmox host disks and over SSH on the NAS, and compares the reallocated sector count with the value saved last month in a small file in the repo. The one disk with errors showed 8 as before, so it reports warn but no growth.

The certificate role asks Caddy through openssl s_client for the expiry of each public name and warns under 21 days. All were above 60 days.

The link role calls the SNMP script from last week for each switch port that has a server. All gave 1000 Mbps, and the CRC counter on the NAS port was still zero after the cable swap.

The update role lists images with newer tags than the pinned ones, using the update script's list mode, and the apt role lists pending security updates on every host. There were 6 pending on the LXC.

Some issues came up. The SMART role needs sudo on the NAS, and the NAS user cannot sudo without a password. I used the smartctl path allowed in the sudoers file for that user, and noted it.

The SNMP community string is a secret, so it is in the vault file with the other credentials. The playbook asks for the vault password once.

Remaining: the restic integrity role and the report formatting. The roles are tagged so I can run just one. A dry run of the four finished in 90 seconds.

I did not schedule it yet, since the output should be read by a person first, and then maybe sent to my email.

summary: Finished the second half of the monthly maintenance playbook, covering restic integrity, certificate expiry, pending updates and link speeds, and its first run found one slow port.
body:
Today I finished the monthly maintenance playbook that I started last week with the SMART checks. The second half adds four checks: restic integrity for both repositories, certificate expiry for every Caddy hostname, pending package updates on the VMs, LXC containers and the Pi, and the negotiated link speed of each wired host.

For restic, the role runs 'restic check --read-data-subset=5%' against the NAS repository and the cloud bucket. A full read of the bucket would cost egress and take most of a day. A random 5% slice each month should cover the whole repository over a year or two, and the playbook prints the subset it used so a failure can be reproduced. The NAS check took 11 minutes and the bucket check took 19. Both passed with no errors.

The certificate check uses the 'openssl s_client' command from the Proxmox host against each name in the Caddy list. It fails the play if any certificate has fewer than 21 days left. I tested it by temporarily lowering the threshold to 90 days, and it correctly flagged all of them. Then I put it back to 21.

The pending updates check runs 'apt list --upgradable' and counts the results. It does not install anything, because the weekly container script and my own judgment decide that. It only reports the counts and lists security updates separately.

The link speed check reads /sys/class/net/*/speed over SSH and compares it with the expected speed in host_vars. On the first run it flagged the Pi at 100 Mb/s instead of 1000. The cable is the cause, and I will swap it on the weekend. The other hosts were all at the expected speed. It is good to know the check catches the kind of problem I only found by accident with the Samba transfers.

The playbook writes a short summary to a file and posts it to an Uptime Kuma push monitor, so a month without a run turns the monitor red. What is left is a systemd timer on the Proxmox host to run it on the first of each month, and a note in the runbook about what each failure means.

summary: Checked the SSD cache wear on the NAS after yesterday's report and found the daily write volume is low enough for years of life, so no purchase yet
body:
The maintenance report showed 61 percent wear on the NAS SSD cache, so I looked at how fast it moves. The SMART data has total bytes written and the power-on hours.

The drive has written 38 TB in about 2.6 years, which is about 40 GB per day. Its rated endurance is 150 TB, and the wear indicator of 61 percent is stricter than that number suggests. By the byte count, there would be 8 more years.

The wear percentage and the byte count disagree, which happens when the firmware counts write amplification. I used the faster of the two and assumed about 14 months to the point of 100 percent, as a pessimistic case.

The cache is only a read cache, so a failure costs only speed. I checked in DSM that it is not configured as read-write, and that was right.

I decided to buy nothing now, and added the wear value to the report with a warn at 80 percent. That gives a few months of notice, which is enough to order a drive.

summary: Power cut at night: the UPS chain shut everything down cleanly, but Home Assistant came back with the Zigbee stick on a different device path, which I fixed with a stable udev name
body:
A power cut of about 25 minutes happened in the night. The UPS log on the Pi showed the switch to battery at 02:11, the low-battery shutdown signal at 02:31, and the NAS going down last, as designed in the pull-the-plug test.

When the power came back, the Proxmox host started on its own, the NAS mounted first and Jellyfin waited for it, as the start-up order fix from earlier does. DNS answered from both servers within a few minutes. Those parts worked without help.

Home Assistant was up, but all Zigbee devices were unavailable. The integration log said it could not open /dev/ttyUSB0. The USB stick had enumerated as /dev/ttyUSB1 on this boot, because another USB serial device, the UPS cable, grabbed the first number.

As a short fix I changed the path in the integration settings and the devices returned after a restart. But that only holds until the next reorder, so I fixed it properly.

On the Proxmox host, I looked up the stick's vendor and product IDs and serial with udevadm info. I wrote a udev rule that creates /dev/zigbee for that serial, and put it in the Ansible role for the host. The USB passthrough in the VM definition now uses the vendor and product ID instead of the host port, so it follows the stick.

In the Home Assistant VM, the stick appears as a serial device, and I set the integration to the by-id path, which contains the serial and so is stable.

To test it, I unplugged and replugged the stick and then rebooted the VM. The devices were back in 40 seconds with no manual step. I also swapped the USB port, and it still worked.

The check for this was added to the maintenance playbook: it fails if the integration's configured path is not a by-id path. That is a quick grep on the config storage file.

Other things I checked after the outage: the restic job that was due at 03:00 had been skipped, and ran at boot because the timer is persistent. It finished at 06:20, a bit late, and the Uptime Kuma push arrived. The router's DHCP leases survived, and the ISP prefix did not change this time.

The battery of the UPS showed 100 percent again after 5 hours of charging. The runtime estimate was 36 minutes at the current load, and the cut used about 60 percent of it, so there is margin.

I wrote the incident in docs/power.md with the times, since it is the first real test of the whole shutdown chain.

summary: After the power cut, I audited every service for hardcoded device paths and found two more that would break on a reboot, then fixed them with stable names in the repo.
body:
The Zigbee stick moved to a different device path after the power cut, so I looked for other places where the repo depends on device names that can change. I grepped the compose files, the Ansible roles and the Proxmox VM configs for /dev/ttyUSB, /dev/sd and /dev/net paths.

Three hits turned up. The Zigbee one was already fixed with the udev rule. The NUT driver config on the Pi pointed at a USB bus path that depends on the port, and the Proxmox VM for Home Assistant passed through a USB device by bus and port number rather than by vendor and product id.

I changed the NUT config to match on the vendor and product id of the UPS and left the serial empty because the UPS does not report one. The Home Assistant VM now passes through by vendor and product id too. I edited the roles/nut template and the host_vars for the Proxmox host.

To test, I moved the UPS cable to another USB port on the Pi. Before the change upsc failed with a driver not connected error. After the change, the driver found the UPS on the new port after I restarted nut-driver, and upsc showed the battery at 100 percent.

I did not do the same test with the Zigbee stick because the udev rule is already tested. I ran the Ansible playbook with --check first, and it showed only the two expected changes. Then I ran it for real and both services restarted cleanly.

I also added a short note to the runbook that says to use ids and not paths for any new USB device. Left to do is a power test of the whole chain again, which I want to do on a day when nobody is watching a film.

summary: Pulled the plug on the UPS input in a planned test and confirmed the whole shutdown chain and the clean startup now work with the stable USB names.
body:
This evening I repeated the power failure test on purpose, since the real one had exposed the device path problem. I told the household first, closed Jellyfin sessions and made sure no backup was running.

I unplugged the UPS from the wall at 20:40 and watched the logs. NUT on the Pi saw the on-battery state straight away. The low-battery threshold is set generously, so the shutdown did not start at once. I had lowered the delay for the test to two minutes so the test would not take long.

After the delay, the Pi sent the shutdown signal. The NAS shut down first, then the Proxmox host, which stopped its VMs in order. Home Assistant went down cleanly in about forty seconds. The Proxmox host took about three minutes in total because of the Jellyfin container.

Then I plugged the UPS back in. The UPS powers the machines on again only when the battery has some charge, and the NAS and Proxmox booted by themselves through their BIOS and settings. Everything was back in about eight minutes.

I checked the points that went wrong last time. The Zigbee stick appeared under the stable name. The NUT driver found the UPS. Pi-hole answered on both DNS servers. Uptime Kuma showed all monitors green after ten minutes, and it recorded the outage as one gap.

One small thing I noticed: the NAS volume check ran after boot because of the shutdown, and it only took a few minutes. I put the delay back to its normal value in the host_vars and committed the change with the test result in the message.

summary: Looked at why Uptime Kuma notified me about the outage only after the services were already back, and moved its alerts to a channel that does not depend on the home network.
body:
During the power test, the alert from Uptime Kuma arrived about ten minutes after the machines had come back. That made me think about what would happen in a real outage: the Kuma container runs on the Proxmox host, so it is down at the same time as everything else.

There are two parts to this. First, a monitor can only tell me about its own downtime after it returns. Second, the notification goes through an email service over the internet, which needs the router to be up as well.

I looked at the options. A monitor outside the house would be the real answer. I decided on a free external heartbeat service that expects a ping from Kuma every five minutes and sends me a message if it stops. The push monitor in Kuma supports this.

I added a push monitor in the Kuma config on the Ansible side and put the heartbeat URL in the secrets file, not in the compose file. The sync script created it without errors. I then stopped the Kuma container for seven minutes to see if the external service would react.

It did, with a message on my phone after the grace period. When I started the container again, the recovery message arrived within a minute.

The limit is clear: a message says the house is silent, not why. I wrote that in the runbook. I did not add more monitors from outside, because one heartbeat is enough for a home setup.

summary: Tried a newer kernel on the Proxmox host to fix a rare network hang, saw it fail to boot cleanly with the NIC driver, and went back to the old kernel.
body:
The Proxmox host has had one network hang in a month where the NIC stopped answering until I reset the link. The log showed a TX timeout from the e1000e driver, which is a known problem with some hardware offload settings.

I first tried the usual fix of turning off TSO and GSO for the interface. That is easy to put in the interfaces file with a post-up line. I did that and left it for two days, and it was fine, but a rare problem proves nothing in two days.

So I also installed the newer opt-in kernel from the Proxmox repository to see if the driver was improved. After the reboot the NIC came up, but the boot took very long, and the log had a message about firmware loading failing for the driver. Network came up late and the VMs started before the bridge was ready, so two of them had no link.

I did not want to debug that, so I pinned the previous kernel with proxmox-boot-tool and rebooted. Boot time returned to normal and the bridge came up before the VMs.

I kept the offload workaround in the Ansible role for the host, with a comment that explains why it is there. I removed the newer kernel package. If the hang comes back, I will look at the NIC itself, or put in a cheap PCIe card.

summary: Planned and started moving the Caddy config into an Ansible role, because the reverse proxy was the last service still edited by hand on the host.
body:
Caddy was the last service that I still edited directly on the VM. Everything else is built from the repo, so a rebuild of the proxy would need the runbook and memory. I started to fix that today.

First I copied the live Caddyfile and compose file into the repo to see the real state. They differed from the old copy in the repo in three places: a new site block for Home Assistant with websocket support, a header change for Jellyfin, and the DNS challenge token now read from the secrets file.

I designed the role like the Pi-hole one. It has a template for the Caddyfile with a list of sites in the variables, a template for the compose file, and a handler that validates the config with caddy validate before reloading. Validation inside the container uses docker exec so that it checks the same binary that runs.

The site list in the variables has name, upstream and an optional extra block. Eight sites fit that, and two special ones use the extra block for headers. I kept the Caddyfile readable, since I will be reading the generated file during problems.

The secrets file stays outside the role and is managed with ansible-vault, as before. The role only mounts it into the container as an env file.

I ran the role with --check --diff against the live VM. The diff showed only whitespace and the order of the site blocks. I fixed the order in the template to match, and the diff went to zero except for a comment line.

I did not apply anything yet. Next is a test on a scratch VM with a staging certificate, so I do not hit the rate limit of the real certificate authority. That is for the next session.

summary: Built a scratch VM from the new Caddy role and got a staging certificate, which proved the role works from nothing.
body:
I cloned the template VM in Proxmox and ran the new Caddy role against it. For the test I pointed the ACME setting to the staging endpoint with a variable, so no real certificates were issued.

The first run failed because the role did not install Docker on the scratch machine. The common role does that, so I added it to the test playbook and not to the Caddy role.

The second run worked. Caddy started, validated its config and requested a certificate for a test name through the DNS challenge. The staging certificate was issued in about forty seconds.

I checked with curl --resolve that the proxy answered for two of the sites, using a dummy upstream. Both gave the expected response and headers. Then I destroyed the VM. Next is the switch of the real proxy to the role.

summary: Applied the Caddy role to the real proxy VM, and all sites kept working with certificates unchanged after a short reload.
body:
This evening I ran the Caddy role against the live proxy. I did it at a quiet time and kept a copy of the old Caddyfile and compose file in /root on the VM.

The play showed three changes: the Caddyfile because of the comment line, the compose file because of a label and a restart of the container. The handler validated the config first and only then reloaded it.

After that I checked every site from the laptop and from a phone on mobile data. All eight answered, and the certificates had the same expiry dates as before, so nothing had been re-requested.

Uptime Kuma showed no gap longer than one check interval. I removed the old copy of the files from the VM after an hour. The reverse proxy is now built from the repo like the rest, and I updated the restore runbook to say so.

summary: Investigated why Jellyfin transcoding stutters on the Proxmox host and found the container has no access to the Intel iGPU render device, then fixed it and tested hardware transcoding.
body:
A family member told me that films stutter on the TV when the client asks for transcoding. I opened the Jellyfin dashboard during playback and saw ffmpeg using almost 100 percent of all CPU cores. That means software transcoding, which a small server handles badly.

The host has an Intel CPU with an integrated GPU, so hardware transcoding should be possible. I checked the host first. ls /dev/dri showed card0 and renderD128, and vainfo on the host listed the H.264 and HEVC profiles. So the hardware was fine.

Inside the Jellyfin container there was no /dev/dri at all. Jellyfin runs in an LXC container with Docker inside, so the device has to pass through two layers. In the Proxmox container config there was no device entry, so the first layer was missing.

I added a dev entry for /dev/dri/renderD128 to the LXC config with the right gid for the render group. In the container, the render group had a different gid than on the host, which is a common cause of permission errors. I set the gid in the entry to the container value.

Then I added the device to the Jellyfin compose file with the devices key and group_add for the render group. I restarted the LXC and the container.

vainfo inside the container worked now. In the Jellyfin settings I selected VA-API as the hardware acceleration and enabled the HEVC decoding options that the chip supports. Tone mapping stays off, because that needs more features than this iGPU has.
