For the test I started a 4K HEVC film on a client that forces transcoding to 1080p. CPU use stayed around 15 percent, and intel_gpu_top on the host showed the video engine busy. The film played without stutter for ten minutes.

I wrote the LXC device entry into the Ansible role for the Jellyfin container, so a rebuild keeps it. The gid is a variable now. I also put a line in the runbook about the two layers.

One point remains open. The ffmpeg log shows a fallback to software for one old file format, which is expected. I will watch whether that matters for anything people actually watch.

summary: Checked what the new hardware transcoding does to power use at the UPS and found about 20 W less during playback, which gives a longer runtime on battery.
body:
After the iGPU change, I wanted to know the effect on the load at the UPS, since the shutdown timing is based on runtime. NUT reports the load as a percentage of the UPS capacity.

I played the same film as before with transcoding and read upsc every ten seconds for five minutes. With software transcoding the load was about 38 percent in an earlier note. With hardware transcoding it was 29 percent, about 20 W less by my estimate for this UPS size.

Idle load without playback is 22 percent, so the difference is only during transcoding. The estimated runtime at idle is unchanged. The shutdown thresholds stay as they are. I put the numbers in the UPS section of the runbook.

summary: The monthly maintenance playbook reported a TLS certificate expiring in nine days for the Home Assistant site, and I traced it to a renewal that was blocked by an old DNS record.
body:
The monthly playbook flagged the Home Assistant certificate with only nine days left, while the others had weeks. Caddy should renew at thirty days, so something had failed.

The Caddy log showed repeated errors for that name: the DNS challenge could not be cleaned up because a stale TXT record for _acme-challenge was still in the zone from an earlier failed attempt. The provider refused to create a second one with the same name.

I deleted the old TXT record in the provider's panel and restarted the Caddy container. It renewed in under a minute. The playbook check now shows 89 days. I added a line to the runbook about this error message, since it will probably come back.

summary: Wrote a small script to export the Uptime Kuma monitors and compare them with the Ansible definition, so drift between the two shows up in the monthly run.
body:
Kuma monitors get edited by hand in the web interface when I am in a hurry, and then the repo no longer matches. I wrote a script that exports the monitors through the API and compares them with the YAML file in the repo.

The script prints three lists: monitors only in Kuma, monitors only in the repo, and monitors whose interval or URL differ. On the first run it found two monitors that existed only in Kuma, both added during the power test, and one interval that differed.

I added the two to the YAML and set the interval in the repo to the value I wanted. The script now reports no differences. I hooked it into the monthly playbook as a task that fails on any drift.

summary: The first scheduled run of the Ansible update playbook updated the containers in the wrong order and Caddy restarted before its backends, so I added ordering and a pause between groups.
body:
The new update playbook ran on its own for the first time at 03:00 and I read the log this morning. Everything ended up updated, but the monitor in Uptime Kuma showed about four minutes of failed checks for Jellyfin and Home Assistant. The cause was the order: the playbook looped over the hosts in inventory order, so the proxy VM pulled its image and restarted first, and the backends followed one by one.

Caddy itself was fine. It came back within seconds and kept its certificates. The failures came from the backends restarting while it was already serving, so the first requests to them got 502 responses until their health checks passed. Nothing was lost, but the alert at night is exactly what the playbook was meant to avoid.

I changed three things in the repo. First, the inventory now has three groups, data services, application services and proxy, and the playbook runs them in that order with serial set to one inside each group. Second, after each group a task waits until every container in it reports healthy, with a timeout of five minutes, and stops the run if one does not. Third, the Uptime Kuma pause is now set before the first group and lifted after the last, so a normal update produces no alerts at all.

I tested it in two steps. A dry run with --check showed the new order and the wait tasks, and then I ran it for real against the application group with an image that had a newer tag. Jellyfin took about 40 seconds to become healthy, Home Assistant about 90, and the playbook waited for both without error. A full run with nothing to update took under two minutes.

One thing is left open. The health check of Home Assistant looks a bit tight for its slow start, and I want to look at it separately before the next scheduled run. I also want the playbook to send a short summary of what changed to the alert channel, so I do not have to read the log each time.

summary: First scheduled run of the new update playbook rolled back Home Assistant after a failed health check, and I found the check was too strict for its slow start.
body:
The timer ran the update playbook at night, and in the morning the summary reported one rolled-back service: Home Assistant. Everything else was updated and healthy.

I read the playbook log. The new Home Assistant image had been pulled and started, and the health check waited its two minutes. Home Assistant took longer than that to answer after an update, because it migrates its database on first start. The playbook decided it had failed and went back to the old image.

That was bad in a quiet way. The old image then started on a database that had already been migrated, and Home Assistant refused to load it with a message that the database schema is newer than supported.

I restored the database from the nightly backup of the VM data and started the new image by hand. It came up after almost four minutes, and all integrations loaded, including Zigbee.

I made two changes. The health timeout is now a per-service value, and Home Assistant gets ten minutes. Second, I added a flag for services that migrate data on start. For those, the playbook does not roll back automatically but raises the alarm and leaves the new container running.

I tested the timeout with a manual run for Home Assistant alone, and the check passed after four minutes without a rollback. I noted the incident in the runbook, under the update section.

summary: Set up a restic check that restores a random sample of files from the cloud bucket every month and compares checksums, since an integrity check alone does not prove a restore works.
body:
The monthly playbook runs restic check, which verifies the repository structure and a share of the data. That tells me the repository is consistent, but not that I can get my files back from the cloud bucket at a sane speed. I added a restore sample test for that.

The task picks a random snapshot from the last month and then fifty random files from it. I used restic ls with json output and a small Python filter that selects files under a size limit, so the test does not download big media files. The files are restored into a temporary directory on the data disk.

Then the task compares each restored file with the live version by sha256. Files that changed since the snapshot would cause false alarms, so the comparison uses the file's modification time in the snapshot: if the live file has a newer mtime, it is skipped and counted separately.

The first run was against the NAS repository. Of fifty files, forty-seven matched and three were skipped because they had changed. The run took 40 seconds. Good.

The cloud run was slower: 3 minutes for the same count, mostly due to the latency of each request. All forty-nine non-skipped files matched. The download volume was small, so the egress cost is negligible, and I checked the bucket pricing page to be sure.

I made the sample size a variable, and added the elapsed time to the report so a slowdown in the cloud path would be visible month to month. A failure sends a notification and marks the playbook run as failed.

One more thing I did: I ran the check with a wrong repository password on purpose, and the task failed with the restic error and did not report a pass. A test that cannot fail is useless, so that mattered.

I updated the runbook with the new check and with the expected times. Later I want to add a full restore of one small service per quarter, but that is a bigger task and I will plan it separately.

summary: Reviewed the WireGuard setup after a phone could not connect from a hotel network, and found the UDP port is blocked there, so I added a second listener on port 443.
body:
A phone failed to bring up the VPN from a hotel network yesterday. The handshake never completed. At home and on mobile data it works, so the config is correct, and the network was the problem.

I looked at what the hotel might allow. Most guest networks pass only web traffic, and often UDP 443 is allowed because of QUIC, while the WireGuard port 51820 is dropped. I could not test the hotel again, so I tested from a phone with a hotspot of a friend whose provider blocks other UDP ports. The same failure.

The fix is a second listening port. The router forwards UDP 443 to the WireGuard host, and WireGuard itself listens on one port only. So I did the redirect on the host with an nftables rule that maps UDP 443 to 51820. That way there is one interface and one set of keys.

I put the rule in the Ansible role for WireGuard in a drop-in file for nftables, and made the role open the port in the host firewall. The router rule is manual, and I wrote it in the runbook with the exact menu path.

Next, the client side. I made a second profile for the phone and the laptop with the endpoint set to the same name and port 443. The profile has a different name so I can switch between the two. PersistentKeepalive stays at 25 because carrier NAT closes mappings fast.

Test: from the hotspot with blocked ports, the 443 profile connected in two seconds, and I could open Jellyfin and Home Assistant through the tunnel. The old profile still failed there, as expected, and worked on the home network.

I checked one risk: DNS inside the tunnel. Both DNS servers are reachable through the tunnel and the phone resolved local names. Pi-hole shows the VPN client under its own name since the earlier fix for per-client logging.

There is a small cost. The 443 profile gets traffic that looks like unknown UDP to some deep-inspection firewalls, so it may still fail in strict places. I do not have a fix for that and will not try one. The port 443 profile is enough for now.

summary: A disk in the Proxmox host showed a growing count of pending sectors, so I moved the VM storage to the spare disk, ran the extended test, and decided to replace it.
body:
The monthly SMART task reported the Proxmox host's SSD with a rising wear indicator, and the NVMe log showed media errors for the first time. The count was small, but it was zero last month, and this disk holds all VMs and the LXC containers.

I started with a fresh backup. I ran the vzdump of every guest to the NAS, outside the nightly schedule, and verified that the archives listed correctly. That took forty minutes.

Then I checked the numbers properly with smartctl -a and nvme smart-log. Percentage used was 41, which is not high, but media and data integrity errors was 6. Available spare was still 100 percent. The error log had entries with read errors in one region.

A drive with six media errors and no spare use is not necessarily dying, but I do not want the VM disks on it. I had an older SATA SSD in a drawer that is healthy. I added it as a second storage in Proxmox, and moved the disks of the less critical guests to it with the move disk function while they ran. The Home Assistant VM I moved while it was stopped, to avoid a write during the copy.

The copy of the largest disk took twenty-five minutes. After the moves, I ran the extended self-test on the NVMe disk from the host. It finished without a failed status, but the error counter went up to eight during the test, in the same area.

That settled it. I ordered a new NVMe drive of the same size, with a better endurance rating than the old one, since the Home Assistant recorder and the Jellyfin metadata write a lot.

Until it arrives, the guests run from the SATA SSD. I checked the speed with a quick fio run: sequential speeds are lower, but random IO is fine for these services, and Jellyfin seems unaffected.

I updated the storage definitions in the Ansible variables for the host, so that the repo shows the current state, with a comment that it is temporary. The restore runbook has the same note.

When the new disk is here, I will install it, restore or move the guests back, and wipe the old one. I will also add the NVMe error counter to the monthly check as a hard failure, not a warning.

summary: The new NVMe drive arrived, and I installed it, added it as storage, and moved the guests back from the temporary SATA disk without downtime except Home Assistant.
body:
I shut down the host for the swap since the board has no hot-plug. The UPS-driven shutdown order kept things tidy. After the new NVMe was in, the host booted from its own boot disk, and the new drive showed up as nvme1n1 with a clean SMART log.

I created a new LVM-thin storage on it and added it in Proxmox under the name from the Ansible variables, so the earlier names in the repo are valid again. Then I moved the guest disks back one by one with the move disk function and the option to delete the source. Most moved while running. Home Assistant was stopped for the move and was down for about eight minutes.

I checked that everything started on reboot and that backups still worked with a manual vzdump of two guests. The temporary storage definition is removed from the variables and from the runbook.

The old NVMe I wiped with a secure erase, labelled and put in the drawer. The NVMe error counter is now a hard failure in the monthly playbook.

summary: Looked into a slow web interface on the NAS and found a runaway indexing service eating memory, then limited it and moved the media index to run at night only.
body:
The NAS web interface took ten seconds to open this morning, and file browsing from the laptop was slow. Over SSH, top showed the memory almost full and a lot of swap use. The biggest process was the media indexing daemon, using more than 1.5 GB.

The indexer runs whenever it notices new files. Since I added the new metadata directories and more media a few weeks ago, it had been reindexing in the background with little pause. The NAS has only 4 GB of RAM, so that is a real strain on it.

I looked at what I actually use. The indexing is for the NAS's own media apps, and I do not use them because Jellyfin does the job. So the simplest fix is to turn the indexing off for the folders that Jellyfin owns, and keep it only for the photo share, where I use the NAS's search.

I removed the media and metadata folders from the indexed folders in the settings. Then I stopped the indexer, which freed the memory at once. Swap use stayed high for a while, so I ran swapoff and swapon through SSH to clear it, which took about a minute with the load low.

After that the web interface opened in two seconds. I let the NAS run for a few hours and checked memory again: 1.1 GB used by all services, no swap.

I also looked at the other packages that start with the NAS. Two of them I never use, a video station and a note app. I stopped them and disabled their autostart. That gave back another 300 MB.

The lesson for the repo is that the NAS settings are not under Ansible, as the NAS has no good module for them. So I wrote the settings I changed in a document in the repo under docs, with the list of enabled packages and the indexed folders. If the NAS needs a reset one day, I will not have to remember it.

I added a memory check to the monthly playbook that reads free memory and swap use over SSH and warns when swap is above 500 MB. I ran it and it reports a pass now.

I am not sure the memory is enough over time. If the problem comes back, the better answer is to add RAM, since the model has a free slot, and a module is cheap.

summary: Planned the migration of Pi-hole's long-term query logs to a separate small store, after the FTL database on the Pi grew to 2 GB and slowed down the dashboard.
body:
The Pi-hole dashboard on the Pi takes several seconds to load its charts, and the FTL database file has grown to 2 GB. The default retention is 91 days, and I increased it a year ago because I liked looking at old numbers. The Pi now runs from a USB SSD, so space is not a problem, but the queries are slow and the database is written all the time.

I looked at the data first. A sqlite query on the queries table showed about 38 million rows. Most of them are from the same few noisy clients: a smart TV, the robot vacuum and a phone with a chatty app. Those make up two thirds of the rows.

I considered three options. One is cutting the retention back to 30 days, which solves the speed at once. Another is keeping the long history in a separate place by exporting rows weekly. The third is ignoring the noisy clients in the log. I do not look at old data much. I mostly want the last month, and long-term trends for counts only.

So my plan has three steps. First, set the retention to 45 days. Second, before pruning, export daily counts per client and per domain category into a small CSV file kept in the repo data directory, which is enough for trends, a few kilobytes per day. Third, stop logging the TV and the vacuum at the DNS level by using the privacy setting that hides their domains, but still lets them be blocked.

I wrote a draft of the export script in Python with sqlite3 that reads the FTL database in read-only mode and writes one CSV line per client per day. I ran it against a copy of the database and checked that the sums matched the totals of the dashboard for three random days. They did.

The second DNS server has the same issue, but its database is smaller because it is newer. I will use the same settings on both through the Ansible role, and the sync script does not copy the database, so there is no conflict.

A risk I thought about: pruning a large sqlite file takes a while and locks the database, so the DNS service could stall. I will do it in a quiet hour, with the second server answering the queries, which is exactly why it exists.

Tomorrow I will run the export for real, set the retention in the role, and apply it to the Pi at night. After that I will vacuum the file and compare the dashboard loading time. The script and the plan are committed.

summary: Ran the Pi-hole log cleanup: exported daily counts, cut retention to 45 days, vacuumed the FTL database from 2 GB to 400 MB, and the dashboard loads in under a second.
body:
This morning I carried out the plan from yesterday for the Pi-hole database. I started with the export script on the real database, in read-only mode. It wrote 5,400 lines of daily counts for about fifteen months and took less than a minute. I checked a few random lines against the dashboard to be sure.

Then I changed the role. The retention variable is 45 days now, and the template sets it in the FTL config. I applied the role to the second DNS server first, as the test, since its database is small. It restarted FTL without trouble and clients kept resolving.

For the Pi, I stopped DNS service on it deliberately. Clients and the VPN fall back to the second server, and I watched the query counter there go up as expected. On the Pi I ran the role, which restarted FTL, and FTL started deleting old rows at startup.

The delete took about four minutes and the file was still 2 GB afterwards, because sqlite does not shrink a file by itself. I stopped FTL again and ran sqlite3 with VACUUM on the database. That took six minutes and left a file of about 400 MB. Then I started FTL and checked that the gravity database and the lists were untouched.

The Pi was back in service after about fifteen minutes in total. Both servers gave identical answers in the check script that compares them.

The dashboard now opens in under a second, and the query log page works with the filters again. For the noisy devices I set the privacy level for their group, but I found that the setting is global in this release, not per client. So I left it out and kept full logging, since the shorter retention solved most of the problem.

I added the export script to a weekly timer on the Pi so the CSV continues to grow before rows are deleted. The runbook has a short section about the history file and where it lives. Open point: the CSV is in the repo data directory, which the backup covers, but I want to check that it does not grow into something large. At the current rate it is under 1 MB a year, so it is fine.

summary: After the Pi-hole log cleanup I moved the long-term query statistics into a small daily-counts store and a weekly report, so history survives the 45-day retention.
body:
The cleanup this morning cut retention to 45 days, which means older detail is gone for good. I wanted to keep the trend data, so I built a small script that runs nightly on the Pi and writes the daily totals into a SQLite file outside the FTL database.

The script reads the FTL database read-only through sqlite3 and groups queries by day, by client and by status (allowed, blocked, cached). It writes one row per day and client into /srv/dns-stats/daily.sqlite. The first run imported the export from this morning, which gave 212 days of history.

I put the script in the repo under ansible/roles/pihole/files/dns-daily.py and added a systemd timer at 03:10. The timer is templated by the role, so a rebuilt Pi gets it again. The stats directory is a bind path on the data partition, not on the SD card, to avoid writes on the card.

The weekly report is a second small script that prints the top ten blocked domains, the share of blocked queries and the busiest client. It sends the text to the notification channel I moved Uptime Kuma to last month. The first report said 23 percent of queries were blocked, and the busiest client was the smart TV, with about 4 times the queries of the laptop.

The TV result made me check its behaviour. It asks for the same telemetry domains about every 5 seconds. I did not block more yet, because the TV breaks when its update check fails, so I only noted it in the role's README.

I added the stats file to the restic backup paths for the Pi. A test run showed the file is 380 KB, so it costs nothing. I also ran a restore of it into /tmp and opened it with sqlite3 to make sure it is readable.

One problem came up: the timer fired while FTL was vacuuming and the read hit a lock for 8 seconds. I set a busy timeout of 30 seconds in the script and it passed. Next I want a small graph in Home Assistant from this file, but that is not urgent.

summary: The weekly DNS report ran by itself for the first time and its numbers matched a manual count, so the stats pipeline on the Pi is trusted now.
body:
Yesterday's report was only a first run on imported data. Today the timer produced the nightly rows for a real full day, and I compared them with a manual query on the FTL database.

The manual count for the previous day was 41,870 queries, and the daily table had 41,870. The blocked count differed by 2, which I traced to queries that arrived between the end of the day boundary and the timer. I changed the script to use a fixed end timestamp at midnight instead of the current time.

After the change I deleted that day's rows and re-ran the script, and both counts were equal. The script is now idempotent: it replaces the rows of a day instead of appending, so a repeated run does no harm.

I also checked the timer log with journalctl and saw no lock waits. The run took 1.4 seconds.

The change went into the repo with a commit message about the boundary. I applied the role to the Pi with ansible-playbook and it reported one changed task, the script file.

Nothing else is left for this topic. The Home Assistant graph is a later idea.

summary: Added a Home Assistant sensor graph of daily blocked-query share from the Pi stats file, using a tiny HTTP endpoint instead of exposing the database.
body:
I wanted the DNS trend visible on the Home Assistant dashboard without giving it file access to the Pi. The stats file stays on the Pi, and I wrote a very small read-only script that serves the last 30 days as JSON on the LAN.

The script is a Python http.server handler of about 40 lines. It listens on port 8099 only on the LAN address and answers a single path. It runs as a systemd service with a dedicated user, which has read access only to the stats directory.

In Home Assistant I added a REST sensor that polls it every hour. The sensor value is the blocked share of the latest full day, and the 30 days are an attribute. A history graph card shows the value over time.

The first attempt showed the sensor as unavailable. The cause was the Pi firewall, which only allowed port 80 and 53 from the LAN. I added 8099 to the role's nftables rules for the Home Assistant address only.

After that the sensor showed 22.8 percent. I checked that another LAN machine could not read the endpoint, and it was refused as intended.

Both the service and the firewall rule are in the Ansible role. I did not add authentication, since the data is only daily counts and the rule limits the source.

The card is on the network dashboard now, next to the UPS values.

summary: Investigated why the nightly restic backup to the cloud bucket took 3 hours more than usual and found a new Jellyfin metadata folder with a million tiny files.
body:
The backup alert showed a duration of 5 h 40 min, compared to the usual 2 h 30. I looked at the restic log for the cloud job to see where the time went.

The scan phase was normal, but the upload phase had a long tail of small files. The summary listed 1.1 million new files, which is far more than any day before. The new files were under the Jellyfin config path, in a folder named metadata/library.

I traced it to the change of hardware transcoding a few weeks ago. Since then, Jellyfin had been generating trickplay images, small thumbnails for scrubbing, for the whole library. Each video got a folder with hundreds of small JPEG files.

I checked the size with du: the folder had 14 GB in 1.1 million files. The size was not the problem, the file count was, because each file costs a request to the bucket.

I had three options. I could turn off trickplay, exclude the folder from the backup, or keep it. The images can be regenerated from the media, so the backup is not needed for them, and the feature is useful.

I chose to exclude the folder. I added the path to the restic exclude file in the repo, under the Jellyfin section, with a comment that the data is regenerable.

I also thought about the restore runbook. It says Jellyfin metadata is restored from backup, so I added a line that trickplay is regenerated after a restore and takes several hours.

The next run was manual. It finished in 2 h 21 min, and the snapshot had only 312 new files. The old snapshots still hold the folder, so the repository did not shrink yet.

I ran forget with the existing retention and a prune would free the space later. I started the prune at the end, and it will run for a while. I will check the repository size tomorrow.

summary: The restic prune after the trickplay exclusion finished and the cloud repository shrank from 1.9 TB to 1.7 TB, with the backup duration back to normal.
body:
The prune I started two days ago finished overnight. It took about 9 hours, mostly repacking.

The repository size in the bucket went from 1.9 TB to 1.7 TB according to restic stats. That is less than the 14 GB per snapshot would suggest, because most of the data was deduplicated across snapshots.

The last two nightly runs took 2 h 24 min and 2 h 28 min, so the extra time is gone. Uptime Kuma push monitor stayed green.

I ran a restic check with a small read subset after the prune and it reported no errors. The monthly sample restore compares checksums too, and I will see it in the next run.

Nothing more needs doing here.

summary: Planned and started a second Pi-hole instance sync with Gravity Sync replaced by a small Ansible-driven rsync of the lists, because the sync tool broke after the Pi-hole update.
body:
The second DNS server has been running for a while, and its blocklists were copied by a sync tool. After the last Pi-hole update the tool stopped working and printed a schema error about the gravity database.

I first looked at whether the tool had an update, and it did not. Rather than wait, I decided to manage the lists as configuration in the repo, which fits the Ansible approach for everything else.

The plan has three parts. The adlists, the allow and deny entries and the group settings become YAML files in the pihole role. A task applies them on both servers with the pihole CLI. A check compares the counts on both.

Today I did the first part. I exported the current adlists from the primary with sqlite3 on gravity.db and wrote them into group_vars/pihole/lists.yml. There were 14 adlists, 31 allow entries and 9 deny entries.

I found two adlists that return 404 now, and I removed them from the file. One allow entry was for a domain that no longer exists, and I removed it too.

Then I wrote the apply task. It uses pihole-FTL sqlite3 with insert-or-ignore statements for each entry and then runs pihole -g to update gravity. I tried it first on the secondary in check mode, which only prints the statements.

The statements looked right, but I noticed the group assignments were missing. Entries without a group assignment do not apply to any client. I added a join step that assigns each entry to the default group.

I ran it for real on the secondary. After gravity finished, the count of blocked domains was 1,214,330, and the primary showed 1,214,330 after the same run. The two servers agree again.

What is still open is the removal of entries. The task only adds, so an entry deleted from the YAML would remain. I will handle that next, with a delete of entries that are not in the file.

The old sync tool is still installed and its timer is failing. I disabled the timer for now so it stops raising alerts, and I will remove it when the new way has run for a few days.

summary: Made the Pi-hole list sync remove entries that are no longer in the YAML and added a count comparison check that alerts through Uptime Kuma when the two servers differ.
body:
This continues the list sync from this morning. The apply task only added entries, so I added the removal part.

The task now reads the existing entries of each type from gravity.db and builds the difference against the YAML. Entries in the database that are not in the file are deleted. I limited this to entries with the comment field set to ansible, so manual entries added through the web interface are not touched.

For that I changed the insert statements to write the comment ansible. The existing entries had no comment, so the first run would not own them. I ran a one-time update to mark all current entries with the comment, after checking that they equal the YAML.

To test it, I added a fake deny entry by hand with the ansible comment, then ran the playbook. It was removed. Then I added one without the comment, and it stayed. That is the behaviour I wanted.

The second part is the check. A small script on the monitoring VM asks both servers for the gravity domain count over the API and compares them. If the difference is more than 1000 domains, which can happen between gravity runs, it reports down.

I made it a push monitor in Uptime Kuma, and defined it in the Ansible monitor list so the drift script from earlier knows it. The first push was up with a difference of 0.

I also tested the failing case by stopping FTL on the secondary for a minute. The check went down after the next interval, and came back up after the restart.

The old sync tool is still disabled. I will remove it after a week of normal runs. The topic is finished except for that cleanup.

summary: Upgraded Proxmox from the current minor release and found that the Caddy VM lost its static IPv6 address after reboot, which I traced to a changed cloud-init network option.
body:
I applied the pending Proxmox package updates after checking the release notes. They contained a new qemu version and the usual kernel package, but I stayed on the old kernel as before.

Before the update I made a vzdump snapshot backup of the guests that matter, the proxy VM, Home Assistant and the DNS VM. The backups went to the NAS and took 14 minutes.

The host rebooted without trouble and all containers started. The monthly checks looked fine until I opened a site over IPv6, which timed out. IPv4 worked.

I logged in to the Caddy VM and saw that the interface had only a link-local IPv6 address. The static global address I had configured was missing. The ULA address was missing too.

The VM uses a cloud-init drive for its network config. After the qemu update, the generated network file looked different: the ipv6 line in the Proxmox VM config was set to auto, and the static address was no longer in it.

I compared with the file in the repo. The Terraform-like definition does not exist here, so the VM settings are in an Ansible task using qm set. The task sets ipconfig0 with ip and gw only for IPv4, and the IPv6 address had been added by hand months ago. The new qemu version regenerated the cloud-init drive, so the manual part was lost.

That means my earlier setup was not fully in the repo, which is exactly the kind of drift I try to avoid. I added the ip6 and gw6 values to the qm set task, with the address in the group variables.

I ran the task and rebooted the VM. The interface came up with both addresses, and the site answered over IPv6 within a few seconds.

I then checked the other guests for the same issue. The DNS VM had it configured in the playbook, so it was fine. The Home Assistant VM uses DHCPv6 and SLAAC, which came up correctly.

I also updated the AAAA records check in the monthly playbook. It now tests that each public site answers over IPv6 from the monitoring VM, not just that the record exists.

The remaining work is to run the full playbook once from scratch against a scratch VM, to be sure no other manual setting hides there. I will do that this week.

summary: Ran the VM definition playbook against a scratch clone and found no more hand-made settings, only a missing tag and a different disk cache mode.
body:
Following the IPv6 surprise yesterday, I wanted to know whether other VM settings exist only on the host. I cloned the proxy VM definition into a scratch VM with the playbook and compared the two configs with qm config.

The diff was short. The real VM had a tag named prod and the scratch had none. The real VM used cache=writeback on its disk, while the playbook left the default.

The tag is harmless, but I added it to the task for cleanliness. The cache mode matters a bit. Writeback is faster, but with the UPS and the clean shutdown it is acceptable. I wrote it into the variables so it is deliberate.

All other values were equal, including the CPU type, memory and the boot order.

I destroyed the scratch VM afterwards and ran the playbook against the real one in check mode. It reported no changes, so the repo matches the host now.

summary: Answered the question whether the Raspberry Pi SD card is a risk for Pi-hole and decided to move the root filesystem to a USB SSD that I already had.
body:
I asked myself how long the SD card in the Pi will last, since it holds the primary Pi-hole. I checked the writes with iostat and the card's total written bytes, which the kernel does not expose, so I used the daily average over a day of 1.2 GB.

That is low after the log cleanup, but SD cards fail suddenly and without SMART data. The card is about two years old.

I have a small 120 GB SATA SSD and a USB adapter in a drawer. Booting the Pi from USB is supported on this model after an EEPROM update, and I checked the version with rpi-eeprom-update. It was recent enough.

The plan is to clone the card to the SSD with rsync, change the cmdline root and boot order, and keep the card as a spare. I wrote the plan down in the repo notes and will do it in the next session.

summary: Moved the Pi root filesystem from the SD card to a USB SSD and booted from it, with Pi-hole back online after about six minutes of downtime.
body:
Today I did the move planned in the morning. The secondary DNS server took over during the downtime, so the clients did not notice anything.

First I attached the SSD and partitioned it with a boot partition of 256 MB and a root partition for the rest. I formatted them and mounted them under /mnt/new.

I stopped FTL and the stats timer to get a consistent copy. Then I ran rsync with the archive, hard links and xattr options, excluding /proc, /sys, /dev, /run and /mnt. The copy was 5.8 GB and took three minutes.

Next I changed the PARTUUID values in /mnt/new/etc/fstab and in cmdline.txt on the new boot partition. I forgot the cmdline first, and the first boot hung with a message that the root device was not found. I booted the card again, fixed the file, and tried once more.

The second boot worked. I confirmed with findmnt that / was on the SSD, and the speed with hdparm was 280 MB/s compared to about 40 MB/s on the card.

The EEPROM boot order already preferred USB after SD, so I set it to try USB first with rpi-eeprom-config. I took the card out afterward and put it in the drawer with a label.

I applied the Ansible role to check for drift, and it changed nothing except the fstab, which the role manages for the data path. I adjusted the template so it does not conflict.

The dashboard in Pi-hole loads faster now. The whole thing took about an hour. I will watch the SSD for a week for USB resets in dmesg.

summary: Replaced the hand-written container update script remnants with a health report that lists image age and pending updates per service, and fixed an outdated Jellyfin tag pin it revealed.
body:
The update playbook updates containers, but I had no overview of how old each image is or which ones are pinned. I wrote a report task that collects this data.

The task runs docker image inspect for each running container on each host and gets the creation date of the image and the tag. It then asks the registry for the newest tag that matches the same major version, using skopeo list-tags. The result is a table with service, current tag, newest tag and age in days.

I put the logic in a small Python script under scripts/image-report.py, since doing the version comparison in Jinja would be unreadable. The script handles tags like 10.9.3, v2024.1 and latest. For latest it only shows the age.

The first report ran against all 31 containers. Most were current. Eight were behind by a patch version, which is expected for the ones I pinned on purpose.

The report found one real problem. Jellyfin was pinned to a tag from nearly a year ago in the compose file of the media VM. I had pinned it after a bad update long ago and never moved it forward. It was 9 minor versions behind, and the release notes listed security fixes.

Before updating, I read the notes between the two versions for breaking changes. There was a database migration in one of them, so I made a backup of the Jellyfin config directory and a Proxmox snapshot of the media VM.

Then I changed the tag and ran the update playbook for that group only. The migration took about four minutes, with the web interface showing a maintenance page. Then it started normally.

I tested playback of a movie with hardware transcoding, and checked that the render device was still mapped, using vainfo inside the container. Both worked, and the library scan found no changes.

The report also found an old Pi-hole container image still around on the Pi, left from before the move to the package install. I removed the container and the image to free 300 MB.

I added the report to the monthly maintenance playbook, with a threshold: pending updates older than 90 days show as a warning, and security pins older than 180 days as an error. The first monthly run will show it.

The remaining question is what to do with pins in general. I added a comment above each pin in the compose files that states the reason and a date to review, so the pins do not get forgotten again.

I committed everything in two commits, one for the report and one for the Jellyfin update. The snapshot of the media VM stays for three days in case of problems.

summary: Planned and began the replacement of the 4 TB NAS disk that reports reallocated sectors, starting with a full backup check and ordering a matching drive.
body:
The weekly SMART summary from the NAS showed disk 3 with 24 reallocated sectors, up from 8 two weeks ago. The other three disks are clean. The pool is a Synology Hybrid RAID with one-disk redundancy, so a failing disk is not an emergency, but a second failure during a rebuild would be.

I first looked at what the numbers mean. The reallocated count is rising slowly and there are no pending sectors yet. The extended test on the disk completed without read errors. That says the drive is degrading but still readable.

Before touching anything, I checked the backups. The restic job to the cloud had succeeded last night, and the local copy on the Proxmox host disk too. I ran a restore of a random folder of 2 GB from the cloud bucket and compared checksums, which matched.

I also looked at which data is only on the NAS. The photo archive and documents are in both backups. The media library is not in the cloud, because it is large and can be recovered, so a double failure would cost me the library. That is a known and accepted risk.

The disks are 4 TB drives from the same batch, bought together about three years ago. I looked up the model and the Synology compatibility list. The same model is still sold, and a newer one of the same size has a similar price.

I decided to buy the same size and a different batch, a drive from the NAS-rated line with a 3-year warranty, and ordered one. It arrives in two days according to the shop.

In the meantime I checked the rebuild time. With 4 TB disks and the pool being 70 percent full, the repair should take about 10 hours. The NAS load during the repair is higher, so I plan it for a night when no one watches media.

I wrote the procedure in the repo notes as a checklist. It covers a fresh backup before the swap, a SMART test of the new drive on another machine through the USB dock, the hot swap in the web interface, and the check that the pool is healthy after the repair.

I also lowered the SMART alert threshold in the Uptime Kuma push check for the NAS. It alerted at 50 reallocated sectors before. Now it alerts when the count rises by more than 10 in a week, which would have warned earlier. I put the new value in the monitor definition in Ansible.

The next step is the swap once the drive arrives. I do not plan to power the disk down before, since the pool works and the risk is in changing too much at once.

summary: Tested the new NAS drive in the USB dock before installing it and found it healthy after a full surface test, with no reallocated sectors.
body:
The drive arrived yesterday evening. Before putting it into the NAS I wanted to be sure it is not defective, since new drives do fail early.

I connected it to the Proxmox host through the USB dock and looked at it with smartctl. The model and capacity were right, and the power-on hours were 3, which is plausible for a factory test. Reallocated and pending counts were 0.

I started a short SMART test, and it passed in two minutes. Then I started the extended test, which the drive estimated at 480 minutes. In parallel I ran badblocks in read-write mode on the whole drive, which writes four patterns and reads them back. It is destructive, and the drive is empty, so that is fine.

The USB dock gave only about 150 MB/s. The badblocks run took 19 hours. I checked the progress now and then, and it showed 0 errors in each of the patterns.

The extended SMART test also finished with no errors. After both tests, the counts were still 0, and the temperature peaked at 41 degrees in the open dock.

I recorded the serial number and the test results in the notes file in the repo, so I have them for the warranty. I also labelled the drive with the date of the test on a sticker, which is a habit from the earlier disk.

The drive is ready for the swap. I plan it for tonight when the nightly backup is done, since the repair puts load on the NAS and I do not want the two to overlap.

One decision I made: I will not shut the NAS down. The bays are hot swap, and the web interface supports the deactivation of the failing disk first. That keeps the services up during the swap.

I also checked the UPS state, which showed full charge and 52 minutes of runtime, so a power cut during the repair would be covered. The clean shutdown chain was tested earlier.

I prepared the commands for monitoring the repair over SSH, mainly cat /proc/mdstat, to see the progress without the web interface. The speed can be limited with the sysctl for the md sync speed, and I will leave it at the default for now.

Tonight's swap is the next entry for this topic.

summary: Swapped the failing NAS disk for the tested one and started the pool repair, which was at 12 percent after the first hour.
body:
After the nightly backup finished at half past seven, I started the swap. First I checked that the pool was healthy except for disk 3 and that the last backup was complete.

In the Storage Manager I chose the failing disk and deactivated it. The NAS gave a warning that the pool would run without redundancy, and I confirmed it. The disk bay light went off after a few seconds.

I pulled the drive out and put the new one in the same bay. The system detected it within 10 seconds and listed it as not initialized. The pool showed as degraded, as expected.

In the repair wizard I selected the new drive. The wizard warned that all data on it will be deleted, which is fine. It started the repair at once.

Over SSH, /proc/mdstat showed the resync with an estimated finish of 9 hours 40 minutes and a speed of about 110 MB/s. After the first hour it was at 12 percent. The load average rose to about 3, and the web interface was still responsive.

I watched the Jellyfin library, and it kept working, with slower thumbnails. The Samba shares worked as well. I paused the monthly maintenance timer for tonight so it does not add load or false alerts about the degraded pool.

The Uptime Kuma NAS push check reported a warning for the degraded state, which is the intended behaviour of the check. I let it alert, and will see it clear when the repair is done.

The failing drive is on my desk. I will wipe it with a single pass of zeros before throwing it away, since it holds personal data, and I will do that tomorrow in the dock.

The next entry is the check after the repair.

summary: The NAS repair finished with a healthy pool, and I wiped the old drive, re-enabled the paused timer and confirmed the SMART alert threshold works on the new disk.
body:
The repair finished after 9 hours 22 minutes, a bit earlier than the estimate. The pool status changed to healthy, and the Uptime Kuma check cleared by itself at the next push.

I ran a data scrub on the pool afterward to check consistency, since the repair rebuilds parity from the other disks. The scrub took about 6 hours and reported no errors. I started it at noon and it ended in the evening.

The SMART values of the new drive after the repair showed 0 reallocated and 0 pending sectors. The temperature in the NAS was 36 degrees, which is the same as the other disks.

I re-enabled the monthly maintenance timer that I paused on the evening of the swap. I ran the playbook once by hand to see that it works with the new disk, and the SMART section listed all four disks as passed.

Then I wiped the old drive in the USB dock. I used dd with zeros over the whole disk. It took about 7 hours at the dock speed, and it ended with no write errors, interesting since the drive had reallocated sectors, but those were handled by the firmware.

I also tested the changed alert threshold on purpose. I cannot create reallocated sectors, so I ran the check script with a fake previous value in its state file. The jump of 12 produced the warning, and the normal case produced no alert. I restored the state file after the test.

The old drive is still within warranty according to its serial number. I looked at the manufacturer page, and a return with a SMART report is possible. I decided to send it in after the wipe, as the replacement might serve as a spare, since the pool has no hot spare.

I documented the whole operation in the repo notes, with the times, so the next swap is quicker. The note includes the mdstat output and the commands for the scrub.

The decision on the spare: when the replacement arrives, I keep it in the drawer, labelled, and tested in the dock before storing it. That closes the topic of the failing disk.

summary: Filed the warranty return for the old NAS drive with the SMART report and noted the shipping details in the repo notes.
body:
I filled in the return form on the manufacturer's page for the drive that was replaced. It asks for the serial number, the model and a description of the failure.

I described it as a growing number of reallocated sectors, 24 at the time of removal, with the extended test completed. I attached the smartctl output I had saved before the swap.

The form gave me a return number and an address in the same country. Shipping to them is paid by the sender. The drive was already wiped, which the process allows, and I put it in an anti-static bag in a box.

The estimated time for the replacement is two to three weeks according to the page. I wrote the return number, the date of sending in relative terms and the expected arrival in the notes file.

I also added a reminder as an Uptime Kuma push monitor with a long interval, which alerts if I have not marked the return as received within five weeks. It is a bit unusual use of the tool, but I want one place for alerts.

The drive goes to the post office tomorrow morning. Nothing else is open.

summary: The morning Ansible update run failed on the Home Assistant host with a full /var/lib/docker, and I pruned old image layers and set a weekly prune in the playbook.
body:
The update playbook reported a failure when pulling the new Home Assistant image: no space left on device. The host is a small VM with a 16 GB root disk.

I logged in and ran df, which showed the root at 100 percent. docker system df listed 9.1 GB of images, most of them reclaimable. These were old layers from earlier updates, since the update playbook pulled new images but never removed the old ones.

I ran docker image prune with the all option and a filter for images older than 7 days. It freed 7.4 GB. The root was at 46 percent afterward.

The pull was repeated and worked. The health check passed after the slow start, which I loosened some weeks ago, and Home Assistant stayed on the new version.

The real fix is in the playbook. I added a task at the end of the update run that prunes unused images older than a week on each host. I made it a separate tag so I can skip it, and I added a check that logs the free disk space before and after.

I also looked at the other hosts for the same risk. The media VM has a 64 GB disk with 40 percent used, and the proxy VM had 71 percent used of a small 8 GB disk, which is a bit tight. The prune task will help there too.

As a last step I added a disk usage check to the monthly maintenance playbook that warns above 80 percent for each guest, so this shows up before an update fails.

I ran the playbook in check mode and then for real on all hosts. The proxy VM went from 71 to 52 percent.

summary: Investigated random Wi-Fi drops of the Raspberry Pi sensor node near the garage and traced them to a power supply that sags under load, then replaced it and logged the voltage.
body:
Home Assistant showed the temperature sensor Pi in the garage as unavailable several times a day, each time for a few minutes. I looked at the logs on both sides to find a pattern.

On the Pi, journalctl showed the Wi-Fi interface losing its connection and reconnecting, with the line brcmfmac: brcmf_cfg80211_connect failed in some cases. There were also kernel messages about under-voltage detected, which I almost missed in the noise.

The vcgencmd get_throttled command returned 0x50005, which means under-voltage now and in the past, and throttling. That points to the power supply, not the access point.

I checked the access point signal first to be sure. The signal at the Pi was minus 71 dBm, which is weak but usable. The drops did not correlate with other devices in the garage.

The Pi was powered by a phone charger with a long thin cable, about 3 meters, because the socket is far from the shelf. The sensor reads a USB camera in addition, which raised the current draw to about 1 A at times.

I had a proper 5.1 V 3 A supply for the Pi model and a short cable in the drawer, and I used an extension on the mains side instead of the DC side. I replaced the charger and the cable and moved the plug.

After the change, get_throttled returned 0x0, and it stayed 0 over several hours of load, with the camera on. I wrote a small script that logs the throttle value every minute into the journal, to see if it comes back.

The Wi-Fi drops did not stop completely. I saw one in the afternoon, but there was no under-voltage message at that time. I looked at the Wi-Fi power saving mode, which on this Pi is on by default and is known to cause drops. I set power_save off with iw and made it permanent with a small systemd unit.

Since then there were no disconnects over about six hours, which is a short time but is longer than the interval before.

I added the Pi to the Ansible inventory properly. It was not managed by it, since I had set it up by hand long ago. The new role contains the Wi-Fi power save unit, the throttle logger and the Home Assistant sensor script.

I also created an Uptime Kuma monitor that pings the Pi, with a 5 minute interval, so that a drop is counted and I can compare the days. Before the change, I estimate 6 drops a day from the Home Assistant history.

If it happens again, the next suspects are the Wi-Fi channel and the antenna position. I will watch the history for two or three days before changing something else.

summary: The garage Pi stayed connected for two days after the power fix, so I closed the topic and used the monitor data to check the Wi-Fi signal margin.
body:
The garage Pi had no drops in the past two days according to the Uptime Kuma monitor. The uptime of that monitor was 100 percent, compared with about 97 percent before the change.

The throttle log showed 0x0 every minute. There were no under-voltage lines in the journal. The power supply was the main cause, and the power save setting probably added to the problem.

The Wi-Fi signal margin was still on my mind. At minus 71 dBm the link works, but a change in the garage, like parked car metal, could break it. I checked the signal history with a small iw loop that I ran for a day and wrote into a file.

The values were between minus 68 and minus 76 dBm, with the lower values in the late evening. The noise floor was around minus 95, so the margin is about 20 dB at worst. The link rate stayed at 54 Mbit/s or more, which is far more than a temperature sensor needs.

I considered a second access point or a powerline adapter and decided against it. The sensor data is tiny, and the margin is fine. I noted the numbers in the repo so I can compare later.

One leftover from the investigation was the USB camera. It is not used by anything in Home Assistant now. It was a test from last year, and it consumed power and USB bandwidth. I removed it from the role and unplugged it.

I also added the Wi-Fi signal to Home Assistant as a diagnostic sensor, read from the Pi with the same small script that reports the temperature. The values appear in the history so I do not need the loop again.

The Ansible role for the Pi ran clean on the second run, with no changes.

I am marking this closed. If drops reappear, the first step is to read the throttle log and the signal sensor.

summary: Reviewed the WireGuard peer list, removed three unused peers and rotated the keys of the two phones, with the config managed from one vars file.
body:
I had not looked at the peers of the WireGuard server for a long time, and the monthly playbook does not cover them. I listed them with wg show and compared the last handshake time of each.

There were nine peers. Three of them had no handshake for more than 200 days. One was an old laptop that I had sold, one was a test phone, and one I could not identify by its name, which was just peer7.

For the unknown one, I looked in the git history of the config. The key was added in a commit with the message hotel test, which was the second listener work. It was a temporary key for a test client and had never been removed.

I removed all three from the vars file, where the peers are defined as a list with name, key and address. The template generates the server config from it. I applied the role and the peers were gone from wg show.

The second part was the key rotation for the two phones, since their keys are over two years old. The server config does not hold private keys, so I generated new pairs on a trusted machine with wg genkey. I made QR codes for the phones from the client configs with qrencode, scanned them, and deleted the files afterward.

I updated the public keys in the vars file and applied the role. The phones connected again within a minute, with the new handshake times in wg show. I tested access to the NAS and Home Assistant through the tunnel from mobile data.

I also checked that the 443 listener still works for the hotel case. A connection test from a phone with the port forced showed a handshake as well.

The unused address space is now free and I wrote a comment in the vars file on which addresses are taken. I added a check to the monthly playbook that lists peers with a last handshake older than 120 days as a warning, so stale peers show up.

The vault holds the peer private keys only for the server itself. I verified that nothing with client private keys is in the repo by grepping for the PrivateKey string and found only the server one in the vault.

All done for now. The next review of the peers will come with the monthly run.

summary: Checked the new monthly peer warning and the image report in the first full monthly run, and fixed a false alert for the WireGuard laptop that is only used on trips.
body:
I ran the monthly maintenance playbook by hand to see the new checks from this week together. The output was long, but most sections passed.

The image report listed 6 containers with pending patch updates, all within the 90 days limit. The disk usage check passed on all guests, with the proxy VM at 54 percent. The Pi throttle check was clean.

The WireGuard peer check raised a warning for the work laptop. Its last handshake was 140 days ago, which is above the 120 day threshold. The laptop is real and still in use, but I only use it on trips, so the warning is a false alert in practice.

I added an optional field to the peer definition named stale_ok with a number of days. For this laptop I set 300. The check reads the field and uses it instead of the default. Peers without the field keep 120.

I ran the check again and it passed. I also tested it with a fake peer that had a low stale_ok and an old handshake, which produced the warning, and then removed the fake peer.

The summary at the end of the run now shows a single line of counts for warnings and errors. It was 0 errors and 0 warnings after the fix.

The run took 4 minutes 10 seconds in total. I committed the change with the explanation of the field in the README of the role.

Nothing else is pending from this week.

summary: Replaced the nightly cron mail with an Uptime Kuma push monitor for the restic jobs, so a silent backup failure now raises an alert within an hour.
body:
The nightly restic jobs only reported by mail, and I noticed the mail had been going to a folder I never read. I wanted a signal that does not depend on someone reading it. The new design is a push monitor in Uptime Kuma for each of the two repositories, the NAS and the cloud bucket.

The backup wrapper script now calls the push URL with status up only after restic exits with code 0 and the snapshot count has grown. On any other exit code it calls the URL with status down and includes the last line of the restic error in the message. The push URLs live in the Ansible vault and are templated into the script, so nothing secret is in the repo in plain text.

I set the heartbeat interval to 26 hours with two retries. That is long enough to survive a slow night, and short enough to notice a missed run the same day. The cloud job usually ends at about 03:40, so the margin is fine.

To test it I ran the NAS job with a wrong repository password. The monitor went down within a minute and the notification reached my phone through the existing channel. Then I fixed the password and the next run turned it green again.

I also tested the case where the script never runs. I disabled the timer on the Proxmox host and let the heartbeat expire in a shortened test setting of one hour. The alert came after the grace period as expected, and I restored the real value afterwards.

One thing I found is that the wrapper treated restic exit code 3, which means some files could not be read, as a failure. For the Jellyfin cache folder that happens now and then when a file vanishes during the run. I made code 3 count as up with a warning text instead, because the snapshot is still created.

The old mail stays as a second path for now. Open: write the same push monitor for the monthly restore sample check, which still reports only to the log.

summary: Added the monthly restore sample check to Uptime Kuma as a push monitor with a 35-day heartbeat, so a skipped monthly run becomes visible.
body:
Following the backup monitors from a few days ago, I gave the monthly restore sample check its own push monitor. The heartbeat is 35 days, which allows for a month with a late run. The script calls the push URL as up only when all sampled checksums match.

If one file differs, the script now sends down with the file path in the message. I tested this by editing a copy of one restored file before the compare step, and the alert showed the right path.

The URL went into the vault like the others. I ran the playbook in check mode first and then for real, and only the script and the timer environment changed. The next real run is in about three weeks, so the first true proof will come then. I wrote that into the repo notes.

Nothing else changed.

summary: Investigated why the Caddy certificate renewal log showed repeated DNS challenge timeouts and found Unbound was caching the negative answer for the TXT record for too long.
body:
Caddy logged several failed attempts of the DNS challenge for the wildcard certificate before it succeeded on a later try. The certificate was still valid for weeks, so nothing was broken yet, but the retries looked wrong.

I first checked the API token of the DNS provider and it was fine. The TXT record was created each time. The failure message said the record was not found during propagation checks, even though the provider showed it.

Then I queried the record through Pi-hole and through the provider directly. Direct queries returned the record after a few seconds. Through Pi-hole and Unbound the answer stayed NXDOMAIN for about five minutes. Caddy resolves through the local servers, so its check kept hitting the cached negative answer.

The cause was the negative cache TTL that comes from the SOA of the zone, which is 300 seconds. Unbound honored it for the challenge name after the first lookup, which Caddy does before the record exists.

I considered lowering the cache-max-negative-ttl in Unbound globally. That would increase upstream queries for every blocked or missing name, so I did not want it. Instead I used the Caddy option that sets resolvers for the challenge and pointed it at the public resolver of the provider only for this purpose.

I edited the Caddyfile template in the Ansible role, with the resolvers line inside the tls block. After a reload I forced a renewal on the test hostname with the staging CA. It passed on the first attempt in about 40 seconds.

I also lowered the propagation timeout in the config back to the default, because I had raised it earlier as a workaround and that hid the problem.

The real wildcard renews in about three weeks. I added a note to check the Caddy log then. If the staging result holds, this topic is closed.

summary: Wrote an Ansible role for the Raspberry Pi base setup, so the USB SSD root, Unbound and Pi-hole settings can be rebuilt from the repo.
body:
After moving the Pi to the USB SSD, I realized that the Pi was still the one machine with hand-made settings. I started a role called pi_base to change that.

The role covers the packages, the static address, the journald size limit, the weekly fstrim timer for the SSD, and the Unbound config files. Pi-hole itself stays managed by its own installer, but the role writes the setupVars equivalent and the adlist YAML that already exists.

I ran it in check mode against the Pi. The diff showed three differences: a sysctl file I had added by hand during the Wi-Fi investigation, a different journald limit, and an old cron line for a log rotation script that is no longer needed.

I added the sysctl file to the role and removed the cron line. For journald I kept the role value of 200 MB.

Then I ran it for real. Unbound restarted once and Pi-hole answered all queries during the restart, because the second server took over in the meantime, as intended.

I also tried a dry rebuild on a spare SD card with a fresh image. The role failed on the first run because the apt cache was empty and a package was missing, so I added an update_cache step. The second run completed.

Still open: the USB boot settings in the EEPROM are not in the role, only in the notes. I will think about whether that is worth automating.

summary: Planned and began moving Home Assistant from a VM to a container on the Docker host, after the VM's disk use and slow boot made upgrades painful.
body:
The Home Assistant VM has been the most awkward guest: it takes four minutes to boot, its disk image is 32 GB for a few hundred megabytes of real data, and upgrades have broken the health check twice. I decided to look at running it as a Docker Compose service next to the others.

First I listed what the VM needs: the USB Zigbee stick, the mDNS discovery on the local network, the data in the config folder, and the add-ons. I went through the add-ons one by one. Only three are in use: the MQTT broker, the file editor and a backup helper. The broker can run as its own Mosquitto container, and the others are not needed.

The Zigbee stick is the main risk. In the VM it is passed through by USB ID. The container host is itself a VM, so I would need the passthrough on that one. I tested this by attaching the stick to the Docker host VM in Proxmox and checked that /dev/serial/by-id showed it.

For discovery I chose host networking for the container, since the integrations use multicast. That works with the current VLAN layout.

Then I wrote the compose file with a pinned image tag, the config volume on the NVMe storage, and a health check that is more patient than the old one, with a 120 second start period. This comes from the rollback lesson of the first update run.

I copied the config folder from a snapshot of the VM to a scratch directory and started the container on a different port. It came up, loaded the integrations, and complained about two things: the add-on based MQTT address and a missing supervisor-only sensor. Both are expected.

I did not switch anything yet. The old VM keeps running and stays the production instance.

Next steps: build the Mosquitto service with the same credentials, move the Zigbee stick during a short window, and compare the entities between old and new. I wrote the plan into the repo notes with a rollback path, which is simply to start the VM again and move the stick back.

summary: Built the Mosquitto container and verified that the Zigbee and sensor devices publish to it, as the second step of the Home Assistant move.
body:
This continues the Home Assistant container plan from earlier today. The first thing it needs is a broker that does not live inside the old VM.

I added a Mosquitto service to the compose stack with a pinned tag, a config file with password authentication and no anonymous access, and persistence on a small volume. The users are templated from the vault: one for Home Assistant, one for the Zigbee bridge, one for the garage sensor node.

I tested it from my laptop with mosquitto_pub and mosquitto_sub, with the right password and with a wrong one. The wrong one was rejected, as the log showed.

The garage Pi sensor node publishes to the old broker address. I changed its config through Ansible to the new host name and restarted its service. Its values appeared on the new broker within a few seconds.

The Zigbee bridge was the harder part. It runs on the same stick that would have to move to the new host, so I cannot test it side by side. Instead I looked at its settings file and confirmed which topics it uses, and I wrote down the base topic so the names will stay the same.

One mistake: I first forgot to open the broker port in the host firewall rules from the IoT VLAN, and the sensor node showed connection refused. Adding the rule to the Ansible firewall vars fixed it.

I left the old broker running. For a while both exist, and only the garage node uses the new one.

Next: move the stick and the bridge in a short window, and then switch the container to production.

summary: Moved the Zigbee stick and bridge to the new Docker host and checked that all 23 devices reconnected without re-pairing.
body:
I did the planned window this morning. First I stopped the bridge in the VM and then detached the stick from it in Proxmox.

I attached the stick to the Docker host VM and started the bridge as a container with the same network key and channel from the saved config. The 23 devices reconnected within about ten minutes, as the battery devices only check in occasionally.

Two door sensors needed a manual wake by opening and closing them. After that, all devices showed a recent last-seen time.

The bridge now publishes to the new Mosquitto broker. Home Assistant in the VM still points to the old broker, so for now it shows the devices as unavailable. That is expected and part of the plan.

I took a copy of the bridge database before the move and stored it with the other backups.

Next is switching the production Home Assistant to the container.

summary: Switched Home Assistant production to the container, with the VM stopped but kept for a week as a fallback, and fixed an MQTT address and a lost mobile app login.
body:
I took a fresh backup of the VM instance first, then copied the config folder again to get the latest state, and started the container on the standard port.

I changed the MQTT integration to the new broker address and credentials. All Zigbee entities came back with their old names, so the dashboards and automations kept working.

Two things needed fixing. The mobile app asked for a new login, because the external URL had a different internal address in the app's cache. I logged in once on each phone. The second was the supervisor-only sensor for the VM disk use, which I deleted from the dashboard.

Caddy still pointed to the VM address. I changed the upstream in the Ansible template to the Docker host and reloaded. The public name worked again after that.

I went through the 12 automations and triggered the three most important ones by hand: the heating schedule, the door alert and the power failure notice. All behaved.

The VM is stopped, not deleted. The container uptime and the health check will be watched for the next days. I will remove the VM after a week if nothing breaks.

summary: Added Home Assistant's config folder to the restic backup and wrote a restore test for it, since the VM snapshots no longer cover it.
body:
With Home Assistant running as a container, the backup coverage changed. The VM was covered by the Proxmox backup, but the container's data is on the Docker host's volume. Without a change, it would be in the general restic job only if the path was included.

I checked the include list in the Ansible vars, and the path was not there. I added the config folder and excluded the home-assistant.log file and the database WAL leftovers to save space.

The SQLite database can be inconsistent if copied while it is written. I added a pre-backup step that asks Home Assistant to create its own backup through the API and puts the file into a folder that restic includes. Then I left the live database out of the job.

I ran the job manually. The snapshot included the new folder and was 180 MB larger.

For the restore test, I restored the snapshot's folder to a temp path and started a second container with it on a spare port. It loaded fine and showed the entities. I removed the test container afterwards.

The monthly sample check might pick files from this folder now, which is good.

summary: Home Assistant on the container had its first night with a problem: the recorder database grew by 900 MB, and limiting excluded entities and purge days fixed it.
body:
Uptime Kuma showed the disk space warning for the Docker host volume this evening, which I had not seen since the move. Home Assistant's database had grown from about 600 MB to 1.5 GB in a single night.

I looked at the recorder and found one entity that updated several times per second: a power sensor reading from a smart plug, which had been misconfigured with a polling interval of 0.2 seconds after the integration was re-added. In the VM it was the same, but the purge was not noticed.

I did three things. First, I set the polling interval for the plug to 10 seconds in the integration options. Second, I added the entity to the recorder exclude list for the raw values and kept only the statistics. Third, I set purge_keep_days to 10 instead of the default and ran a purge with repack.

After the repack the database was 520 MB. I watched the growth for an hour and it was about 1 MB per hour, which is normal.

I added the recorder settings to the Ansible template of the configuration, so a rebuild keeps them. I also added a Kuma check on the free space percentage of that volume at 80 percent.

The topic is closed unless the size grows again tomorrow.

summary: Removed the old Home Assistant VM after a week of stable container operation, and reclaimed 32 GB from NVMe storage after taking one last archive of its disk.
body:
The container ran for a week without a restart caused by a fault. Uptime Kuma showed no gaps, the health check never failed, and the database stayed near 550 MB. I felt it was time to clean up.

Before deleting, I wanted a last safety copy. I exported the VM disk as a compressed image to the NAS, which came to 4.1 GB. Then I wrote a note in the repo with the file name and the reason: it is the only complete copy of the old add-on state.

I checked a few things I might have missed. The VM had a cron job inside for the mobile app geofence sync, which I had not listed. I read its script and found that it is no longer used since the app does it natively. So nothing needed to move.

I also checked the DHCP reservation for the VM. It was still in the router list and the Pi-hole static DNS file. I removed both entries through the Ansible vars, and ran the playbook for the Pi.

Then I removed the VM definition from the Proxmox VM playbook vars, which also had a tag and a backup schedule entry. The playbook run in check mode showed exactly these removals and nothing else.

I destroyed the VM with the purge option. The storage page showed 32 GB freed on the NVMe pool, and the backup job for the Proxmox guests now has one guest less, which cut its time by about eight minutes.

I updated the architecture notes. Home Assistant is now listed as a container on the Docker host, the Zigbee stick passthrough is documented with its USB ID, and the old VM ID is marked as retired.

One remaining question was whether to keep the old MQTT broker address in any config. I searched the repo for the old IP and found two stale mentions, one in a comment and one in a Kuma monitor target for the old VM. I removed both.

The Home Assistant move is complete. The remaining ideas, like a USB passthrough via a network service, are not needed and I dropped them.

summary: Looked into why Jellyfin hardware transcoding stopped working after a kernel update and found the render device permissions had changed inside the container.
body:
A family member reported that a video stuttered on the TV and the Jellyfin dashboard showed the stream was being transcoded by the CPU, with the CPU at 90 percent. Hardware transcoding had worked before.

I checked the playback log and found the error: Failed to open VAAPI device, permission denied on /dev/dri/renderD128. The device was there on the host.

On the host, the group of the render node was render with a numeric ID of 104. After the latest package update, the ID of the render group was 105 on the VM, because a new package had created a group first. The compose file had the group_add with the number 104, which now pointed at a different group.

I confirmed with ls -ln and the container's id output. The fix was to stop using a number and use the group name through a lookup in the Ansible template, which reads the ID with getent on the host and writes it into the compose file.

I ran the playbook, which recreated the Jellyfin container. Then I started a test stream with a forced 1080p to 720p transcode. The dashboard showed the hardware transcode label and the CPU stayed at 12 percent.

I also checked the other containers with a device mapping. Only Jellyfin uses the render node.

I added a small check to the health report that greps for the VAAPI error in the last day of the log, so a repeat shows up early rather than from a complaint.

The issue is solved.

summary: Reviewed the Ansible repository structure after the many recent role additions and merged duplicated variables into group_vars, with no change on the hosts.
body:
The repo grew a lot in the last weeks: new roles for the Pi, the Mosquitto service, the Home Assistant container, and several vars files. I wanted to clean it before it becomes hard to read.

I started with a search for duplicated values. The Docker host address appeared in five places, the NAS address in seven, and the timezone in four. Some of these were comments, but most were real variables with the same value.
