I created a group_vars/all/network.yml for the addresses and a group_vars/docker/main.yml for the shared container settings like timezone, user and group IDs, and the restart policy. Then I replaced the duplicates by references.

After each group of changes I ran the playbooks in check mode with diff. The goal was an empty diff on every host. Twice there was a difference: one template used an old variable name that I had renamed, and one file had a trailing newline difference. I fixed both.

I also renamed three roles to match what they do, for example the role called misc became docker_prune. The playbooks and the README list were adjusted.

The lint run reported 14 warnings before and 3 after. The remaining three are about the use of shell for restic calls, where I do not want to change the behavior now.

Finally I ran the full playbook once for real. It reported zero changed tasks on all four hosts, which is what I wanted to see.

I wrote a short section in the README with the layout and where each kind of variable belongs. No further work is planned on this topic.

summary: Diagnosed a DNS outage in the evening when the first Pi-hole stopped answering, found the USB SSD had disconnected for a few seconds, and added a power setting fix.
body:
Around two in the afternoon, the Uptime Kuma checks for the first Pi-hole went red, while the second one stayed green. Nobody noticed at home, because clients fell over to the second server, which is what it is for. I saw the alert on my phone.

I logged in over SSH, which worked, and Pi-hole's service looked active. But dig against localhost timed out. The FTL log had a line about a database write error, and the kernel log showed the real cause: a USB reset on the SSD, with the message of a disconnect and reconnect of the device, followed by a remount as read-only.

So the root filesystem became read-only after the reset. Unbound and FTL could no longer write their state.

I rebooted the Pi, and it came back normally with a clean filesystem check. The total downtime for the first server was about 25 minutes before I acted.

Then I searched for the cause. The USB to SATA adapter uses UAS, and there are known problems with this mode on some chips. The kernel log at boot showed the adapter using uas. I looked up the chip ID with lsusb and found it is on the list of adapters that behave better with the usb-storage driver and a quirk.

I added the quirk to the kernel command line with the usb-storage.quirks parameter and the flag u, to turn off UAS for this device. This is in the pi_base role now, in the cmdline template.

I also changed the mount options to errors=remount-ro as before, but added a watchdog service, so that if the filesystem becomes read-only, the Pi reboots itself. Without that, a read-only state stays unnoticed for too long.

After the change I ran a disk benchmark with fio. The throughput dropped from 280 to 230 MB/s, which does not matter for Pi-hole.

I also adjusted the Kuma check. The old check only looked at the port, so I changed it to resolve a name and compare the answer, so that a half-dead server is seen as down.

I will watch the kernel log over the next days for more resets. If they come back, the cable and the power of the adapter are next to check. I noted this in the repo.

summary: A week without USB resets on the Pi: the quirk worked, so I closed the SSD topic and wrote the cause and fix into the notes.
body:
I checked the kernel log of the Pi for the days since the UAS quirk. There were no resets, no I/O errors and no read-only events. The uptime is a full week.

I also looked at the watchdog service that I added as a safety net. It has never triggered, and I tested it once on purpose by remounting a spare loop filesystem as read-only. The test showed that the check works and the reboot command is reached.

The Kuma check that resolves a real name had two short red moments of a few seconds. Both were at the time the Unbound cache was restarted by the Ansible run. I raised the retry count to 2 so a restart does not alert.

In the notes, I wrote down the full story: the symptom, the kernel message, the chip ID, the quirk flag and the benchmark result. I also noted that the same adapter model is used in the NAS dock, which only matters if I ever boot from it.

The topic is closed.

summary: Closed the Home Assistant move by checking the container for a month of use, then removing the leftover VM config from Ansible and the old backup job from restic.
body: Four weeks after the switch to the container, I went through what the VM had left behind in the repo. The Ansible inventory still listed the old VM host, and its restic job still ran every night against a machine that no longer existed. I removed the inventory entry, the VM definition and the backup job, then ran the playbook in check mode and saw no changes except the removed items. The Uptime Kuma push monitor for the old job had been paused, so I deleted it to keep the dashboard clean. Home Assistant itself had been stable: no restarts outside the planned updates, and the recorder database stayed near 600 MB after the purge setting. The restore test for its config folder had passed the last three monthly runs. I wrote a short note in the repo about the whole move: the order of the steps, the MQTT address change and the mobile app login that had to be redone. Nothing is left open on this topic, so I marked it closed.

summary: Planned a larger change to give the Docker host a proper staging copy for updates, and built the first part: a clone VM with the same compose files and no access to real data.
body:
Some updates only fail when the real data is there, but several of the recent breaks, like the Home Assistant health check, could have been seen in a copy. I wanted a place where the update playbook runs first.

The idea is a staging VM cloned from the Docker host template, using the same compose files with different variables. It would run the services with test data, on a separate address, with outgoing mail and notifications turned off.

I wrote down the requirements first. It must not touch the real USB stick, the real bucket or the real DNS names. It must start from a clean state with a script, so I do not have to maintain it. And it should use little memory, because the Proxmox host has 32 GB, and 24 are already planned.

Then I created the VM from the template with 4 GB RAM and 40 GB disk on the NVMe pool, using the existing Proxmox playbook with a new entry. It has the tag staging, and no backup schedule.

I added an inventory group called staging. The group_vars for it override the data paths, the host names, the notification settings and the image pull policy. Because I cleaned up the group vars last week, this was only 18 lines.

The first run of the docker role on it worked. The services that started were Caddy with an internal CA, Mosquitto, Home Assistant with an empty config, and Uptime Kuma.

Jellyfin and the backup jobs are not part of staging. Jellyfin needs the media share, and I do not want to mount it. I excluded these by a variable.

A problem came with Caddy: it tried to get real certificates for the staging names, which failed. I set the internal issuer in the staging vars, and then it worked with a local CA.

I also noticed that the Pi-hole static DNS entries do not cover the staging names. I added a few entries for them in the vars.

The next step is to run the full update playbook against staging before production, and to see which differences remain. I wrote this as a plan in the repo notes, along with the memory budget.

summary: Ran the update playbook on the staging VM first and found it pulled a new Mosquitto major version that dropped an old config option, which the real host would have hit.
body:
With the staging VM from yesterday, I ran the container update playbook against it for the first time. Nothing was pinned to a fixed digest, and the playbook pulled the latest allowed tags.

Mosquitto failed to start. The log said unknown configuration variable for an option that I use in the config, a persistence setting that had been renamed in the new release. The real broker is still on the old image, so nothing was broken.

I read the release notes and found that the option name changed and the old name was removed. I changed the template to the new name, which is accepted by the old version too, so the same config works on both.

Then I re-ran staging and the broker started. I connected the garage node's test publisher and saw the message arrive.

I also looked at the image report for other pending major changes. Uptime Kuma and Caddy had only minor updates. Home Assistant had one monthly release, which loaded fine in staging with the empty config.

After that, I ran the playbook on the real host. The Mosquitto update went through and the garage values kept arriving.

I changed the order of the update workflow in the README: staging first, wait for the health checks, then production. A pending item is to automate that order in one playbook, which I will do later.

summary: Wrote one playbook that updates staging, waits for its health checks, and only then updates production, and tested the stop case with a deliberately broken image tag.
body:
The manual order from yesterday is easy to forget, so I made it a single entry point. The playbook update_all.yml now has two plays in a fixed order.

The first play targets the staging group and pulls and recreates the containers. After that, a wait task polls the health endpoints of the staging services with a timeout of five minutes. The checks reuse the same endpoints as Uptime Kuma, with a longer start period for Home Assistant, as learned from the first rollback.

The second play targets production, but only if all hosts in staging passed. I used a play-level condition with a fact set in the first play, and the any_errors_fatal option so that one failed host stops the run before the second play begins.

To test this, I changed the Caddy image tag in the staging vars to a tag that does not exist. The pull failed in the first play and the production play did not start. The output ended with a clear message, and the production services were untouched, which I verified by their container creation times.

Then I tested the second kind of failure, where the image exists but the service is unhealthy. I used a Caddy config with a syntax error, templated only in staging. The container restarted in a loop, and the wait task timed out after five minutes. Again, production was not touched.

After I reset the broken values, I ran the whole playbook for real. Both plays passed, and 3 images were updated in production. The total time was about 11 minutes, of which staging took 7.

I also changed the timer on the Docker host. It now calls update_all.yml from the Proxmox host's controller account, instead of the old playbook. The old one remains in the repo, but the timer does not use it.

One question remains: the monthly run reports to Kuma with its push URL. I added a push call at the end of the second play only, so a stop in staging shows as a missing heartbeat. I think that is correct, since a stopped update needs a look.

Documentation is updated in the README, with the diagram of the order.

summary: The first scheduled run of the staged update stopped in staging because of a Pi-hole image change, and I fixed a DNS entry the new version needed, then confirmed that production followed.
body:
This morning, the Kuma push monitor for the update run showed missing, and the log of the run showed that it had stopped after the first play. That is the intended behavior, and it was the first real case.

The failing service in staging was the Pi-hole container that I added to the staging group a while ago for testing the list sync. It reported unhealthy after the update. The container log said the FTL service could not bind to port 53, because another process had it.

I looked at the staging VM and found that systemd-resolved was listening on the stub address, 127.0.0.53, and the new image tried to bind to all addresses. The old image bound only to the configured interface. So it was a change in the default of the new release.

I had two options. Disable the stub listener on the staging VM, or set the listening mode of Pi-hole explicitly. The production Pi-hole runs natively on the Raspberry Pi, not in a container, so the container exists only for tests. Still, I preferred a setting that is explicit.

I set the environment variable for the interface and the listening mode to the local mode in the compose template, and also disabled the stub listener through the staging vars with a drop-in file for resolved. The container started then and passed its health check.

The update run was started again manually. The staging play passed. The production play updated two images, Caddy and Uptime Kuma, and finished.

Then I checked whether production could have been affected. The Raspberry Pi Pi-hole is not in the update playbook, so it was not. I noted that the staging container should not be taken as proof for the native one.

As a result of this event, I added the expected message to the playbook output when staging fails, with the name of the failing host and service, so I can see the cause in the push message. The Kuma message now says staging failed at pihole on the staging host.

I checked that the heartbeat notification came to my phone, and it was readable.

I also thought about whether the Pi-hole container in staging is worth its upkeep. It cost about 30 minutes today. But it caught a change that would also matter if I ever move Pi-hole to a container. I kept it.

Nothing else is open from this run.

summary: Checked the NAS shares permissions after a family member could not save files into the photo folder, and fixed a group setting that the pool repair had reset.
body:
A family member told me that saving photos into the shared photo folder from the laptop gave a permission denied error. Reading worked.

I looked at the folder's ACL on the NAS over SSH. The group that has write access was listed, but the folder inheritance flag was missing on the top level. New subfolders created by other users did not inherit the group write permission.

I compared with the other shares. They all had the inheritance on. The photo share was the only one that had been changed, and I suspected the time of the pool repair a few weeks ago, when I restored share settings from the exported config after the volume was rebuilt. The export did not include the inheritance flag.

I first tried to fix only the top folder, and it was not enough, as the subfolders created in the meantime had their own ACLs without the group. I used the NAS's recursive permission option on the share, with the group write and inheritance for all subfolders, and kept the owner of each file.

The run took about 12 minutes for 180000 files. After that, the laptop could save into the new subfolders.

I wrote a small check script that lists the shares and prints the inheritance state and the owner group of the top folders. I ran it for all shares, and all were consistent now.

The script is in the repo as scripts/check_nas_acl.sh and runs from the monthly run with the result as a line in the monthly report. If a share differs from the expected list in the vars file, the line is marked and the push monitor shows a warning.

I also saved the share settings export again, and this time I confirmed that it includes the flag by looking at the exported file.

The issue is closed. I told the family member, who confirmed that saving works.

summary: Looked at the cloud bucket costs after the bill rose by a third, and found the cause in old restic snapshots kept by an unchanged retention rule, then tightened the policy.
body:
The monthly bill for the cloud bucket was about a third higher than the month before, so I wanted to find out why before it becomes a habit.

I listed the repository's stats. The raw data size was 1.75 TB, almost the same as after the prune of weeks ago. So the stored size had not grown much. I then looked at the provider's usage page and saw a part I had not expected: the number of API requests and the early deletion fees.

The early deletion fee comes from the bucket's minimum storage duration. When restic prune rewrites packs, it deletes older objects, and objects deleted before the minimum duration are still charged for it. My weekly prune after the Jellyfin changes rewrote many packs.

I checked the prune settings. The playbook runs forget with the keep rules and then prune weekly, with no limit on how much to repack. A single prune had rewritten about 90 GB.

I changed it in two ways. First, prune now runs monthly instead of weekly, and the forget step stays weekly, because forgetting alone does not delete data. Second, I added max-unused 8 percent, so restic tolerates some unused space and does not repack for small gains.

I did a dry run of the prune with the new option. It reported that it would repack only 6 GB and keep about 5 percent unused. This is a clear improvement.

I considered changing the provider's storage class too. The cheaper class has a longer minimum duration, which would make this problem worse, so I left it.

I updated the cloud job vars and ran the playbook. The timers on the Proxmox host showed the new schedule.

I wrote the cost reasoning into the repo notes, with the numbers, so I do not undo the change later without remembering why. The next bill will show whether the fee is gone, and I will compare it then.

summary: Planned a backup of the Docker host's compose directory with a pre-update snapshot step, and wrote the first part: a script that snapshots volumes before each staged update.
body:
The cloud bill work from this morning made me look again at what the restic jobs actually protect, and the staged update playbook came up as a gap. If an update breaks a service in production, the data volumes are only covered by the nightly backup, which can be up to a day old. I wrote down the goal: before production is touched, take a quick snapshot of the volumes that hold state, so a bad update can be rolled back in minutes.

I listed the stateful services first. They are Home Assistant, Mosquitto, Pi-hole, Uptime Kuma, Caddy's data folder and the Jellyfin config, while the media itself lives on the NAS and does not change during updates. The Jellyfin cache and transcode folders are rebuildable, so I left them out. That brought the list down to six paths and about 4.1 GB in total.

I considered LVM snapshots on the Docker host. The VM disk is a plain ext4 volume without LVM, so that was out. A Proxmox snapshot of the whole VM would work but takes the RAM state or needs a pause, and it would also roll back the staging comparison. I settled on a tar copy of the six paths to a local folder on the data disk, taken with the containers of that stack stopped for a few seconds.

I wrote the script as scripts/pre-update-snapshot.sh. It takes a stack name, runs docker compose stop for it, tars the named paths with zstd, then starts the stack again. It writes to /srv/snapshots/<stack>/<timestamp>.tar.zst and keeps only the last three. Mosquitto took under a second and Home Assistant about nine seconds, mostly the recorder database.

I ran it by hand against Pi-hole and Uptime Kuma first. Both stacks came back healthy, and the DNS gap was about four seconds, which the second DNS server covers. I then checked that restoring one archive into a scratch folder gives byte-identical files, using diff -r.

One problem showed up. The first run for Home Assistant failed with a permission error on the Zigbee-related folder owned by a different user. I fixed it by running the tar step with sudo through the existing Ansible become setting, not by changing ownership.

The script is not yet wired into the update playbook. That is the next step, together with a rollback task that restores a chosen archive. I also still need to decide whether the snapshots should be excluded from the restic job, since they duplicate data that is already backed up. For now they sit in a folder that restic does not include.

summary: Wired the pre-update snapshot into the staged update playbook, so production stacks are archived before they are touched, and added a rollback task that was tested on Mosquitto.
body:
Yesterday's snapshot script worked by hand, so this morning I put it into the staged update playbook. The order is now: update staging, wait for its health checks, snapshot each production stack, then update that stack. If a health check fails after the update, the playbook stops and prints the path of the archive it just made.

I used a block with a rescue section per stack. The rescue restores the newest archive and starts the stack again, so a failed update leaves the old state in place. I did not make the rescue automatic for every failure kind. A failure in the snapshot itself aborts the run before anything changes, which seemed the safe choice.

To test it I broke Mosquitto on purpose. I changed the image tag to a version that starts but rejects the existing password file, which is close to what happened with the major version earlier. Staging caught it first as designed, so I added a temporary override to push the change to production anyway. The health check failed after 40 seconds and the rescue restored the archive and the old tag.

The first attempt of the rescue failed. It restored the files but left the new tag in the compose file, so the stack started the broken image again. I made the rescue also reset the compose file from git, using the checkout on the host. After that the second test ended with Mosquitto running the old version and all 23 Zigbee devices still publishing.

The whole run takes about three minutes longer than before, from the stop and tar steps. That is fine for a weekly job. I excluded the snapshot folder from restic after all, because it would only add duplicate data to the cloud bucket right after I tightened the retention. Next I want to run the full playbook once on a normal week and look at the disk use of the three kept archives.

summary: Looked at why the Jellyfin library scan took over an hour and found the scan was walking the NAS share over NFS with attribute caching turned off.
body:
The user noticed new episodes showing up late. I timed a manual library scan: 68 minutes for about 9,000 items.

The mount options in the Docker host's fstab had `noac`, a leftover from a debugging session long ago. With it, every stat call went to the NAS. I changed the options to `ro,nfsvers=4.1,actimeo=60,noatime` and remounted through the Ansible mount task.

The next scan took 11 minutes. I checked that new files still appear: I copied a test video into the share and it was found in the following scan. The media share is read-only for Jellyfin, so the caching cannot cause write trouble.

I left the real-time monitoring switch on and noted the mount option reason in a comment in the group_vars file, so nobody removes it later.

summary: Added a Caddy rule and a small status page so the family can see which services are up without asking, backed by the Uptime Kuma public page.
body:
The user wanted a simple answer for relatives to the question whether Jellyfin is down or just their Wi-Fi. Uptime Kuma already supports status pages, so I created one with four entries: Jellyfin, Home Assistant, Photos and DNS.

Caddy now serves it at status.home on the LAN only, with a reverse proxy to the Kuma port. I kept the admin interface on its own hostname and left it behind the existing basic auth.

I checked that the page shows no IP addresses or internal host names, only the friendly names. One thing I removed was the monitor for the router, since that would only confuse people.

The Pi-hole local DNS entry was added in the Ansible vars, and I tested from a phone on guest Wi-Fi, which correctly could not reach it.

summary: Tested the UPS clean shutdown with a real pull of the mains plug and found the NAS powered off before Proxmox finished, so the shutdown order needed a delay.
body:
I did the test in the evening while the user was home. After the plug was pulled, NUT on the Pi reported on battery and started the sequence after the configured two minutes.

The NAS went down in about 40 seconds, while Proxmox was still stopping the VMs. The VM disks live on local NVMe, so nothing was damaged, but the NFS mounts disappeared under running containers, and the log showed several I/O errors.

I changed the order: the NAS now gets its shutdown command only after the Proxmox host reports done, using a small script on the Pi that waits for the host to stop answering ping. Total time from power loss to everything off is now about 4 minutes, well inside the UPS runtime of 22 minutes at the current load.

I ran the test again and the logs were clean. I put the plug back and verified all services after boot.

summary: Reviewed the failing weekly container update and found one compose file pinned to a tag that the registry had removed, so staging stopped before production as designed.
body:
The staged update playbook stopped at staging this afternoon with `manifest unknown` for the Uptime Kuma image. The tag in the compose file was a specific minor version the maintainers had deleted.

Production was untouched, which confirmed that the gate works. I switched the pin to the current minor version tag, ran staging again, and the health checks passed in about 3 minutes.

I then let the playbook continue on production. All containers came up, and Kuma kept its data since the volume is separate.

To catch this earlier I added a pre-check task that runs `docker manifest inspect` on every image in the compose files and reports missing ones before any pull starts.

summary: Planned and began the move of Pi-hole's gravity and local DNS records into the repo so the second DNS server stays in sync automatically, and built the first sync step.
body:
The second Pi-hole was set up weeks ago by hand, and its local records already drifted from the first. Yesterday the user asked for a lasting fix rather than another manual copy.

Plan in four steps: first, move the local DNS and CNAME records into one vars file; second, template them to both hosts; third, sync adlists and groups; fourth, add a drift check to Uptime Kuma. Not planned: gravity-sync style tools, since I would rather keep one source of truth in git.

Today I did step one. I exported the records from both servers with `pihole-FTL --config dns.hosts` and compared them. The first had 47 entries, the second 41, and 3 entries had different addresses for the same name. Two were stale; one, the printer, was correct only on the second server.

I merged them into `group_vars/dns/records.yml` as 49 entries, after removing 6 for devices that no longer exist, and asked the user about two unknown names. They confirmed both could go.

The template task writes `/etc/pihole/custom.list` and a dnsmasq file for CNAMEs, then restarts DNS only if the file changed. I ran it with `--check --diff` on both hosts and the diffs looked right.

I did not apply it yet. Step two is the real run, scheduled for tomorrow morning when nobody is using the network.

summary: Applied the templated Pi-hole records to both DNS servers and confirmed that every name resolves the same way on each of them.
body:
I ran the playbook on the second Pi-hole first, then on the first. Each restart of the resolver took under 2 seconds, and clients fall back between the two anyway.

To verify, I looped through all 49 names with `dig @server name +short` against each server and diffed the outputs. They were identical. I also tested three CNAMEs through Caddy and they landed on the right hosts.

The printer entry now has the correct address on both. The user's phone had cached the old one, and a reconnect solved it.

Next is syncing adlists and groups.

summary: Synced Pi-hole adlists and group settings between both servers through an Ansible task that edits the gravity database, and checked that gravity updates on both.
body:
Adlists and groups live in gravity.db, so I wrote a task that uses `sqlite3` to insert the lists from a vars file and remove any that are not listed. I made it idempotent by using `INSERT OR IGNORE` and by comparing the address column.

The first server had 9 lists, the second 6. After the run both have 8; I dropped one list that had been dead for months, and one duplicate.

I ran `pihole -g` on both and compared the domain counts: 1,214,630 and 1,214,630. The group assignment for the kids' devices was copied too, and I tested a blocked domain from a tagged device.

One snag: the task needs the FTL service stopped for the write on older versions, but the current version allows it live, so I skipped the stop.

summary: Added a drift check for the two Pi-hole servers as an Uptime Kuma push monitor that fails when records or list counts differ.
body:
The check is a short script run by a systemd timer every 30 minutes on the Pi. It fetches the custom.list checksum and the gravity domain count from both servers over SSH and compares them.

If they match, it calls the Kuma push URL; otherwise it sends a failure status with the message `records differ` or `gravity differs`. The heartbeat interval is 1 hour, so a dead timer also alerts.

To test, I added a temporary entry to only one server. Within one run the monitor went red with the right message. I removed the entry and it went green again.

The script and timer are in the Ansible role for the Pi, and the Kuma token is in the vault.

summary: Investigated slow Home Assistant dashboards in the evening and traced them to the history graphs of a power sensor that wrote a value every second.
body:
The user said the energy dashboard took 10 seconds to open. In the container, the recorder database was 2.3 GB again, though the purge was working.

I queried the states table by entity. One smart plug power sensor produced about 80,000 rows per day, since its integration reports every second. That alone was most of the growth.

I added a throttle with a filter sensor in the config, limited to one update per 30 seconds, and used the filtered version in the dashboard. The raw entity is excluded from the recorder.

After a restart the dashboard opened in about 2 seconds. The old rows will leave with the next purge, and I ran `recorder.purge` with repack once to shrink the file to 1.1 GB.

I documented the pattern in the repo notes for the next chatty sensor.

summary: Wrote a restore runbook for the whole Docker host after realizing that only the data restore was documented and not the order of the rebuild.
body:
The user asked what would happen if the NVMe died tonight. The answer was that the data is safe in restic, but the steps were scattered across notes.

I wrote `docs/rebuild-docker-host.md` with the order: install Debian from the preseed, run the base Ansible role, mount the NAS shares, restore volumes from restic by tag, bring up Caddy, then the others. Each step has the command and the check that proves it worked.

While writing, I found two gaps. The restic password is only in the vault, and the vault key is only on one laptop. I asked the user to put a printed copy of the vault key in the safe, which they agreed to do. The second gap was that Caddy's certificate storage was not in the backup, which would trigger new issuance and could hit rate limits.

I added that folder to the backup paths and ran the backup. Next is a timed dry run of the rebuild on the staging VM to see how long it really takes.

summary: Did the timed rebuild test of the Docker host on a fresh VM from the runbook; it took 74 minutes and exposed four steps that needed fixing in the repo.
body:
I created an empty VM with the same disk size as the host and followed the runbook exactly, using only the repo and the restic repository.

The base role ran in 6 minutes. The first failure was the NFS mount: the role used a hostname that the new VM could not resolve before Pi-hole's search domain was set. I added the search domain to the base role.

The second failure was restic restore with the tag filter, which restored only the newest snapshot of one volume, not all. The fix was `--host` together with `--tag` in the restore script, and a loop over the volume names.

Third, the Jellyfin compose file referenced the render device by a number that differs on the VM; I switched it to a group-based device mapping.

Fourth, Mosquitto's password file was not in the backup, so the devices could not log in. I added it.

After the fixes I ran the restore again from a clean VM. Data restore of 180 GB from the NAS took 31 minutes, and from the cloud bucket I only restored a small sample to save egress. All services were healthy at 74 minutes in total.

I updated the runbook with the real times. The remaining item is a test against the cloud bucket, to be done later in a quiet week.

summary: Fixed the four steps from the timed rebuild test in the repo, removing manual work from the Docker host runbook and cutting the rebuild time estimate.
body:
After the timed rebuild test on the fresh VM, I went through the four steps it had exposed and fixed them in the repo. The first was a missing package, because the docker role assumed the compose plugin was already installed. I added it to the role, and it is now installed from the same repository as the engine.

The second was the order of the restic restore. The runbook said to restore the data before starting the stacks, but the restic password file was only created by a later role. I moved the secrets role before the restore step and noted the dependency in a comment at the top of the playbook.

The third was a hard-coded IP of the old Docker host in the Caddy config. It only mattered on a fresh machine with a different address. I replaced it with a variable from group_vars, and the same variable now feeds the Pi-hole local records.

The fourth was manual: the Zigbee stick needed a udev rule and a passthrough setting in Proxmox before Home Assistant could start. The udev rule is now in the role. The passthrough stays a documented manual step in the runbook, since the Proxmox side is outside this playbook, but I wrote the exact qm set command with the vendor and product ID.

I ran the playbook again against a new clone to verify. It reached a working state without any manual input except the passthrough, and the services passed the Uptime Kuma checks. The run took 58 minutes instead of 74, and most of the remaining time is the restic restore of the media metadata.

I updated the runbook text to match, shortening it from 31 numbered steps to 22. One thing remains open: the Jellyfin config restore is slow because it includes the image cache. I will look at excluding the cache from the backup, but not today.

summary: Excluded the Jellyfin image and transcode caches from restic, which shrank the backup and shortened the rebuild restore by about eight minutes.
body:
The rebuild test had shown that the Jellyfin restore took far longer than the other stacks, so I looked at what the backup contained. The config folder was 11 GB, and about 9 GB of that was the image cache and the transcode temp folder. Both are rebuilt by Jellyfin on its own, so they do not need to be saved.

I added two exclude patterns to the restic job in the Ansible template and checked them with restic backup --dry-run -v. The dry run listed the cache folders as excluded and the rest of the config as included. The next real backup was much smaller, with 1.8 GB total for that stack.

The old snapshots still contain the cache, so a restore from one of them would bring it back. That is harmless but slow, and the retention rule will remove them over the coming weeks. I did not try to rewrite them.

I then repeated the restore sample check for the Jellyfin config on a scratch folder. It took 40 seconds instead of more than eight minutes, and Jellyfin started from that copy with the library and users intact. Posters reloaded on first view, as expected.

The cloud bucket also grows more slowly now, which helps after the cost increase. I noted the exclusion in the runbook so nobody wonders why the cache is missing after a rebuild.

summary: Built the first part of IPv6 prefix change handling, so DNS and firewall entries follow the ISP's rotating prefix instead of breaking after each reconnect.
body:
After the last router reconnect the AAAA records on Pi-hole pointed to a prefix that no longer existed, and some devices with IPv6 first behaved slowly. The ISP hands out a changing /56.

The plan has three parts: detect the new prefix, update the records and firewall, and alert on a change. Today I did the detection and the record update.

Detection runs on the Pi each 5 minutes. It reads the global address of the Pi's interface with `ip -6 addr show scope global`, takes the first 56 bits and compares with the last stored value in `/var/lib/prefix/current`.

When it changes, a script rewrites the AAAA records in the Pi-hole vars from a template that uses only the host suffix and the prefix. I decided against writing it live on the Pi-hole itself, because I want the change to stay visible in git.

So the script commits to a branch-less local clone, runs the DNS role with the new prefix and pushes. I tested by faking a prefix change in the state file. The records were rewritten for 11 hosts, both Pi-hole servers reloaded, and `dig AAAA` returned the new values.

Some hosts use SLAAC with privacy addresses, and those are not in DNS by design. Static suffixes only apply to servers.

What is not done: the firewall rules on the Proxmox host still contain the old prefix in two rules, and the Caddy listener for IPv6 is untouched. That is the next session.

One risk I noted: if the Pi itself loses its address, the script must not write empty records, so it exits when no global address is found.

summary: Finished the IPv6 prefix handling by making the Proxmox firewall rules use an IP set that the prefix script updates, and tested a faked change.
body:
The two firewall rules with the hard-coded prefix were replaced by a named IP set called `lan6`. The prefix script now rewrites the set through `pvesh` after updating DNS.

Caddy listens on all addresses, so it needed no change, but its certificates are by name and stay valid.

I faked a change again and watched: DNS, the IP set and a test connection from a phone over IPv6 all followed within one cycle. The state file is also reported to Kuma as a push message so a prefix change shows up in the log.

I wrote the whole flow into the notes and closed the topic.

summary: Looked at the cloud bucket size after the Jellyfin cache exclusion and confirmed it stopped growing, with the retention rule now pruning old snapshots as planned.
body:
A week after the cache exclusion and the tighter retention rule, I checked the bucket size to see whether the changes had the intended effect. The restic stats command showed 412 GB of raw data, down from 530 GB before the retention change. The daily growth over the last seven days was about 300 MB, mostly Home Assistant and photo uploads.

I also ran restic forget with the policy in dry-run mode on the cloud repository. It listed 14 snapshots as removable, all from before the cache was excluded. The scheduled prune had not yet run on them because it runs only weekly.

I let the next prune happen on its own and did not start it by hand. The estimate from the bucket billing page for this month is lower than last month by about a quarter, which matches the numbers. I wrote the figures into the notes file so the next cost check has a baseline, and I will look again after the prune has finished.

summary: Upgraded Proxmox to the new minor release on the host after a snapshot and a check of all VMs, with one container needing a changed mount option afterwards.
body:
I started in the evening with a backup of /etc/pve and a vzdump of the two VMs and the Pi-hole container. Before the upgrade I read the release notes for anything on the kernel or ZFS, and nothing applied.

The update ran `apt dist-upgrade` and took 9 minutes, then a reboot. The host was back in about two minutes and the VMs started in the configured order.

The Docker host and staging came up fine. The Unbound LXC container did not start. The log said it failed on a bind mount with `idmap` errors; a changed default for unprivileged mount handling was the cause.

I added the explicit `mp0` option with `ro=1` and the right uid mapping in the container config and started it. DNS was out for about 4 minutes, and the second Pi-hole carried it, which is exactly what it is for.

I ran the Ansible check for all hosts afterwards and there was no drift. The container config is now in the repo templates so the fix survives a rebuild.

summary: Planned and built a monthly check that compares the Ansible inventory with what is actually running on Proxmox, to catch forgotten VMs and containers.
body:
The user found an old test VM that still used 8 GB of RAM and was not in any file. That made me want a recurring check instead of a one-time cleanup.

The idea is simple: list all guests with `pvesh get /cluster/resources --type vm --output-format json`, list the guests expected in `inventory/guests.yml`, and report the difference in both directions.

I wrote the script in Python without extra packages, since it runs on the Pi. It prints three groups: unknown running, expected but missing, and stopped for more than 30 days.

The first run found four items. One was the forgotten test VM, one a template that should be marked in the inventory, one an LXC for an experiment from months ago, and one expected guest that had been renamed.

With the user's agreement I deleted the test VM after a last vzdump to the NAS, and the LXC the same way. The template and the rename were fixed in the inventory.

Now the script runs from a monthly timer after the other monthly checks and pushes to a Kuma monitor with a 35-day heartbeat. If the result is not empty, the push is a warning with the list in the message.

I tested the warning path by temporarily adding a fake entry. The message arrived on the phone with the right name.

The reclaimed memory is now free for the staging VM, which was a bit tight at times.

summary: Answered the user's question whether a second Jellyfin transcode stream would still fit the Docker host, by measuring CPU and GPU load with two and three streams.
body:
The user planned a movie night with several people. I started a transcoded stream on the laptop, then on two phones, and measured with `intel_gpu_top` and `docker stats`.

With one 4K to 1080p stream the GPU engine was at 18 percent and CPU about 6 percent. With two it was 35 and 11. With three streams the GPU reached 58 percent and nothing stuttered.

The constraint is the NAS network link at 1 Gbit, which only carried about 80 Mbit for three streams, so there is lots of space.

I told the user that four or five streams are fine. Tone mapping for HDR doubled the GPU load, so that is the actual limit, probably around three HDR streams.

No configuration changes were needed, so I only wrote the numbers into the notes.

summary: Tested restoring from the cloud bucket on a fresh VM instead of the NAS, to prove the backup works if the NAS and the house are both gone, and it worked in 2 hours.
body:
Until now every restore test used the NAS repository. If the NAS was lost, the cloud copy would be the only copy, and it had never been tried end to end.

I created a clean VM and installed only restic, with the bucket credentials and the password from the vault. The first command was `restic snapshots`, which listed everything correctly.

I restored the Home Assistant config, the Caddy folder, the Mosquitto files and the Pi-hole export, which together are about 6 GB. That took 9 minutes and cost 6 GB of egress, so a negligible amount.

Then I restored the Jellyfin metadata at 40 GB to measure the speed: 24 MB/s on average, so the full 180 GB of the Docker volumes would take about 2 hours, as in the title. The media files are not in the cloud copy by choice.

I verified contents with a checksum comparison for 200 random files against the live system, with zero mismatches.

In this test I found that the restore script assumed the NAS path as the default. I changed it to accept a `--repo` argument and documented the cloud command in the runbook.

I then deleted the VM and the downloaded data.

The cloud restore is now proven, and I added the date of the test, as relative time, to the notes as something to repeat in a year.

summary: Planned and started replacing the aging Raspberry Pi SD-based sensor node with a small Ansible-managed image, doing the base role and a read-only root first.
body:
One sensor node in the garage still ran from an SD card, and cards of this kind fail over time. The user asked for a setup that survives power cuts without corruption.

The plan has four steps: apply the Pi base role, make the root file system read-only with a writable tmpfs for logs, move the sensor script to a systemd service, and add a Kuma heartbeat. Today I did the first two.

I flashed a fresh Raspberry Pi OS Lite image to a new card, enabled SSH with a key, and ran the base role from the repo. It installed packages, set the timezone and hostname, and configured NTP in 3 minutes.

An issue came up directly: the role expects the USB SSD root layout from the main Pi. I made that part conditional by a variable `root_on_ssd`, defaulting to true, and set it to false in the host vars for the garage node.

For the read-only root I used the overlay option of `raspi-config nonint enable_overlayfs` and put the boot partition read-only. Data that must persist, such as the sensor buffer, goes to a small separate ext4 partition on the card, mounted with `noatime,commit=60`.

After the reboot I confirmed `findmnt /` showed overlay, and that writing a file in /etc disappeared after another reboot, which is the intended behavior.

One problem is that the overlay also covers the Ansible runs. To change anything I now need to disable it first. I wrote a helper playbook `maintenance.yml` that turns the overlay off, reboots, applies roles and turns it on again.

I tested this cycle once and it took about 4 minutes.

I did not touch the sensor script yet, it still runs from the old card in the garage. The swap is planned after step three.

summary: Moved the garage sensor script into a systemd service on the new read-only node, writing its buffer to the data partition, and tested a power cut.
body:
The script, which reads the temperature sensors and publishes to Mosquitto, was copied into the repo as a role. It runs as a dedicated user with `Restart=always`.

The buffer for values that cannot be sent goes to the data partition with a size cap of 20 MB. I tested by stopping Mosquitto for 10 minutes, then starting it, and the buffered values arrived in order.

Then I pulled the power three times while it was writing. The node booted every time with a clean file system and kept sending data. The data partition had no fsck errors.

The last step is the Kuma heartbeat and the real swap in the garage.

summary: Swapped the new read-only sensor node into the garage, added its heartbeat monitor and confirmed that Home Assistant shows the same sensors with no gap longer than a few minutes.
body:
I took the new card node to the garage, put it in place of the old one with the already replaced power supply, and connected it. It joined the Wi-Fi and the Mosquitto connection within a minute.

Home Assistant showed the temperature and humidity sensors again after about 3 minutes. The entity names were the same since the topic names did not change, so the dashboards and the automations needed no edits.

The Kuma push monitor has a heartbeat of 5 minutes, and the node sends it from a timer. I paused the timer for ten minutes to test the alert, and it arrived as expected.

The old SD card was imaged to the NAS for reference and then wiped. I added the node to the Ansible inventory and to the monthly drift check.

This closes the topic. In a week I want to look at the signal strength graph once more, since the new node sits in the same spot.

summary: Added a weekly restic check that restores a few random files from the NAS repository and compares checksums, after the garage node work reminded me that backups are only proven by restores.
body:
The idea came while finishing the garage node: its data partition is backed up, but nothing proved that single files could come back intact. I wrote scripts/restore-sample.sh, which picks ten random files from the latest snapshot of the NAS repository and restores them into a temporary directory. It then compares their sha256 sums with the live files and prints a short result line.

Files that changed since the snapshot would give false alarms, so the script skips anything modified in the last two days. It also excludes the Home Assistant database and the Jellyfin metadata, which change constantly. The first run picked ten files and eight matched. The other two were log files rotated in between, so I added the log directories to the skip list.

After that the run was clean three times in a row, each taking about 40 seconds. I wrapped it in a systemd timer on the Docker host that runs it early in the morning once a week. The result is sent to Uptime Kuma as a push monitor that goes red if any file differs or the restore command fails. I tested the failure path by pointing the script at a wrong repository password, and the monitor turned red within a minute.

The cloud bucket repository is not covered yet, because every restore from it costs egress. I will add it as a monthly run with only three files. The timer and the script are in the repo under the backup role, and the Ansible run applied them without changes elsewhere.

summary: Made the garage node keep a size-limited journal on its data partition and added a disk-usage push monitor to Uptime Kuma that fails above 80 percent.
body:
Following the list from yesterday, I did both items in the sensor node Ansible role. The journal now goes to a directory on the data partition with SystemMaxUse set to 50M, and a bind mount makes /var/log/journal point there. I first tried setting Storage=persistent directly, but the read-only root made journald fail at boot with a message about not being able to create the directory. The bind mount, ordered after the data partition mount, fixed that.

I rebooted the node twice and confirmed that logs from the earlier boot are visible with journalctl --list-boots.

For the disk alert I wrote a small shell script run by a systemd timer every ten minutes. It reads the use percentage of the data partition and calls the Uptime Kuma push URL with status up, or down when the value is above 80. The push token comes from the Ansible vault and is templated into an environment file.

To test it I filled the partition with a 2 GB file using fallocate, and the monitor turned red in under eleven minutes. After deleting the file it turned green again. The role was committed and applied once more with no changes reported on the second run, so it is idempotent.

The weekly reboot test is still open and I decided to skip it for now, because the power cut test already covered the case.

summary: Answered the user's question about why Uptime Kuma showed Jellyfin as down for six minutes in the night: the weekly update restarted the container and the check interval was too tight.
body:
The user asked why there was a red entry for Jellyfin in the night. I looked at the Uptime Kuma history and found a six minute outage that matched the start of the staged weekly update. Jellyfin was restarted after pulling a new image, and its startup includes a library check that takes a few minutes.

The monitor had a one retry setting with a 60 second interval, so it flagged down quickly. I changed the retries to 6 for that monitor and kept the interval, so only a gap longer than about six minutes alerts. I did not change other monitors.

The real fix would be a health check in the compose file that the update playbook waits for, and that already exists for staging. Jellyfin simply starts slowly. Nothing else was needed.

summary: Planned and began a smart-disk health report for the NAS and Proxmox disks, writing the first script that collects smartctl values into a weekly summary.
body:
Since the disk that showed errors earlier is still in service, the user wanted a regular report rather than checking by hand. I planned it as three parts: collect, compare with last week, and send a summary to the user's mail.

Today I did the collect part. A script in scripts/disk-health.sh runs smartctl -A -H on each disk of the Proxmox host and, over SSH, on the NAS disks. It extracts reallocated sectors, pending sectors, power-on hours and temperature, and writes one JSON line per disk to a file in the repo-managed state directory.

The Synology needed a different path to smartctl, and it returned an error for the USB backup disk because the device type must be given with -d sat. I added a per-disk option for the type in a small vars file.

Test run: seven disks, all passed, and the old disk still shows 8 reallocated sectors, unchanged from last check. The script takes about 20 seconds.

Not done yet: the comparison with last week and the mail. That is the next session. The timer is not enabled yet, so nothing runs on its own.

summary: Found that the disk report mail was marked as spam by the mail provider because of its subject pattern and sender, and fixed it with a clearer subject and a proper sender address.
body:
The user said the weekly disk report had not shown up in the inbox for two weeks. The logs on the Docker host showed the mail left the server fine, with status 250 from the relay each time. So the problem was on the receiving side, and I asked the user to check the spam folder. All the reports were there.

Two things looked suspicious. The sender was root@ followed by the internal hostname, which does not resolve publicly. The subject began with the bare word WARN or OK followed by a long line of disk serial numbers. I changed the msmtp configuration so the sender is a real address of the mail account, and the from-header is set explicitly in the script rather than taken from the system user.

I shortened the subject to the form homelab disk report: all ok, or homelab disk report: 1 warning. The serial numbers moved into the body. A test mail with the new format still landed in spam, though. I then noticed the body was sent as plain text with very long unwrapped lines, and added a fold step at 78 characters.

The second test arrived in the inbox. I marked the earlier mails as not spam, which should help the filter learn. I sent two more test mails, one with the WARN text, and both arrived normally.

The same sender fix applies to the other scripts that mail from the host, such as the update summary and the UPS notice. I changed the shared msmtp file in the Ansible role, so all of them now use the real address. The Ansible run touched only that file on the Docker host and the Pi.

What is left is to watch the next scheduled report and confirm it arrives without help. I also want to check that the UPS mail, which is rare, still gets through, so I will send a manual test of it next time I work on the shutdown script.

summary: Replaced the Docker host's old 1 TB system disk image with a larger virtual disk after the root filesystem reached 91 percent, resizing online and cleaning up old image layers first.
body:
Uptime Kuma's disk monitor warned that the Docker host root filesystem was at 91 percent. I first looked at what was using the space with du and docker system df. Old image layers from the staged updates took 38 GB, because the pre-update snapshots keep the previous images for rollback. Journal logs and old snapshot archives used another 12 GB.

I pruned images older than two weeks, which freed 26 GB. This is not a permanent fix, because the rollback design needs old images to exist for a while. So I also decided to grow the disk instead of fighting it.

On Proxmox I took a snapshot of the VM and checked that the last backup was good. Then I enlarged the virtual disk by 40 GB in the web interface. Inside the VM I ran growpart on the partition and resize2fs on the filesystem, all while the VM was running. The root filesystem showed the new size right away, with no reboot and no container restart.

I checked that all stacks were still healthy in Uptime Kuma and that the Home Assistant recorder had no gaps. The Proxmox snapshot was removed after an hour, since it would otherwise slow the disk down.

I changed the disk size in the Ansible VM definition, so the rebuild from the runbook creates the same size. The rebuild runbook also had a line about the partition layout, and I updated it to say that growpart is expected on first boot.

The prune is now a weekly task in the update playbook. It keeps images used by the latest pre-update snapshot and removes anything older than 14 days. I ran it once by hand and it removed nothing more, which is right.

The disk is at 52 percent now. I added a second Uptime Kuma threshold at 75 percent as an early notice, so growth shows up before it is urgent. The restic backup size did not change, since the images are excluded from it.

summary: Checked that the lock fix held by looking at both backup logs after the evening update test and found no leftover locks on either repository.
body:
Earlier today I changed the update playbook to stop both backup units. This evening I ran another staged update to see the behaviour with the cloud backup active. I started the cloud backup by hand and then launched the playbook.

The playbook printed that it was waiting for restic and continued after the backup ended, about six minutes later. Afterwards restic list locks showed nothing on the cloud bucket and nothing on the NAS repository.

Both timers were enabled again at the end. I also checked the failure path by making a staging task fail on purpose, and the always block started the units again. Everything behaved as designed, so I left it as is.

summary: Began moving Home Assistant's automations and dashboards under version control, and wrote the export step plus a check that detects UI edits that the repo does not know about.
body:
The user pointed out that Home Assistant is the one service whose configuration lives mostly in the web UI and so is covered only by the backup. I planned to bring the YAML-capable parts into the repo and to detect the rest.

I looked at the config directory on the Docker host. Automations are stored in automations.yaml, scenes in scenes.yaml and scripts in scripts.yaml, all plain YAML. Dashboards are in .storage/lovelace as JSON. Integrations are in .storage/core.config_entries and contain secrets, so I decided they stay out of the repo.

I created a directory homeassistant/ in the repo with the three YAML files and the dashboard JSON, copied from the host. A secrets check with grep found one API key in a script, which I moved to secrets.yaml with a !secret reference. secrets.yaml itself is in the Ansible vault.

Then I wrote scripts/ha-pull.sh. It copies the files from the host with rsync into a temporary directory and runs git diff --no-index against the repo copy. If there are differences it prints them and exits with 1. The first run reported one difference: an automation for the porch light that the user had changed in the UI two weeks ago.

I committed that change as the new truth, with a message saying it came from the UI.

The Ansible role now has a task that copies these files to the host, but I set it to run only with a tag, so a normal playbook run does not overwrite UI edits. That is deliberate while the habit of editing in the repo has not yet formed.

What is left: a push monitor that runs the pull script weekly, and a test that Home Assistant accepts a deployed change using its config check command. Both are for the next session.

summary: Finished the Home Assistant repo export: UI edits now get committed through a reviewed diff, and the drift check passes after two days with no unknown changes.
body:
This was the last step of the move of Home Assistant's automations and dashboards under version control, which began a few weeks ago with the export script. Tonight I closed the remaining gap, which was how changes made in the UI get back into the repo without anyone running the export by hand.

The export step now runs as a small Ansible task on the Docker host. It copies automations.yaml, scripts.yaml, scenes.yaml and the dashboard files from the Home Assistant config volume into a working directory of the repo. It leaves out secrets.yaml, the .storage files that hold tokens and the history database. The last one is the 3.1 GB file that I measured earlier, and it must never reach git.

The drift check compares the exported files with the committed ones and already failed twice during testing, which is how I know it works. The first failure came from an automation the user had edited on the phone. The second came from key ordering: the UI rewrites the YAML with a different key order after every save. I added a normalization pass with a sorted dump, and the false positives are gone.

When the check finds a difference, it now does three things:
- it writes the diff to a file under the repo's notes folder
- it sends a push to the Uptime Kuma monitor so the check turns red
- it does not commit anything on its own

I chose that last point on purpose. A UI edit can be a mistake, and an automatic commit would hide it. The user looks at the diff, commits it, or reverts it in the UI.

I tested the whole loop with a harmless change. I renamed a dashboard card in the UI and waited for the nightly run. The monitor went red, the diff showed exactly the one line, and after I committed it the next run turned green again. I also did a restore test on the staging VM: a fresh Home Assistant container with only the repo files started with all automations and the same dashboards, and only the integrations that need a login had to be set up again.

What is left is a short note in the runbook for the Docker host rebuild, which says that the Home Assistant config comes from the repo and the history database from restic. I will write it tomorrow. After two days of nightly runs there have been no unknown changes, so I consider the topic finished.

summary: Answered the user's question about how much space the repo-controlled Home Assistant files and the restic snapshots take, and found the history database is the big part, at 3.1 GB.
body:
The user wondered whether the Home Assistant backup was getting large. I checked the config directory on the Docker host with du. The YAML files and the .storage directory together are under 4 MB. The file home-assistant_v2.db is 3.1 GB, which is almost everything.

The database holds the recorder history. After the earlier fix for the power sensor that wrote every second, the growth slowed, but the retention was still the default ten days and many sensors are recorded that nobody graphs.

I looked at restic stats for the Home Assistant path. A snapshot adds about 600 MB of new data per day because the database file changes constantly, which is deduplicated poorly.

I proposed two options to the user: exclude the database from restic and accept losing history on a restore, or stop it from being backed up and keep a nightly sqlite dump of only the statistics tables. The user chose the first. I added the exclusion to the restic exclude file and noted in the runbook that history starts empty after a restore.

The next backup was 380 MB smaller on the cloud side. I did not shorten the recorder retention.

summary: Replaced the shell loop that pings the family devices for presence with Home Assistant's own router integration after the script began to give false away states.
body:
The user reported that the presence automation set the house to away while people were home. I looked at the old setup: a shell script on the Raspberry Pi pings the phones every minute and posts to Home Assistant through a webhook. Phones in power saving mode ignore pings for several minutes, so they appear away.

I checked the logs and found 14 false away events in the last week, most of them in the evening, when phones sleep.

I added the router's integration in Home Assistant using the router's device list by MAC address, which does not depend on pings. Device state there changes after a configurable timeout, and I set 3 minutes for home to not_home.

To avoid flapping, I changed the presence automation to require not_home for 10 minutes before acting. I removed the ping script and its timer from the Pi role in Ansible and ran the playbook against the Pi to delete them.

The config change went through the repo and the config check from before, which passed. After applying, I watched the states for an hour in the evening with two phones asleep on a table, and neither flipped.

I will check the event count again in a week.

summary: Checked the presence automation a day later and found no false away events overnight, then recorded the thresholds in the repo notes.
body:
This evening I looked at the Home Assistant logbook for the presence entities. Over the night and the morning there were zero away events while all phones stayed in the house, compared with about two per day before the change.

One phone did switch to not_home once for four minutes, when the user switched off wifi. The 10 minute delay in the automation kept it from acting, which is what the delay is for.

I wrote the thresholds in the notes file next to the Home Assistant config: 3 minutes in the integration, 10 minutes in the automation. The reasoning is that the first is about device visibility and the second about reacting. I will look at the logbook again after a week.

summary: Reviewed the Caddy certificate renewals after a warning mail about a certificate expiring in 14 days and found the DNS challenge token had lost a permission.
body:
A warning mail from Uptime Kuma said the certificate for one subdomain would expire in 14 days. Caddy normally renews at 30 days, so a renewal had failed.

I read the Caddy log on the Docker host with docker logs and found repeated lines: acme: error presenting token, and a 403 from the DNS provider's API. The DNS challenge uses an API token stored in the Ansible vault.

I logged into the provider's panel and found that the token was restricted to a zone that the user had moved the previous month, so it no longer matched the zone for that name. Other names were in the old zone and renewed fine, which explained why only one failed.

I created a new token with edit rights for both zones, put it in the vault, and ran the Caddy role. After a restart Caddy obtained the certificate in about 20 seconds, and the log showed certificate obtained successfully.

To prevent a repeat, I changed the Uptime Kuma certificate check to warn at 21 days instead of 14, which gives more time. I also noted in the runbook that token scope must be checked whenever a zone is moved.

I revoked the old token in the panel after confirming that all the names renewed with the new one by running caddy reload and checking each in a browser.

summary: Built a staging copy of the Caddy config with a test domain to catch broken reverse proxy rules before production, and used it on the three rules changed so far.
body:
After the certificate problem this morning, the user asked for a safer way to change Caddy rules. I planned a staging Caddy on the staging VM that loads the same Caddyfile with a different domain variable.

The Caddyfile in the repo was written with the real domain in many places. I turned it into a Jinja template with a base_domain variable and a list of services with their upstream and options. The production output was compared with the old file using diff and was identical apart from whitespace, which made me confident about the template.

On staging I set base_domain to a test subdomain, and used the internal CA of Caddy instead of the public one, to avoid rate limits. The upstreams on staging point to the staging stacks, which exist already from the update playbook.

I added a task to the staged update playbook that runs caddy validate on the generated file in both environments. A syntax error in the template was caught right away when I tested with a missing brace.

Then I used it for real. I ran the three rules changed since the status page work: a header for the status page, a redirect for the old Jellyfin path, and a basic auth rule for the Pi-hole admin. All three worked on staging when tested with curl --resolve.

One rule behaved differently. The redirect worked with the internal CA but curl complained about the certificate until I passed -k, which is expected with an internal CA and not a problem.

Finally I applied to production. The Caddy reload took under a second and no monitor went red.

The remaining weakness is that staging upstreams are not identical to production in all cases, so a rule can pass there and still fail in production. I added that note to the README.

summary: Removed the old basic auth password for Pi-hole admin from the Caddy config and moved it to the vault after noticing it was visible in the repo history.
body:
While reviewing yesterday's Caddy template, I saw that the basic auth hash for the Pi-hole admin was written directly into a variable file that is not encrypted. It is a bcrypt hash, not a password, but it still should not be in plain text.

I moved the hash into the vault file and changed the template to read it from there. I then generated a new password and hash with caddy hash-password, so the old hash in the git history is useless. The user got the new password.

After applying the role, I tested with curl and the old password was rejected with 401, the new one worked. The history still contains the old hash, but it no longer matches anything.

summary: Found why the Synology reported the volume as 'degraded' for a day: a disk had a failing cable, not a failing drive, and fixed it by reseating the drive and checking the rebuild.
body:
The NAS sent an alert mail that the storage pool was degraded. I logged in over SSH and ran cat /proc/mdstat, which showed one member of the array missing, so a rebuild was needed.

The obvious suspect was the old disk with the 8 reallocated sectors. But the missing disk was a different one, in bay 3, and smartctl showed it healthy with zero reallocated sectors and a normal power-on count. The kernel log with dmesg had many lines of ata4: hard resetting link followed by the drive being detached.

That pattern points to a connection problem. I told the user, who reseated the drive in its bay. After that the NAS saw the disk again and started a repair. I checked the progress through mdstat: it estimated about 6 hours for the 8 TB drive.

While it was rebuilding, I paused the weekly backup to the NAS to avoid the load by editing the timer with an override, and I noted in the runbook to remove that override. The cloud backup continued, because it reads from the Docker host.

The repair finished in 5 hours 40 minutes. dmesg stayed clean afterwards, with no more link resets. I ran the disk health script by hand and it showed the same numbers as before for all disks.

I removed the timer override and started the NAS backup manually to catch up. It finished in 31 minutes.

The earlier disk health report would not have caught this, since it looks at SMART values and the disk was healthy. I added a line to the weekly report that counts link reset messages in dmesg per device, so this pattern shows up as a warning.

If the resets come back, the bay or the backplane is the next suspect, and the user would have to move the drive to another bay to test.

summary: Added the link reset count to the disk report and tested that it triggers the WARN subject, then looked at whether the old disk should be replaced soon.
body:
I implemented the dmesg check I had noted after the bay 3 problem. The report script now runs dmesg on the NAS and the Proxmox host, counts lines matching 'hard resetting link' per ata device, and stores the count in the JSON line for the disk.

The mapping from ataN to a disk was the awkward part. On the Proxmox host I used /sys/class/ata_port to find the device behind each port. On the Synology the layout is different, and I had to go through the /sys/block entries and match their path to the ata number. It works on both now, and I put the mapping logic in a function with a comment.

To test it, I faked a count by adding two lines to a copy of the dmesg output in a test mode of the script. The compare step then printed a growth line and the mail subject became WARN. With the real data, the count for bay 3 is 41 from the earlier events, and it will not count as growth unless it rises further. Since dmesg resets on reboot, a lower value than last week is treated as a reset of the counter and not an improvement.

Then I turned to the old disk. I compared its numbers over the last weeks: reallocated sectors at 8 for the whole period, pending at 0, temperature normal. It is also 5 years of power-on time. The user asked what I would do. My view was that it is not urgent, as long as the weekly report stays quiet, but a spare drive of the same size should be bought, so a replacement does not wait for a delivery.

I added this as a reminder in the notes with a threshold: replace when reallocated sectors pass 20 or pending sectors are above 0 for two weeks in a row.

The change to the script is committed and the timer is unchanged.

summary: Planned and did the first part of rotating all service secrets in the vault: made an inventory of every secret, where it is used and how to change it.
body:
The user wanted a rotation of the secrets since some are years old. I decided to start with an inventory, because changing things without a list risks forgetting a consumer.

I went through the vault files and the compose files and listed each secret. There are 23 entries: the Pi-hole admin password, the Caddy DNS token, Uptime Kuma push tokens, the restic repository passwords for the NAS and the cloud, the cloud bucket keys, the mail account password, the WireGuard private keys, the Home Assistant API key and a few service database passwords.

For each I recorded in a YAML file: name, consumer, how to change it, whether a restart is needed, and the risk. The risky ones are the restic passwords, since a lost password means the backups cannot be read. For these, rotating means adding a new key with restic key add and only later removing the old one.

The WireGuard keys are risky for another reason: each phone and laptop holds its own key, so rotating needs the user's devices.

I sorted the list into three groups. Group one is easy and safe: the push tokens, the Pi-hole password, the mail password. Group two needs coordination: the cloud bucket keys and the database passwords. Group three is the restic and WireGuard keys.

I also found two secrets that were no longer used: an old API token for a service that was removed last year and a test token for staging. I marked both for deletion.

The inventory is committed without any secret values. Next I will rotate group one and then go through the others, one at a time, with a check after each.

summary: Rotated the easy group of secrets: Pi-hole admin password, mail password and the Uptime Kuma push tokens, and confirmed that every dependent job still runs.
body:
I took group one from the inventory. First the Pi-hole password: I generated a new one, put it in the vault and ran the Pi-hole role on both servers. I confirmed the login on both.

Then the mail account. The user changed the password at the mail provider and I updated the msmtp config on the Proxmox host and the Docker host through the role. I sent a test mail from each and both arrived.

The push tokens were the largest part with 11 monitors. In Uptime Kuma a push token is changed by regenerating it in the monitor. I regenerated each, updated the vault, and applied the roles that contain the timers. After applying, every monitor was down for a short time until its next run, so I triggered each timer by hand with systemctl start and watched all 11 turn green.

One timer, the drift check for the Pi-hole servers, was missed in the first pass because its token was in a different vars file than I expected. The monitor stayed red until I found it with a grep for the old token over the repo and fixed it. After that, grep found no more uses of the old tokens.

I deleted the two unused tokens from the inventory.

summary: Rotated the cloud bucket keys and the database passwords with a check after each step, and found that the Home Assistant recorder still used the old database password until it was restarted.
body:
This was group two from the inventory. I started with the cloud bucket keys. The provider lets me create a second key pair, so I created one, put it in the vault and ran the backup role. I ran a restic backup by hand to the bucket with the new key and it worked, so I deleted the old key pair at the provider afterwards. Doing it in that order meant the backup was never without access.

Next the database passwords. There are three services with their own database containers. For each I did the same: change the password inside the database with ALTER USER, update the vault, apply the role, restart the service container, and look at its log for connection errors.

Two went without problems. The third was Home Assistant's recorder. After applying the role, the Home Assistant log was quiet, and I thought it was done. An hour later the log showed a recorder error: password authentication failed. The recorder had kept the open connection and only failed when the connection was recycled. The role had changed the environment file but did not restart the container, because the handler only triggers on changes of the compose file.

I fixed the role so the handler also triggers on a change to the environment file, then restarted the container. The recorder connected again, and a short gap of about an hour of history was lost. Since the database is not in restic, there was nothing to restore, and it is only graphs.

I checked the other two services for the same issue, and both had restarted correctly, since their compose files had changed in the same commit.

After this, I ran the full staged update playbook, to see that it still passes with the new credentials. Staging and production both passed.

I updated the inventory file with the dates in relative form, meaning the order in which the entries were changed, and marked group two as done. The restic and WireGuard keys remain, and they need more care.

summary: Rotated the restic repository passwords for the NAS and the cloud by adding a new key, testing a restore with it and only then removing the old key, with the new password stored in two places.
body:
Group three, starting with restic. The risk is a lost password making a repository unreadable, so I planned the order: add a new key, test with it, store it safely in two places, and only then remove the old key.

For the NAS repository I ran restic key add with a new generated password. The listing with restic key list showed two keys. I then restored a small directory from the latest snapshot using only the new password, via RESTIC_PASSWORD_FILE pointing to a temporary file, and compared the files with the originals. They were identical.
