The same steps followed for the cloud repository. The key add took a few seconds, but the restore test was slower, 4 minutes for the sample directory, because of the transfer from the bucket.

The new passwords went into the Ansible vault and, because the vault itself is lost in a total disaster, also into the user's password manager. I asked the user to confirm that both entries were in the manager, and they did. This also closes a gap in the restore runbook, which assumed the vault password was available. I added a line about it.

Then I applied the backup role so the timers use the new password file. I started both backups by hand, and the log showed no authentication errors. The NAS backup took 12 minutes and the cloud backup 15.

Only after that did I remove the old keys with restic key remove, and checked that the key list had one entry each. A backup run after the removal was still fine.

I also searched the repo for the old passwords in scripts and found one in a commented example in a README, which I deleted.

Only the WireGuard keys are left. Since each needs a device, I will do them with the user when the phones are around, and I wrote a short procedure for that in the notes.

summary: Rotated the WireGuard keys for the server and two devices with the user at hand, and checked the tunnel from outside the house on mobile data.
body:
The user was home with a phone and a laptop, so we did the last group. I generated a new key pair on the server through the WireGuard role and put the private key in the vault. For each device I created a new pair on the device itself, so no private key traveled, and added the new public key to the server config in place of the old one.

The phone was done first. After applying the role the old peer was gone, and the new handshake showed in wg show within seconds of activating the tunnel with the new config. The laptop took one more try, since I had left the old server public key in its config, and the handshake did not appear until the user pasted the new server key.

The server key change forced all devices to update at once, so there was a short period when the VPN was not usable.

To be sure, the user switched the phone to mobile data and opened Jellyfin and Home Assistant through the tunnel. Both worked. The rotation is now complete for every group in the inventory, and I marked it so in the file.

summary: Planned the replacement of the oldest NAS disk after the link reset counts kept rising, and ordered a matching drive after checking the SMART history of all bays.
body:
The disk report from the weekend showed bay 3 with 41 link resets in a week even after the cable was reseated, so I sat down to decide what to do about it. I pulled the smartctl history from the weekly summaries in the repo and compared the four drives. Bay 3 has the most power-on hours, 43,800, and the reallocated sector count went from 0 to 8 over the last two reports.

The other three drives look fine. Their reallocated count is 0 and their link resets stay below 3 per week. That points at the drive itself and not at the cable this time.

I checked what the volume can take. The NAS runs SHR with one-disk redundancy, so a replacement means a rebuild of roughly 14 hours for the used 7.2 TB. During that time a second failure would lose the volume, which is why the backup state matters first. I looked at the last restic runs for both repositories and the last check, and all were clean, with the cloud snapshot from last night.

I looked at the drive size options. The old drive is 4 TB, and a new 8 TB drive would not add capacity until all drives are bigger, so I chose another 4 TB drive of a different batch, which keeps the cost low. The user agreed to the order after I showed the numbers.

I wrote a short replacement plan in the repo notes. It covers: run a fresh full backup the evening before, take the SMART long test on the other drives, hot swap the drive, watch the rebuild and pause the heavy jobs during it. I also noted that the weekly restic check and the update job need to move out of the rebuild window.

Nothing was changed on the NAS today. Next step is the swap once the drive arrives, expected in a few days.

summary: Wrote a maintenance-mode switch for the Ansible repo that pauses the update, backup check and disk report jobs and their Uptime Kuma monitors, to be used during the NAS rebuild.
body:
The plan for the NAS disk swap needs the heavy jobs to stay out of the way for about a day, and doing that by hand over SSH is easy to forget to undo. So I built a small maintenance switch.

The role `maintenance` writes a flag file, `/etc/homelab/maintenance`, on each host. The update script, the weekly restic restore check and the disk report timer now look at that file at the start and exit with code 0 and a log line saying they were skipped. A skipped run does not count as a failure.

The monitors were the harder part. Uptime Kuma push monitors go red when a job does not report. I added a call to the Kuma API through a small script that pauses a list of monitors by name and resumes them later. The list lives in `group_vars/all/maintenance.yml`, 11 monitors in total. The API token is read from the vault, and I used the new token from the rotation of last month.

I ran it as a test with the flag on the Docker host only. The update timer fired at the test time, wrote its skip line to the journal and did not touch any container. Then I switched it off and the next run went through normally.

One mistake showed up: the first version paused the monitor of the maintenance script itself, so resume could not be reported. I took it out of the list.

I added two playbooks, `maintenance_on.yml` and `maintenance_off.yml`, and a line in the notes. The off playbook also prints which monitors are still paused so none is left behind. It is ready for the swap.

summary: Swapped the failing NAS disk in bay 3 for the new drive after a fresh backup, and started the rebuild, which the Synology estimated at about 15 hours.
body:
The new drive arrived this afternoon. Before touching anything I ran maintenance_on.yml, then started a manual restic backup to the NAS repository and to the cloud bucket. Both finished clean, and I ran restic check on the cloud one with a subset read, which passed.

I looked at SMART on the new drive first, using a USB dock on the desk. It showed 0 hours and no errors, and I started a short self test, which passed. Then I hot swapped bay 3 with the user at the NAS. The Synology noticed the new disk within a few seconds, and I started the repair of the volume from the storage manager.

The estimate is about 15 hours. Over SSH I watched `cat /proc/mdstat` for a while and the speed was around 140 MB/s at the start, so it looks realistic. I reduced nothing else, since all heavy jobs are paused by the maintenance flag.

Services were fine. Jellyfin streamed a test file from the degraded volume without stutter, though the read speed was lower. Home Assistant has nothing on the NAS except the backups, which are paused.

I wrote the exact time of the swap and the old drive serial number in the notes so the old disk can be matched to the warranty. The old drive is labeled and put aside, to be wiped later.

Next check is tomorrow morning when the rebuild should be done. Maintenance stays on until the volume is healthy and a consistency check has run.

summary: Wrote a small script that logs rebuild progress from the NAS every ten minutes, so the rebuild can be reviewed in the morning without staying logged in.
body:
Since the rebuild runs overnight I did not want to rely on checking by hand. I wrote `scripts/nas-rebuild-log.sh`, run from the Pi with a loop in tmux.

Every ten minutes it connects to the NAS over SSH and reads the mdstat line, the temperature of all four drives through smartctl and the count of kernel messages mentioning ata errors. It appends one line to a log file in the repo's ignored folder.

The first lines show 6.1 percent done, drive temperatures between 34 and 39 degrees and no ata errors. The new drive is the warmest at 39 degrees, which is normal during a rebuild.

I added a simple stop condition. If the ata error count rises by more than 5 between two runs, the script sends the disk report mail with a WARN subject. The test of this path used a fake threshold of 0, and the mail arrived with the proper sender and was not marked as spam, so the earlier fix still works.

The tmux session survives my own SSH logout. I checked that by logging out and back in and found the session and its log still growing.

Tomorrow I read the log, then run maintenance_off.yml when the volume shows healthy.

summary: Confirmed the NAS volume is healthy after the rebuild, ran a consistency check, and ended maintenance mode with every monitor green again.
body:
The rebuild had finished in about 14 hours. The log from the loop showed a steady speed, a maximum temperature of 41 degrees, and no ata errors at all. The volume status in the Synology changed from degraded to healthy.

I started the data scrub in the storage manager as a consistency check. It ran for around 6 hours and reported no errors. SMART on the new drive afterward shows 0 reallocated sectors and 0 link resets.

Then I ran maintenance_off.yml. It removed the flag files on all hosts and resumed the 11 Uptime Kuma monitors, and its list of still-paused monitors was empty. All push monitors went green within their intervals, except the weekly check, which will report on its normal schedule.

I ran a normal restic backup to the NAS repository to check that writing to the rebuilt volume works, and it finished in the usual time. The restic check of the NAS repository passed too.

I updated the disk report script, since it had the old drive serial number in a comment, and noted the swap in the repo notes with the date relative to the rebuild. The old drive will be wiped with a full overwrite on the desk dock before it is thrown away.

summary: Looked into why the weekly update left the Home Assistant container on an old image tag, and found the compose file pinned a version that the update script skips.
body:
The user noticed that Home Assistant still showed the old version in its settings, although the update script reported success. I looked at the compose file for it in the repo and found the image was pinned to an explicit version tag, set during an upgrade that broke something a long time ago.

The update script runs `docker compose pull` and then up. With a pinned tag the pull does nothing, so the script was right about its own result and the pin was the cause. I searched all compose files for pins and found three: Home Assistant, Uptime Kuma and Caddy. Caddy's pin was deliberate, because of the custom build with the DNS plugin.

I added a comment above every pin that says why it exists. For Home Assistant I raised the tag by one minor release instead of moving to latest, so there are no big jumps. I read the release notes first and found one breaking change for a router integration, not used here.

Before the change I took a Proxmox snapshot of the Docker host VM and made a copy of the Home Assistant config. After the update the container started, the recorder connected to the database and the dashboards loaded. The drift check from the repo export showed no unknown changes.

I left Uptime Kuma pinned for now because its next release changes the database. I wrote that in the notes as a task for later.

summary: Answered the user's question how long the house can run on the UPS, by reading the logged load and runtime values from the last power test.
body:
The user asked how long the servers would stay up in a power cut before the clean shutdown starts. I looked at the NUT logs from the last test in the repo notes and at the current values from upsc.

The load is currently 62 W, and the UPS reports an estimated runtime of about 21 minutes. The shutdown is configured to start at 40 percent battery or 5 minutes remaining. In the test it began after about 11 minutes.

The order of the shutdown is the VMs first, then Proxmox, then the NAS. The whole sequence took 3 minutes in the test.

One point I told the user: the battery is now older, and the runtime fell from 26 minutes to 21 over the last year. It should still be fine, but the replacement of the battery should be planned around the third year. I put that as a reminder in the notes.

summary: Found that the Pi-hole gravity update on the second DNS server had been failing silently for a week because of a full tmpfs, and fixed the job and its monitoring.
body:
While looking at the DNS query graphs I saw that the second Pi-hole blocked clearly fewer domains than the first. Its gravity database was a week older.

I logged into the second server and ran `pihole -g` by hand. It failed with `No space left on device` while writing to /tmp. The tmpfs there is only 64 MB, and the larger blocklist added a while ago no longer fits during the merge step.

I first considered raising the tmpfs, but the machine has little memory. Instead I pointed the temporary files to the disk with the TMPDIR setting in the gravity cron entry and checked that the run finishes. It took 48 seconds and the domain count matched the first server at 1,014,220 entries.

The cron job had logged the error, but nothing alerted me, since the monitor only checked if the DNS answers. I added a push monitor to Uptime Kuma that the gravity job calls on success, with a limit of 36 hours. I also put the TMPDIR change into the Ansible role so it applies to both servers.

I ran the role on the first server too, to be sure the two stay equal, and nothing changed there except the cron line. I tested the monitor by stopping the job once, and the alert came after the limit as expected.

The lesson for the notes: a check of the answer is not a check of the freshness of the lists.

summary: Built a weekly consistency check between the two Pi-hole servers that compares gravity counts and local DNS records, and reports differences in the disk report mail.
body:
After the gravity problem of this morning I wanted a check that would show any drift between the two DNS servers, not only the failed job. I wrote `scripts/dns-compare.sh` in the repo.

It asks both servers over SSH for three values: the number of domains in gravity, the checksum of the local DNS records file and the checksum of the CNAME file. It prints a line per value with OK or DIFF. The result goes into a small text block.

First I ran it manually. The counts matched, but the local records checksum differed. The reason was an old test record for a VM that I had removed from the first server only. The sync was done by hand in the past and was never part of Ansible.

I moved the records into a template in the repo, `pihole_local_dns.j2`, with the records as a list in group_vars. Both servers now get the same file from the same source. I ran the role, the checksums became equal, and Unbound on both servers kept running.

The weekly timer runs on the Pi, on the same day as the disk report, and adds the block to that mail. If any line says DIFF the subject changes to WARN, using the logic that already exists in the report. I tested that by editing one record on the second server by hand, and the warning mail came with the right subject.

I restored the record afterwards. One open point is the DHCP leases, which are not shared between the servers, and I do not plan to change that.

summary: Started to move the VM and container backups from Proxmox into a separate job with its own retention, since the vzdump jobs had been running too long next to restic.
body:
The backup window had been getting longer again. I looked at the Proxmox task log of the last 10 nights and saw that the vzdump of the VMs took between 52 and 78 minutes, and overlapped with the restic run at the start.

The cause is the overlap on the NAS. Both write to it at the same time, and the NAS is the bottleneck, at around 95 MB/s over its single link. When they overlap, both slow down.

I changed the order. The vzdump job now starts at 01:30 instead of 02:00, and the restic job from the Docker host starts at 03:15. I put both times into the Ansible variables so they are visible in one place, `backup_schedule.yml`.

I also looked at the vzdump retention. It kept 7 daily and 4 weekly copies for every guest, including the test VM that nobody needs and the media container with 400 GB of data. I made a list of guests with their size and the number of copies they really need. The media container only holds files that restic already saves, so I plan to exclude it from vzdump.

I wrote the new job definitions as a draft in the repo but did not apply them. The user wants to read the list of guests and the retention first. I attached the table to the notes.

Next step is applying the schedule change tonight and observing the first run.

summary: Applied the new backup schedule and the reduced vzdump guest list, then checked that the first night finished earlier without overlap.
body:
The user read the guest table and agreed with it, with one change: keep the Home Assistant VM at 14 daily copies, because it is the most painful one to lose.

I applied the change through the playbook for Proxmox. The test VM and the media container are excluded now. Home Assistant has its own retention of 14 daily copies, the other guests keep 7 daily and 4 weekly.

I checked the job definition on the Proxmox host with `cat /etc/pve/jobs.cfg` and compared it with the repo. It matched, so no drift from the web interface.

The first night with the new times finished as follows: vzdump ran from 01:30 to 02:22, 52 minutes, and restic started at 03:15 and ended at 03:51. There was no overlap. Before, the combined run took up to 2 hours 20 minutes.

The NAS space used by the vzdump folder will fall as the old copies of the excluded guests age out. I did not delete them by hand, since the retention will do it, and I noted the expected freed space of 410 GB.

Both push monitors stayed green. I left a note to read the vzdump task log again in a week.

summary: Diagnosed a Home Assistant automation that did not turn off the garage light, which came from the new read-only sensor node reporting door state with an old name.
body:
The user said the garage light stayed on overnight. I looked at the automation in the repo and it triggers when the garage door sensor has been closed for 10 minutes.

In the Home Assistant log I found that the entity `binary_sensor.garage_door` had been unavailable since the afternoon of two days ago. The node still sent its data, and Uptime Kuma had no alert, since the heartbeat monitor only checks that the node is alive.

The cause was in the sensor service. A change in the script made earlier this month renamed the MQTT topic from `garage/door` to `garage/door_state`, but the Home Assistant discovery config still listed the old topic. The drift check watches the UI changes, not the topic names.

I fixed the topic in the discovery file in the repo and restarted the integration. The entity came back and showed the right state within a few seconds. I closed and opened the door to confirm, and the light automation ran.

I also made the automation more robust: if the sensor is unavailable for more than 30 minutes, a notification goes to the phone. That should catch the same problem from a different side.

summary: Added a check to the sensor node's deploy that compares the MQTT topics it publishes with the topics in the Home Assistant discovery files, so a rename cannot break an entity silently again.
body:
Following the garage door problem I wanted a check that stops a rename like that before it reaches the house. I wrote `tests/check_topics.py` in the repo.

It reads the topic names from the sensor service config on the node role and the topic names in the discovery YAML of Home Assistant. It then prints every topic that appears on only one side. A mismatch exits with code 1.

I ran it on the current state and it found no difference, since I had fixed it this morning. To make sure it works, I reverted the fix in a temporary copy, and it reported `garage/door` as missing on the sensor side and `garage/door_state` as unknown on the Home Assistant side.

I hooked it into the git pre-commit hook of the repo. The hook only runs the check when files in those two folders change, so other commits stay fast. It takes under a second.

I also added the check to the playbook for the node as a pre-task, so a deploy stops on a mismatch.

One limit remains: it cannot see topics built from variables. There is only one of them, the temperature topic, and I listed it by hand in an allow list with a comment.

summary: Checked the weekly update run for the Docker host and found that all containers updated cleanly, with the Home Assistant image now one release behind only because of the pin.
body:
I looked at the log of last night's update run. All 17 containers were pulled and restarted, and none logged an error. The restart of Jellyfin was inside the longer check interval, so Uptime Kuma showed no downtime.

Home Assistant stayed on its pinned tag, as intended. A newer minor release exists, so I read its notes again. It changes the way the recorder handles purge, and I want to try it with a snapshot first.

I left the pin as it is. The old image layers took 3.4 GB, so the cleanup step ran and freed it. The root disk is at 58 percent.

summary: Wrote and tested a runbook script for the full rebuild of the Docker host VM from Ansible and restic, and timed a trial run on a spare VM at 47 minutes.
body:
The restore tests so far proved that data comes back, but the setup of the host itself, the services and the compose files, had only been tried in pieces. I wanted one path from an empty VM to a working Docker host and wrote it down as `runbook/docker-host.md` with a helper script, `scripts/rebuild-docker-host.sh`.

The script takes the name of a new VM and does these steps in order: run the base and Docker roles of Ansible, fetch the vault key from the place the notes describe, deploy the compose files, restore the data volumes from the restic repository on the NAS, and start the services in groups. The groups are DNS and Caddy first, then the databases, then everything else.

I created a spare VM on Proxmox with the same disk size and ran it. The first try failed in the restore step, since the restic password file was expected at a path that exists only on the real host. I changed the script to read the password from the vault with a clear error message if missing.

The second try went through. The timeline was 9 minutes for the roles, 21 minutes for the restore of 38 GB, and 17 minutes for the start and the health checks. In total it took 47 minutes.

On the spare VM I checked each service. Caddy served the staging test domain, Pi-hole answered queries, and Home Assistant came up with its history database and the right dashboards. Jellyfin started, but showed an empty library until the NAS media share was mounted, which the script does not do on purpose. I added that as a line in the runbook.

Two issues remain. The Uptime Kuma push tokens on the spare VM were the real ones, so for a minute the test sent heartbeats for the real monitors. I added a flag, `--dry-monitors`, that replaces the tokens with dummy ones for trial runs. The second is that the certificates were requested again for the real names, so a trial should use only the staging domain, which I also made the default.

After the run I deleted the spare VM. The runbook now has the order of the steps, the times and the two traps, and I told the user where it is.

summary: Answered the user's question whether the old NAS drive can be reused, and recommended a full wipe and keeping it only as a cold spare for tests, not in the array.
body:
The user asked if the drive taken out of bay 3 is good for anything. I read its last SMART values: 8 reallocated sectors, growing, and the link resets that led to the swap. That is a drive on its way out.

I said it should not go back into the NAS or hold any backup. It can serve as a test disk on the desk dock, for example for practicing a restore or testing scripts, where losing the data costs nothing.

Before any reuse I advised a full overwrite with `shred` or a secure erase, since it held personal files. The user will do that at the desk.
